chapters.title: Book 1
paragraphs: You are great, O Lord, and greatly to be praised: great is Your power, and Your wisdom has no measure. And man wants to praise You. Man, only a small part of what You have created; man, who carries his mortality around with him, the evidence of his sin and the evidence that You resist the proud: even so, man wants to praise You, this small part of Your creation. You rouse us so that praising You becomes our delight, because You made us for Yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in You. Lord, let me know and understand which should come first, calling on You or praising You? And again, which comes first, knowing You or calling on You? Who can call on You without knowing You? Someone who does not know You might call on You as something other than what You are. Or is it rather that we call on You in order to come to know You? Yet how shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe without a preacher? And they that seek the Lord shall praise Him: for those who seek will find Him, and those who find Him will praise Him. Let me seek You, Lord, by calling on You, and let me call on You as one who believes in You, since You have been preached to us. My faith calls on You, Lord: the faith You gave me, the faith You breathed into me through the Incarnation of Your Son and through the ministry of the Preacher.

And how am I to call on my God, my God and Lord, when calling on Him means calling Him into myself? What room is there in me into which my God could come? Where could God come into me, the God who made heaven and earth? Is there really anything in me, O Lord my God, that can hold You? Do heaven and earth hold You, then, the heaven and earth You made, and in which You made me? Or, because nothing that exists could exist without You, does it follow that everything that exists holds You? In that case, since I exist too, why do I ask You to come into me, when I would not exist at all unless You were in me already? Why? Because I have not gone down into hell, and yet You are there as well: for if I go down into hell, You are there. So I could not exist, my God, could not exist at all, unless You were in me; or rather, unless I were in You, of whom are all things, by whom are all things, in whom are all things. Even so, Lord, even so. Where, then, am I calling You to, when I am already in You? Or from what place could You come into me? Where could I go beyond heaven and earth, so that my God might come into me from there, He who has said, I fill heaven and earth?

Do heaven and earth hold You, then, since You fill them? Or do You fill them and still overflow, because they cannot hold You? And once heaven and earth are full, where do You pour out whatever is left of Yourself? Or do You need nothing at all to hold You, since You hold all things, and whatever You fill, You fill by holding it? The vessels that are full of You do not hold You up; even if they were shattered, You would not spill out. And when You are poured out upon us, You do not fall to the ground; instead You raise us up. You are not scattered; instead You gather us together. But when You fill all things, do You fill them with the whole of Yourself? Or, since all things together cannot take in the whole of You, does each take in a part of You? And do they all take in the same part at once? Or does each thing have its own part, the larger things more and the smaller things less? Is one part of You, then, greater and another smaller? Or are You entirely present everywhere, while nothing takes in the whole of You?

What are You, then, my God? What, I ask, but the Lord God? For who is Lord except the Lord? Or who is God except our God? Highest, best, mightiest, most all-mighty; most merciful and yet most just; most hidden and yet most present; most beautiful and yet most strong; steadfast, yet beyond our grasp; unchangeable, yet changing all things; never new and never old; making all things new, and bringing the proud into old age without their knowing it; always at work, always at rest; always gathering, yet lacking nothing; bearing up, filling and sheltering all things; creating, nourishing and bringing to maturity; seeking, though You have everything. You love, but without the heat of passion; You are jealous, but free from anxiety; You repent, but You do not grieve; You are angry, yet calm. You change Your works, but Your purpose stays the same; You take back what You find, though You never lost it. You are never in need, yet You rejoice at gain; never greedy, yet You demand interest. More than is due is paid to You, so that You become the debtor; yet who has anything that is not Yours? You pay debts, though You owe nothing; You cancel debts, and lose nothing by it. And what have I just said, my God, my life, my holy joy? Or what does anyone say when he speaks about You? Yet woe to those who say nothing, since even the most eloquent are struck dumb.

If only I could rest in You! If only You would come into my heart and make it drunk, so that I might forget my troubles and embrace You, my one and only good! What are You to me? Have pity on me, and teach me to put it into words. Or what am I to You, that You require me to love You, and if I do not, You are angry with me and threaten me with heavy sorrows? Is it such a small sorrow, then, not to love You? Oh, for Your mercies' sake, tell me, O Lord my God, what You are to me. Say to my soul, I am your salvation. Say it so that I can hear. Look, Lord, my heart is before You; open its ears, and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Let me run after that voice and take hold of You. Do not hide Your face from me. Let me die, so that I may not die; only let me see Your face.

The house of my soul is narrow; make it wider, so that You can come in. It is falling into ruin; rebuild it. There are things inside it that must offend Your eyes; I admit it, and I know it. But who will make it clean? Or to whom else should I cry out, if not to You? Lord, cleanse me from my secret faults, and spare Your servant from the power of the enemy. I believe, and that is why I speak. Lord, You know. Have I not confessed my offenses to You, speaking against myself, and have You not, my God, forgiven the wickedness of my heart? I do not argue my case against You, for You are the truth; I am afraid of deceiving myself, in case my iniquity should lie to itself. So I do not argue my case against You; for if You, Lord, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could endure it?

Still, let me speak before Your mercy, I who am dust and ashes. Let me speak all the same, since it is Your mercy I am speaking to, and not some man who would laugh at me. Perhaps You too laugh at me; yet You will turn back and have compassion on me. For what do I want to say, O Lord my God, except that I do not know where I came from into this dying life, or should I call it a living death? From the very start the comforts of Your compassion took me up, as I was told by the parents of my flesh, from whose substance You once formed me; I do not remember it myself. And so the comforts of a woman's milk received me. It was not my mother or my nurses who filled their own breasts for me; You gave me the food of my infancy through them, according to Your ordinance, by which You distribute Your riches through the hidden springs of all things. You also made me want no more than You gave, and made my nurses glad to give me what You gave them. For with an affection taught by heaven they gladly gave me what they had in abundance from You. This good that came to me from them was good for them as well. In fact it did not come from them but through them; for all good things come from You, O God, and from my God comes all my health. I learned this only later, as You proclaimed Yourself to me through these very gifts of Yours, both within me and outside me. At the time all I knew was how to suck, to settle contentedly into whatever pleased me, and to cry at whatever hurt my flesh; nothing more.

After that I began to smile, first in my sleep and then when awake. That is what I was told about myself, and I believed it, because we see other babies do the same; I have no memory of it myself. Then, little by little, I began to notice where I was, and I wanted to make my wishes known to those who could satisfy them, and I could not. My wishes were inside me and those people were outside, and none of their senses could reach into my spirit. So I threw my limbs about and made noises at random, the few signs I could manage, and such as I could manage, meant to resemble what I wanted, though in truth they resembled it very little. And when I was not obeyed at once, because what I wanted would have harmed me or could not be understood, I was furious with my elders for not submitting to me, and with people who owed me no service for not serving me, and I took my revenge on them with tears. This is what I have learned babies are like, from watching them; and that I was like this too, those babies, without knowing it, have shown me better than my nurses, who did know.

And look, my infancy died long ago, and I am alive. But You, Lord, live forever, and nothing in You dies. For before the foundation of the worlds, and before anything that can even be called "before," You are, and You are God and Lord of all that You have created. In You stand, fixed forever, the first causes of all the things that do not last; the sources of all changeable things remain unchangeable in You; and the eternal reasons of all things that are without reason and bound to time live in You. Tell me, Lord, tell Your suppliant; You who are all pity, tell me, Your pitiable one: did my infancy follow some earlier stage of my life that had died before it? Was it the time I spent in my mother's womb? I have been told something about that, and I have seen pregnant women with my own eyes. And before that life, O God my joy, what then? Was I anywhere, or anybody? I have no one to tell me this: not my father or my mother, not the experience of others, not my own memory. Are You laughing at me for asking such things, and telling me to praise You and acknowledge You for what I do know?

I acknowledge You, Lord of heaven and earth, and I praise You for the first beginnings of my being and for my infancy, which I do not remember at all. For You have arranged that a person should infer much about himself from others, and take much about himself on trust from the word of simple women. Even then I existed and was alive, and toward the end of my infancy I was already looking for signs by which I could make my feelings known to others. Where could such a creature come from, if not from You, Lord? Can anyone be his own craftsman? Or is there some channel, coming from anywhere else, through which being and life can flow into us, except from You, O Lord, in whom being and life are one and the same? For You Yourself are supremely Essence and Life. You are the highest, and You do not change; today does not come to its end in You, and yet it does end in You, because all such things exist in You as well. They would have no way of passing away unless You held them in being. And since Your years do not fail, Your years are a single today. How many of our years and our fathers' years have already flowed through this "today" of Yours, taking from it their measure and the shape of whatever being they had; and still others will flow through it, and take from it the shape of their own degree of being. But You are still the same, and everything belonging to tomorrow and beyond it, and everything belonging to yesterday and before it, You will do today, You have done today. What does it matter to me if someone cannot understand this? Let him rejoice too, and say, What is this? Let him rejoice even so, and be glad to find You without working it out, rather than work it out and fail to find You.

Hear me, O God. Alas for the sins of men! A man says this, and You have pity on him, because You made him, though You did not make the sin that is in him. Who reminds me of the sins of my infancy? For in Your sight no one is clean of sin, not even a baby who has lived only a single day on earth. Who reminds me? Does not any tiny child, in whom I see what I cannot remember of myself? What, then, was my sin back then? Was it that I cried with my mouth wide open for the breast? If I did the same now, craving food suited to my age, I would rightly be laughed at and scolded. So what I did then deserved a scolding; but since I could not understand a scolding, custom and reason both ruled it out. As we grow up we root these habits out and throw them away; and I have never seen anyone, even when pruning, knowingly throw away what is good. Or was it good, even for a time, to cry for things that would have done harm if they had been given? to be bitterly resentful that free people, and its elders, even the very people who brought it into the world, did not wait on it? that many others, wiser than itself, did not jump at its every nod? to do its best to hit and hurt them, because they did not obey orders that would have hurt it if they had been obeyed? So the innocence of infants lies in the weakness of their limbs, not in their will. I have seen and known for myself a jealous baby. It could not yet talk, but it went pale and stared bitterly at its foster-brother. Who does not know this? Mothers and nurses claim they can calm such things by some remedy or other. Unless this too is innocence: when the fountain of milk is flowing richly and abundantly, to refuse to let another share it, though that other is in desperate need and still depends on that one food for its very life. We put up with all this gently, not because it is no evil or only a slight one, but because it will disappear as the years go by; for though we tolerate them now, the very same tempers are completely intolerable when we meet them in someone older.

You, then, O Lord my God, gave life to me as an infant, and gave me a body which, as we see, You equipped with senses, fitted together with limbs, and shaped with beauty, and into which, for its well-being and safety as a whole, You planted all the drives of a living thing. And You command me to praise You for these things, to confess to You, and to sing to Your name, O Most High. For You are God, almighty and good, even if You had made nothing but this, which no one but You could make: You, whose Unity is the pattern of all things; who make all things beautiful out of Your own beauty; and who order all things by Your law. As for this stage of my life, then, Lord, which I do not remember, which I know only on others' word, and which I suppose I lived through by watching other infants (however sound that guess may be), I am reluctant to count it as part of the life I am living in this world. It lies hidden from me in the darkness of forgetfulness just as much as the time I spent in my mother's womb. But if I was shaped in iniquity, and in sin my mother conceived me, where, I beg You, my God, where, Lord, or when was I, Your servant, ever innocent? But look, I pass over that period now; what have I to do with a time of which I can recall no trace?

Moving on from infancy, I came to boyhood; or rather, boyhood came to me and took the place of infancy. Yet infancy did not leave (for where would it have gone?), and still it was there no longer. I was no longer an infant without speech; I was now a boy who could talk. This I remember, and later I worked out how I learned to talk. It was not that my elders taught me words by setting them before me in some fixed method, as they taught me my letters a little later. Instead I wanted to express what was in my heart by cries, by broken sounds and by all sorts of movements of my limbs, so that I could get my way, and yet I could not express everything I wanted, or to everyone I wanted. So, with the understanding You gave me, my God, I myself practiced the sounds in my memory. When people named something, and turned toward it as they spoke, I saw and held on to the fact that the sound they made was their name for the thing they meant to point out. That they meant this thing and not another was clear from the movement of their bodies, which is a kind of natural language shared by all peoples: the expression of the face, the glance of the eyes, the gestures of the limbs and the tone of the voice, which show how the mind feels as it seeks, holds, rejects or avoids things. In this way, by hearing words over and over in their places in different sentences, I gradually gathered what they stood for; and once I had trained my mouth to these signs, I used them to say what I wanted. So I exchanged with the people around me these everyday signs of what we wanted, and ventured further into the stormy company of human life, while still depending on my parents' authority and at the beck and call of my elders.

O God, my God, what misery and what mockery I went through then! As a boy I was told that the right way to live was to obey my teachers, so that I might get on in this world and excel in the arts of the tongue, which serve to win the "praise of men" and deceitful riches. Next I was sent to school to learn to read and write, and I had no idea, poor wretch, what use any of it was; yet if I was lazy about learning, I was beaten. Our forefathers thought this was right, and many who had gone through the same life before us had laid out the weary paths we were made to walk, piling up toil and grief for the sons of Adam. But we discovered, Lord, that people prayed to You, and from them we learned to think of You, as well as we were able, as someone great, who could hear us and help us even though You were hidden from our senses. So, as a boy, I began to pray to You, my help and my refuge. I broke the knots that tied my tongue in order to call on You, and small as I was, I begged You with no small feeling not to let me be beaten at school. And when You did not hear me (not that this was to hand me over to folly), the grown-ups, even my own parents, who wanted no harm to come to me, laughed at my beatings, which were then my great and heavy misfortune.

Is there anyone, Lord, so great of soul, clinging to You with such intense love (for a kind of stupidity can do the same, after a fashion); is there anyone, I say, whom devout attachment to You has filled with so great a spirit that he can think as lightly of the rack and the hooks and other such tortures (which people all over the world beg You in great dread to spare them), while loving those who fear them most bitterly, as our parents made light of the torments our teachers inflicted on us as boys? For we did not fear our torments any less, nor pray to You any less to escape them. And yet we did sin, by writing or reading or studying less than was demanded of us. It was not, Lord, that we lacked memory or ability; by Your will we had enough of both for our age. But what we loved was play, and for that we were punished by people who were doing exactly the same thing themselves. Only, the idleness of grown-ups is called "business," while that of boys, which is really the same, is punished by those grown-ups; and no one feels sorry for the boys, or for the men either. Would any sound judge approve of my being beaten as a boy because I played ball, and so made slower progress in the studies I was to learn only so that as a man I could play a more disgraceful game? And what else was the man who beat me doing? If some fellow teacher got the better of him in a trivial dispute, he was more eaten up with bitterness and envy than I was when a playmate beat me at ball.

And yet I sinned in this, O Lord God, Creator of all things in nature and the One who orders them, but of sin only the One who orders it: O Lord my God, I sinned by going against the orders of my parents and of those teachers. For whatever their motive in wanting me to learn, I could have put that learning to good use later. I disobeyed them not because I had chosen something better, but because I loved play: I loved the proud thrill of winning my contests, and I loved having my ears tickled by lying stories, which only made them itch the more; and the same curiosity shone more and more from my eyes, eager for the shows and games of my elders. Yet the people who put on these shows are held in such esteem that nearly everyone wants the same for their own children; and still they are quite willing to see those children beaten if the same shows keep them from the studies by which they hope they will grow up to put on such shows themselves. Look on these things with pity, Lord, and deliver us who call on You now; deliver also those who do not yet call on You, so that they may call on You and You may deliver them.

So, as a boy, I had already heard of eternal life, promised to us through the humility of the Lord our God, who stooped down to our pride; and from my mother's womb, since she put great hope in You, I was already being signed with the mark of His cross and seasoned with His salt. You saw, Lord, how once, when I was still a boy, I was suddenly seized by a pain in my stomach and came close to dying. You saw, my God, since You were already my guardian, how eagerly and with what faith I begged the devotion of my mother, and of Your Church, the mother of us all, for the baptism of Your Christ, my God and Lord. The mother of my flesh was deeply alarmed, since with a heart pure in Your faith she was laboring even more lovingly to bring my salvation to birth. She would have rushed to have me consecrated and cleansed by the health-giving sacraments, confessing You, Lord Jesus, for the remission of sins, if I had not suddenly recovered. So my cleansing was postponed, as though I would have to be soiled again if I lived, because after that washing the stains of sin would bring a greater and more dangerous guilt. At that time I already believed, as did my mother and the whole household, apart from my father; yet he did not overcome the power of my mother's piety in me, so as to keep me from believing, as he himself did not yet believe. For she was eager that You, my God, rather than he, should be my father; and in this You helped her to win out over her husband, whom she obeyed although she was the better of the two, since in this too she was obeying You, who have commanded it.

I ask You, my God, and I would like to know, if You would like it too, why my baptism was put off at that time. Was it for my good that the reins were, so to speak, loosened on me so that I could sin? Or were they not loosened? If they were not, why do we still hear it said on every side, of one person or another, "Leave him alone, let him do what he likes; he is not baptized yet"? Yet where the health of the body is concerned, no one says, "Let him be wounded even more; he is not healed yet." How much better it would have been, then, if I had been healed at once, and if my family and I had taken care that my soul, once its health was restored, was kept safe in the keeping of You who gave it. Better, truly. But how many great waves of temptation seemed to hang over me once boyhood was past! My mother foresaw them, and she chose to expose to them the clay from which I might later be shaped, rather than the finished likeness itself.

Even in boyhood, though, when far less was feared for me than in my youth, I did not love my studies, and I hated being forced into them. Yet I was forced, and that was good for me; but I did not do good, for I would not have learned unless I had been made to. No one does good against his will, even if what he does is good. Nor did those who forced me do good; the good I received came from You, my God. For they gave no thought to what use I would make of what they forced me to learn, beyond satisfying the insatiable desires of a wealthy poverty and a shameful glory. But You, by whom the very hairs of our head are numbered, used the error of all those who pressed me to learn for my benefit; and my own error, in refusing to learn, You used for my punishment, a fitting penalty for one who was so small a boy and so great a sinner. So by means of those who did not do good, You did good to me, and by means of my own sin You justly punished me. For You have commanded, and so it is, that every disordered affection should be its own punishment.

But why did I hate Greek so much, which I was taught as a boy? Even now I do not fully understand it. For I loved Latin; not what my first teachers taught me, but what the so-called grammarians taught. Those first lessons, where you learn to read, write and count, I found just as much of a burden and a punishment as any of the Greek. Yet where did this come from too, if not from the sin and vanity of this life, since I was flesh, and a breath that passes away and does not come back? Those first lessons were certainly better, because they were more certain: through them I gained, and still keep, the ability to read whatever I find written and to write whatever I wish myself. In the others, by contrast, I was made to learn by heart the wanderings of some Aeneas or other while forgetting my own, and to weep for dead Dido because she killed herself for love; and all the while, with dry eyes, I put up with my own wretched self dying among these things, far from You, O God my life.

For what is more wretched than a wretch who has no pity on himself, who weeps over the death of Dido, which came from loving Aeneas, but does not weep over his own death, which came from not loving You, O God? You light of my heart, You bread of my inmost soul, You Power who give strength to my mind and life to my thoughts: I did not love You. I committed fornication against You, and all around me, as I did so, the cry rang out, "Well done! Well done!" For the friendship of this world is fornication against You, and "Well done! Well done!" keeps ringing out until a man is ashamed not to be that kind of man. And I did not weep over this, I who wept for Dido, dead, "seeking by the sword a stroke and wound extreme," while I myself was seeking a worse extreme, the furthest and lowest of Your creatures, having abandoned You, earth going down into earth. And if I had been forbidden to read all this, I would have been upset at not being able to read what upset me. Madness like this is considered a nobler and richer kind of learning than the lessons in which I learned to read and write.

But now, my God, cry out in my soul, and let Your truth tell me, "Not so, not so. That first schooling was far better." For look, I would sooner forget the wanderings of Aeneas and everything of that kind than forget how to read and write. It is true that curtains hang over the entrances of the grammar schools; but they are not so much a sign of some hidden mystery as a cover for error. Let those I no longer fear not shout me down, while I confess to You, my God, whatever my soul wishes, and accept the condemnation of my evil ways, so that I may love Your good ways. Let neither the sellers nor the buyers of grammar shout me down. For if I ask them whether it is true, as the poet says, that Aeneas once came to Carthage, the less educated will answer that they do not know, and the more educated that he never did. But if I ask how the name "Aeneas" is spelled, everyone who has learned this will give me the right answer, according to the signs people have agreed on among themselves. And again, if I ask which could be forgotten with less harm to the business of life, reading and writing or these poetic fictions, who cannot foresee the answer that anyone would give who has not entirely forgotten himself? So I sinned as a boy when I preferred those empty studies to the more useful ones, or rather, when I loved the one and hated the other. "One and one make two"; "two and two make four": to me this was a hateful singsong; while "the wooden horse full of armed men," and "the burning of Troy," and "Creusa's shade and sad similitude" were the spectacle my vanity loved most.

Why, then, did I hate Greek literature, which tells the same kind of tales? For Homer too was skilled at weaving such fictions, and is most sweetly vain; yet to me as a boy he tasted bitter. I suppose Virgil would taste the same to Greek boys, if they were forced to learn him the way I was forced to learn Homer. It was the difficulty, of course, the sheer difficulty of a foreign language, that sprinkled gall, as it were, over all the sweetness of the Greek stories. I did not understand a single word, and I was pressed hard, with cruel threats and punishments, to make me understand. There was a time too, in infancy, when I knew no Latin at all; yet I learned it just by paying attention, without any fear or pain, amid the cuddles of my nurses and the jokes of people who smiled at me and played with me and cheered me on. I learned it without any pressure of punishment driving me, because my own heart drove me to bring its thoughts to birth, and I could only do that by learning words, not from people who taught me but from people who talked with me, and into whose ears I in turn brought to birth whatever I was thinking. This makes it plain that free curiosity does more to help us learn such things than frightening compulsion. Yet compulsion holds in check the wanderings of that freedom, through Your laws, O my God, Your laws, from the teacher's cane to the trials of the martyrs; for Your laws are able to mix for us a healthy bitterness, calling us back to You from the deadly pleasure that lures us away from You.

Hear my prayer, Lord; do not let my soul give way under Your discipline, and do not let me give up confessing to You all Your mercies, by which You have pulled me out of all my worst ways, so that You might become sweeter to me than all the attractions I used to chase; so that I may love You with all my strength and hold on to Your hand with all my heart, and so that You may still rescue me from every temptation, right to the end. For look, O Lord, my King and my God: let whatever useful thing I learned as a boy serve You; let it serve You that I speak, write, read and count. For while I was learning vain things, You gave me Your discipline, and You have forgiven me the sin of taking delight in those vain things. It is true that I learned many useful words in them; but those words can just as well be learned in things that are not vain, and that is the safe road for young feet to walk.

But woe to you, you torrent of human custom! Who can stand against you? How long before you run dry? How long will you keep rolling the sons of Eve into that vast and terrifying ocean, which even those who have climbed onto the cross can barely cross? Did I not read in you of Jove, the thunderer and the adulterer? Of course he could not have been both; but this way the pretended thunder could give sanction to real adultery and act as its go-between. And which of our gowned teachers now gives a serious hearing to a man from their own school who cries out, "These were Homer's fictions; he transferred human things to the gods. If only he had brought divine things down to us!" Yet it would be truer to say, "These are his fictions, certainly; but by giving a divine nature to wicked men, he made sure that crimes would no longer be counted as crimes, and that whoever committed them would seem to be imitating not depraved men but the gods of heaven."

And yet, you hellish torrent, the sons of men are thrown into you, with fees paid, to learn such things; and it is made into a grand public affair when this goes on in the forum, in full view of laws that grant a salary on top of the pupils' fees. And you pound against your rocks and roar, "This is where words are learned; this is where you gain eloquence, which is essential for winning your case and setting out your views." As if we would never have known words like "golden shower," "lap," "beguile," "temples of heaven," or the other words in that passage, unless Terence had brought a worthless young man onto the stage who holds up Jupiter as his model for seduction,
"Gazing at a painting where the tale was shown, Of Jove descending in a golden shower Into the lap of Danae, to beguile a woman."
And then see how he stirs himself up to lust, as if on heaven's authority:
"And what a god! Great Jove, Who makes heaven's highest temples tremble at his thunder,
And I, a poor mortal man, am I not to do the same? I did it, and I did it with all my heart."

The words are not learned one bit more easily because of all this filth; but thanks to the words the filth is committed with less shame. I do not blame the words, which are like choice and precious vessels, but the wine of error that drunken teachers poured out for us in them; and if we did not drink it too, we were beaten, and there was no sober judge to whom we could appeal. And yet, O my God, in whose presence I can now remember this without harm, I learned all this willingly, poor wretch, and took great delight in it, and for this I was called a promising boy.

Bear with me, my God, while I say something about my intelligence, which was Your gift, and about the nonsense I wasted it on. A task was set for me, which troubled my soul a good deal, with praise or disgrace depending on how I did, and the fear of a beating as well: I had to speak the words of Juno, raging and grieving that she could not
"Turn back this Trojan prince from Latium."

I had heard that Juno never said any such words; but we were made to go astray, following in the footsteps of these poetic fictions, and to say in prose roughly what the poet had said in verse. And the one whose speech won the most applause was the one in whom the passions of rage and grief stood out most strongly, clothed in the most fitting language, while the dignity of the character was kept up. What good was it to me, O my true life, my God, that my recitation was applauded above so many others of my own age and class? Was not all that smoke and wind? Was there nothing else on which I could exercise my wit and my tongue? Your praises, Lord, Your praises, through Your Scriptures, could have propped up the still tender shoot of my heart; then it would not have trailed away among these empty trifles, a filthy prey for the birds of the air. For there is more than one way of offering sacrifice to the rebellious angels.

But why wonder that I was carried away into vanities like this, and wandered out of Your presence, O my God, when the models set before me were men who were ashamed and embarrassed if they were criticized for some barbarism or solecism in telling about something they had done that was not bad in itself, yet who gloried in the praise they got when they told about their own disordered lives in rich, polished and well-ordered speech? You see these things, Lord, and You keep silent: long-suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth. Will You keep silent forever? Even now You are drawing out of this horrible pit the soul that seeks You and thirsts for Your delights, whose heart says to You, I have sought Your face; Your face, Lord, will I seek. For to be in darkened affections is to be far from You. It is not with our feet, or by moving from place to place, that we leave You or come back to You. Did that younger son of Yours look for horses or chariots or ships, or fly off on visible wings, or travel by the movement of his legs, so that in a far country he could squander in riotous living everything You had given him when he set out? You were a loving Father when You gave it, and more loving still to him when he came back with nothing. So it is in lustful affections, which is to say darkened ones, that the true distance from Your face lies.

Look, O Lord God, look patiently, as You always do, at how carefully the sons of men keep the agreed rules of letters and syllables handed down by those who spoke before them, while they neglect the eternal covenant of everlasting salvation that they have received from You. So much so, that someone who teaches or learns the inherited rules of pronunciation will give more offense to people by dropping the aspirate and saying "uman being," against the laws of grammar, than if he, a "human being," hates a "human being," against Your laws. As if any enemy could do him more harm than the hatred that inflames him against that enemy; or as if he could wound the one he persecutes more deeply than he wounds his own soul by his hostility. Surely no knowledge of letters is so deeply ingrained as what is written in the conscience: "that he is doing to another what he would hate to suffer from another." How hidden You are, O God, who alone are great, dwelling in silence on high, and by an unwearying law scattering the blindness that punishes lawless desires! A man in pursuit of a reputation for eloquence, standing before a human judge, surrounded by a crowd of human beings, and attacking his enemy with the fiercest hatred, will be extremely careful not to murder the word "human being" by a slip of the tongue; but he takes no care at all not to murder a real human being through the fury of his spirit.

This was the world at whose door I lay as a boy, unhappy as I was; this was the arena where I was more afraid of committing a barbarism than I was careful, if I did commit one, not to envy those who had not. I say these things and confess them to You, my God: the things for which I was praised by the people whom at the time I thought it the whole of virtue to please. For I did not see the pit of vileness into which I had been cast away out of Your sight. In their eyes, what could have been fouler than I already was, when I displeased even people like them? With countless lies I deceived my tutor, my teachers and my parents, out of love of play, eagerness to watch silly shows, and a restless urge to imitate them. I also stole from my parents' cellar and table, either because greed had me in its grip or so that I would have something to give other boys, who sold me their games, though they enjoyed them every bit as much as I did. In these games, too, I often hunted for unfair victories, while being beaten myself by a vain desire to come out on top. And what did I so hate to put up with, and attack so fiercely when I caught it, as the very thing I was doing to others? And if I was caught and attacked for it, I would rather fight than give in. Is this the innocence of childhood? No, Lord, it is not. I beg Your mercy, my God. For these very sins, as the years go by, pass over from tutors and teachers, from nuts and balls and sparrows, to magistrates and kings, to gold and estates and slaves, just as heavier punishments take over from the cane. So it was the small stature of childhood, O our King, that You praised as a sign of humility, when You said, Of such is the kingdom of heaven.

And yet, Lord, to You, the most excellent and most good Creator and Ruler of the universe, thanks would be due to You, our God, even if You had meant me to be no more than a boy. For even then I existed, I was alive, I could feel; and I had an instinct to take care of my own well-being, a trace of that mysterious Unity from which I came. With an inner sense I watched over the wholeness of my senses, and in these small pursuits, and in my thoughts about small things, I learned to delight in truth. I hated being deceived; I had a strong memory; I was well equipped with speech; I was comforted by friendship; I avoided pain, degradation and ignorance. In so small a creature, what was not wonderful, what was not worthy of praise? But all these are gifts of my God. I did not give them to myself; and they are good, and all of them together are me. So He who made me is good, and He is my good, and before Him I rejoice in every good thing I had, even as a boy. For this was my sin: that I looked for pleasures, heights and truths not in Him but in His creatures, myself and others, and so I fell headlong into sorrows, confusions and errors. Thanks be to You, my joy, my glory and my confidence, my God; thanks be to You for Your gifts; but keep them safe for me. For in that way You will keep me safe, and what You have given me will grow and be made complete, and I myself will be with You, since it was You who gave me even my being.

chapters.title: Book 2
paragraphs: I want now to call to mind my past foulness and the carnal corruptions of my soul, not because I love them, but so that I may love You, O my God. I do it for love of Your love, going back over my most wicked ways in the bitterness of remembering them, so that You may grow sweet to me (You sweetness that never fails, You happy and secure sweetness), and so that You may gather me up again out of the scattered state in which I was torn to pieces when I turned away from You, the One Good, and lost myself among many things. For there was a time in my youth when I burned to have my fill of things below, and I dared to run wild in various shadowy loves. My beauty wasted away, and I stank in Your eyes, pleasing myself and eager to please in the eyes of men.

And what was it that delighted me, except to love and to be loved? But I did not keep to the measure of love that runs from mind to mind, the bright boundary line of friendship. Instead, out of the muddy concupiscence of the flesh and the bubbling springs of youth, mists rose up that clouded and darkened my heart, until I could not tell the clear light of love from the fog of lust. The two boiled together in confusion inside me, swept my unsteady youth over the cliffs of unholy desires, and sank me in a whirlpool of shameful deeds. Your anger had gathered strength over me, and I did not know it. I had been deafened by the clanking of the chain of my mortality, the punishment for my soul's pride, and I went further away from You, and You let me go. I was tossed about, poured out, scattered, and I boiled over in my fornications, and You kept silent, O my joy so slow in coming! You kept silent then, and I went further and further from You, into more and more barren seedbeds of sorrow, with a proud dejection and a restless weariness.

Oh, if only someone had brought order to my distress, and turned to good use the fleeting beauties of these lowest things in Your creation, and set a limit to the pleasure they give! Then the surging tides of my youth might have spent themselves on the shore of marriage, if they could not be calmed, and been kept to the purpose of raising a family, as Your law prescribes, O Lord. For in this way You shape the offspring of this death of ours, since You are able with a gentle hand to blunt the thorns that were shut out of Your paradise. For Your omnipotence is not far from us, even when we are far from You. Otherwise, I ought to have listened more carefully to the voice from the clouds: Nevertheless such shall have trouble in the flesh, but I spare you. And, It is good for a man not to touch a woman. And, He that is unmarried thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but he that is married cares about the things of this world, how he may please his wife.

I should have paid closer attention to these words, and, cut off for the kingdom of heaven's sake, waited more happily for Your embraces. But I, poor wretch, foamed like a stormy sea, following the rush of my own tide and abandoning You, and I broke through all Your limits; yet I did not escape Your scourges. For what mortal can? You were always there, severe in Your mercy, sprinkling the bitterest disappointment over all my unlawful pleasures, so that I would look for pleasure without disappointment. But where to find that I could not discover, except in You, O Lord, who teach us through sorrow, who wound us in order to heal, and who kill us so that we may not die away from You. Where was I, and how far was I exiled from the delights of Your house, in that sixteenth year of the age of my flesh, when the madness of lust took command over me (a madness that human shamelessness gives free license, though Your laws do not license it), and I surrendered myself to it completely? Meanwhile my family took no care to catch me as I fell by means of marriage; their only concern was that I should learn to speak superbly and become a persuasive orator.

For that year my studies were interrupted. I had come back from Madaura, a neighboring town where I had gone to study grammar and rhetoric, and the money for a longer stay away, in Carthage, was being put together for me; and that was due more to my father's determination than to his means, since he was only a poor freeman of Thagaste. To whom am I telling this? Not to You, my God; but in Your presence I am telling it to my own kind, to the human race, or to whatever small part of it may come across these writings of mine. And to what end? So that whoever reads this may reflect on the depths from which we must cry to You. For what is closer to Your ears than a heart that confesses and a life of faith? Who did not praise my father at the time, because he went beyond what his household could afford to give his son everything he needed for a long journey for the sake of his studies? Many citizens far richer than he did nothing of the kind for their children. And yet this same father did not care how I was growing toward You, or how chaste I was, as long as I was fluent in speech, however barren I remained of Your cultivation, O God, who are the one true and good Lord of Your field, my heart.

But in that sixteenth year, when I was out of school for a time and living with my parents (a period of idleness forced on us by my family's narrow means), the brambles of unclean desires grew up over my head, and there was no hand to pull them out. What is more, when my father saw me at the baths, growing into manhood and clothed in restless youth, he told my mother about it with delight, as if already looking forward to grandchildren from this. He was rejoicing in that tumult of the senses in which the world forgets You, its Creator, and falls in love with Your creature instead of You, drunk on the invisible wine of its own will, which turns aside and bends down to the very lowest things. But in my mother's breast You had already begun Your temple and laid the foundation of Your holy dwelling, whereas my father was still only a catechumen, and a recent one at that. So she was shaken with a holy fear and trembling; and though I was not yet baptized, she feared for me the crooked ways in which people walk who turn their backs to You and not their faces.

Alas for me! Do I dare to say that You kept silent, O my God, while I wandered further away from You? Were You really silent to me then? And whose words were they, if not Yours, that You sang in my ears through my mother, Your faithful one? None of them sank into my heart so as to make me act on them. For she wanted me, and I remember how she warned me in private with great anxiety, "not to commit fornication, and above all never to defile another man's wife." This seemed to me a woman's advice, which I would have blushed to follow. But the words were Yours, and I did not know it. I thought You were silent and that it was she who was speaking, when through her You were not silent to me at all; and in her You were despised by me, her son, the son of Your handmaid, Your servant. But I did not know it, and I rushed headlong in such blindness that among boys my own age I was ashamed of being less shameless than they were. I heard them boasting of their disgraceful deeds, and the more degraded they themselves were, the more they boasted; and I took pleasure not only in the pleasure of the act but in the praise it won. What deserves blame, if not vice? Yet I made myself worse than I was so as not to be blamed; and when I had not sinned in some way that would put me level with the depraved, I would claim to have done what I had not done, so as not to seem more contemptible for being more innocent, or of less account for being more chaste.

See what companions I walked the streets of Babylon with, and how I rolled in its mud as if it were a bed of spices and precious ointments. And to make me stick all the faster at its very center, the invisible enemy trampled on me and seduced me, because I was easy to seduce. The mother of my flesh had by now fled from the center of Babylon, though she still moved more slowly in its outskirts; but though she had urged me to be chaste, she did not take the same care over what she had heard about me from her husband, so as to keep within the bounds of married love what she sensed was harmful now and dangerous for the future, if it could not be cut back to the quick. She did not see to this, because she was afraid that a wife would be a shackle and a hindrance to my hopes. Not the hopes of the world to come, which my mother placed in You, but my hopes of learning, which both my parents were too eager for me to attain: my father, because he hardly thought about You at all, and about me only empty dreams; my mother, because she reckoned that the usual course of study would not only do me no harm, but would even help me somewhat toward attaining You. That, at least, is my guess, as I recall my parents' characters as best I can. Meanwhile the reins were loosened for me, far beyond any proper severity, to spend my time in amusement, and even to run to dissipation in whatever took my fancy. And over everything there was a mist, cutting me off, O my God, from the brightness of Your truth; and my iniquity burst out as if from very fatness.

Theft is certainly punished by Your law, O Lord, and by the law written in human hearts, which not even wickedness itself can erase. For what thief calmly puts up with another thief? Not even a rich thief will put up with one who steals out of need. Yet I wanted to steal, and I did it, driven not by hunger or poverty but by being sick of doing right and glutted with wickedness. For I stole something I already had plenty of, and of much better quality. Nor did I want to enjoy the thing I stole; what I enjoyed was the theft itself, and the sin. There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit that was tempting neither in looks nor in taste. A gang of us good-for-nothing youths set out late one night to shake it and strip it (we had kept up our games in the streets until then, as was our pernicious habit), and we carried off huge loads, not to eat ourselves but just to throw to the pigs, though we did taste a few. We did it simply for the sake of doing what we liked, because it was forbidden. Look at my heart, O God, look at my heart, which You pitied at the bottom of the bottomless pit. Now let my heart tell You what it was looking for there, so that I was evil for nothing, with no motive for wrongdoing except the wrongdoing itself. It was foul, and I loved it. I loved to perish; I loved my own fault, not the thing for which I was at fault, but the fault itself. Foul soul, leaping down from Your firmament to utter destruction, seeking nothing from the shameful act but the shame itself!

For beautiful bodies have their attraction, and so do gold and silver and all things; in bodily touch the harmony of one body with another counts for a great deal, and each of the other senses has its own object, suitably matched to it. Worldly honor too has its splendor, and so does the power to command and to overcome others, which is also where the thirst for revenge comes from. And yet, to obtain all these, we must not leave You, O Lord, or turn aside from Your law. The life we live here also has its own charm, because of a certain measure of beauty it has and its harmony with all the beautiful things here below. Human friendship, too, is made sweet by a precious bond, because it makes one out of many souls. Sin is committed for the sake of all these and things like them, when, through an excessive leaning toward these goods of the lowest order, the better and higher goods are abandoned: You, O Lord our God, and Your truth, and Your law. For these lower things have their delights, but not like my God, who made all things; for in Him the righteous delights, and He is the joy of the upright in heart.

So when we ask why a crime was committed, we do not usually believe the answer unless it turns out that there could have been a desire to gain one of those goods we called lower, or a fear of losing one. For they are beautiful and attractive, even though, compared with the higher goods that bring happiness, they are poor and lowly. A man has committed murder. Why? He was in love with the victim's wife or with his estate; or he wanted to rob him to make a living; or he was afraid of losing something of the kind to him; or he had been wronged and was burning for revenge. Would anyone commit murder for no reason, simply for the pleasure of murdering? Who would believe it? Even that raging and savage man, of whom it was said that he was evil and cruel for no reason at all, still has a reason given for it: "so that," the writer says, "his hand or heart should not grow slack through idleness." And to what end? So that, by keeping in practice at crime, he could take the city and win honors, power and riches, and be free from fear of the laws and from the troubles caused by his household's needs and by his awareness of his crimes. So not even Catiline himself loved his crimes; what he loved was something else, for the sake of which he committed them.

What was it, then, that I loved in you, wretch that I was, you theft of mine, you deed of darkness in my sixteenth year? You were not lovely, because you were a theft. But are you anything at all, that I should speak to you like this? The pears we stole were beautiful, because they were Your creation, You most beautiful of all, Creator of all, O good God, God the highest good and my true good. Those pears were beautiful, but it was not them that my wretched soul wanted; I had plenty of better ones, and I picked those only in order to steal. Once I had picked them, I threw them away, and my only feast from them was my own sin, which I relished with pleasure. For if any bit of those pears got into my mouth, what gave it its flavor was the sin. And now, O Lord my God, I ask what it was in that theft that delighted me; and look, there is no beauty in it at all. I do not mean the kind of beauty there is in justice and wisdom; nor the kind that is in the mind and memory and senses and bodily life of a human being; nor the way the stars are glorious and beautiful in their spheres, or the earth and the sea, teeming with young life that is born to take the place of what dies away; no, not even that false and shadowy beauty that belongs to the vices that deceive us.

For pride imitates loftiness, whereas You alone are God, exalted over all. And ambition, what does it seek but honor and glory, whereas You alone are to be honored above all, and glorious forever? The cruelty of the powerful wants to be feared; but who is to be feared except God alone? What can be seized from His power or slipped out of it, and when, or where, or by what route, or by whom? The caresses of the lustful want to be taken for love; yet nothing is more tender than Your love, and nothing is loved more healthily than that truth of Yours, bright and beautiful beyond all things. Curiosity poses as a desire for knowledge, whereas You know all things supremely. Even ignorance and foolishness hide under the names of simplicity and harmlessness, because nothing is found simpler than You; and what is more harmless than You, since it is the sinner's own works that harm him? Laziness pretends to want rest; but what sure rest is there apart from the Lord? Extravagance likes to be called plenty and abundance; but You are the fullness and never-failing wealth of incorruptible pleasures. Wastefulness casts a shadow of generosity; but You are the most lavish Giver of every good. Greed wants to own many things; and You own all things. Envy fights for excellence; what is more excellent than You? Anger seeks revenge; who takes revenge more justly than You? Fear shrinks from anything unusual or sudden that threatens the things it loves, and it takes precautions for their safety; but to You what is unusual or sudden? Or who can separate from You what You love? Or where, except with You, is there unshaken safety? Grief pines away over lost things that its desires took pleasure in, because it would like nothing to be taken away from it, just as nothing can be taken away from You.

This is how the soul commits fornication: she turns away from You and looks outside You for what she cannot find pure and untainted until she comes back to You. So all who put themselves far from You and set themselves up against You are imitating You in a perverse way. But even by imitating You like this, they show that You are the Creator of all nature, and so there is nowhere they can go to get away from You altogether. What, then, did I love in that theft? In what way did I imitate my Lord, even if corruptly and perversely? Did I want to break Your law at least by stealth, since I could not do it by power, so that, a prisoner, I could mimic a crippled freedom by doing with impunity what I was not allowed to do, a darkened likeness of Your omnipotence? Look: here is Your servant, running away from his Lord and catching hold of a shadow. What rottenness! What a monstrous life, what a depth of death! Could I take pleasure in what was not allowed, for no other reason than that it was not allowed?

What shall I render to the Lord, that my memory can recall these things and my soul is not frightened by them? I will love You, O Lord, and thank You, and confess to Your name, because You have forgiven me these great and wicked deeds of mine. I put it down to Your grace and Your mercy that You have melted my sins away like ice. I put down to Your grace as well whatever evil I did not do; for what might I not have done, when I even loved a sin for its own sake? Yes, I confess that everything has been forgiven me, both the evil I did of my own will and the evil I did not do because You guided me. Who is there who, weighing his own weakness, dares to credit his own strength with his purity and innocence, and so loves You less, as if he had needed less of Your mercy, by which You forgive the sins of those who turn to You? For anyone who was called by You, and followed Your voice, and avoided the things he reads me recalling and confessing about myself, should not scorn me, who was sick and was cured by that Physician through whose help he himself was not sick, or rather was less sick. And for this let him love You just as much, or even more; for he sees that the One who restored me from such a deep wasting sickness of sin is the same One by whom he was kept from a wasting sickness of sin as bad.

What fruit did I get then, wretch that I was, from those things that I now blush to remember? Above all from that theft, in which I loved the theft itself and nothing else, when it was itself nothing, and I all the more wretched for loving it? And yet I would not have done it alone. That, as I remember, was my state of mind then: alone I would never have done it. So in it I also loved the company of the accomplices I did it with. Then it is not true that I loved nothing but the theft? No, in fact I loved nothing else, because that company was also nothing. What is the truth of it? Who can teach me, except the One who lights up my heart and uncovers its dark corners? What is it that has come into my mind to ask about, to discuss and to consider? For if I had loved the pears I stole back then, and wanted to enjoy them, I could have done it alone, if committing the theft had been enough to get me my pleasure; I would not have needed to inflame the itch of my desire by rubbing against accomplices. But since my pleasure was not in those pears, it was in the crime itself, and it was the company of fellow sinners that produced it.

What, then, was this state of mind? It was certainly far too foul, and woe to me for having it. But still, what was it? Who can understand his errors? It was the fun of it, which tickled our hearts, so to speak, that we were fooling people who had no idea what we were doing and would have strongly objected. Why, then, did my delight in it depend on my not doing it alone? Is it because people do not usually laugh alone? Usually no one does; yet sometimes laughter overcomes people on their own, when no one else at all is with them, if something very funny strikes their senses or their mind. Yet I would not have done this alone; alone I would never have done it. Look, my God, here before You is the living memory of my soul. On my own I would never have committed that theft, in which what pleased me was not what I stole but the fact that I stole it; on my own I would not have enjoyed doing it at all, and I would not have done it. O friendship too unfriendly! You mysterious seducer of the soul, you hunger to do harm for sport and mischief, you craving for other people's loss without any desire for my own gain or for revenge! But when someone says, "Come on, let's do it," we are ashamed not to be shameless.

Who can unravel that most twisted and tangled knot? It is filthy; I do not want to dwell on it, or even look at it. It is You I want, O Righteousness and Innocence, beautiful and lovely to all pure eyes, a satisfaction that never cloys. In You there is perfect rest, and a life that nothing can disturb. Whoever enters into You enters into the joy of his Lord; he shall not fear, and he shall do excellently in the All-Excellent. I slid away from You, my God, and wandered too far astray from You, my stay, in these years of my youth, and I became to myself a barren land.

chapters.title: Book 3
paragraphs: I came to Carthage, and all around me a cauldron of shameful loves sizzled and sang in my ears. I was not yet in love, yet I was in love with loving, and out of a need hidden deeper within me I hated myself for needing too little. I went looking for something to love, in love with love itself; I hated safety, and a road without snares. For inside me there was a famine of that inward food, Yourself, my God; yet that famine did not make me hungry. I had no longing at all for food that does not perish, not because I was full of it, but because the emptier I was, the more it disgusted me. That is why my soul was sick and covered in sores; it threw itself outward in misery, craving to be scratched by contact with things of the senses. Yet if those things had no soul, they would surely not have been loved. To love and to be loved was sweet to me, and sweeter still if I could also enjoy the body of the one I loved. So I fouled the spring of friendship with the filth of concupiscence, and clouded its brightness with the hell of lust; and though I was foul and disgraceful, in my overflowing vanity I longed to seem elegant and refined. So I rushed headlong into love, in which I wanted to be caught. My God, my Mercy, with how much gall did You in Your goodness sprinkle that sweetness for me! For I was loved, and I secretly reached the bond of enjoyment, and I let myself be happily tied up in painful chains, so that I might be beaten with the red-hot iron rods of jealousy, and suspicions, and fears, and angers, and quarrels.

The theater also swept me away, full of pictures of my own miseries and of kindling for my own fire. Why is it that a person wants to be made sad by watching mournful and tragic events, which he would never want to suffer himself? Yet as a spectator he wants to feel grief over them, and that very grief is his pleasure. What is this but a pitiful madness? For the less free a man is from such feelings himself, the more these scenes move him. And yet, when he suffers in his own person, it is usually called misery; when he suffers along with others, it is called mercy. But what kind of compassion is it that is spent on invented, staged sufferings? The listener is not called on to help, only invited to grieve; and the more he grieves, the more he applauds the actor who plays these fictions. And if the disasters of these people, whether from ancient history or pure invention, are acted in such a way that the spectator is not moved to grief, he walks out bored and finding fault; but if he is moved, he stays riveted, and weeps with enjoyment.

So are sorrows loved too? Surely everyone wants to be happy. Or is it that, while no one likes being miserable, people do like being merciful, and since mercy cannot exist without feeling pain, sorrows are loved for this one reason? This too flows from that vein of friendship. But where does that vein go? Where does it flow? Why does it run down into a torrent of boiling pitch, into the monstrous surges of foul lusts, into which it changes and turns of its own accord, twisted and thrown down from its heavenly clearness? Should compassion then be rejected? Not at all. Let sorrows sometimes be loved, then. But beware of uncleanness, my soul, under the protection of my God, the God of our fathers, who is to be praised and exalted above all forever; beware of uncleanness. For I have not stopped feeling pity now. But back then, in the theaters, I rejoiced with the lovers when they wickedly enjoyed each other, even though this was only make-believe in the play; and when they lost each other, I grieved with them as though I were full of compassion, and yet I delighted in both. Now, though, I pity far more the man who rejoices in his wickedness than the man who is thought to have suffered hardship by losing some ruinous pleasure and missing some wretched happiness. This is certainly the truer mercy, but there is no pleasure in its grief. For although the one who grieves for the wretched is approved for performing a duty of love, the one who is truly compassionate would still much rather there were nothing for him to grieve over. For if there were such a thing as ill-willed good will (which can never be), then the one who pities truly and sincerely could wish that there were wretched people, so that he might pity them. So some grief may be approved, but none should be loved. That is how it is with You, O Lord God: You love souls far more purely than we do and pity them far more incorruptibly, yet You are wounded by no sorrow. And who is equal to these things?

But I, wretched as I was, loved to grieve back then, and went looking for something to grieve over. When the suffering was someone else's, and invented, and acted out on a stage, the performance that pleased me most and drew me most powerfully was the one that brought tears to my eyes. What wonder is it that I, an unhappy sheep straying from Your flock and impatient of Your care, became infected with a foul disease? That is where my love of sorrows came from: not sorrows that would pierce deep into me, for I did not love to suffer the things I loved to watch, but sorrows that, when I heard those fictions, would lightly scratch my surface. Yet after them, as after poisoned fingernails, came burning swelling, abscesses, and festering sores. When my life was like this, was it life at all, O my God?

And all the while Your faithful mercy hovered over me from far off. In what grievous sins I wasted myself away! I followed a sacrilegious curiosity, so that, having abandoned You, it led me down into faithless depths and the deceitful service of demons, to whom I offered my evil deeds as sacrifices; and in all of it You were scourging me. I even dared, while Your feasts were being celebrated within the walls of Your Church, to desire and to carry on an affair that deserved death as its fruit. For this You struck me with heavy punishments, though they were nothing compared with my guilt, O You my exceedingly great mercy, my God, my refuge from those terrible destroyers among whom I wandered with a stiff neck, drawing ever further away from You, loving my own ways and not Yours, loving the freedom of a runaway.

The studies that were called respectable were also aimed at the law courts and their quarrels, so that I might excel there, where the craftier a man is, the more he is praised. Such is the blindness of human beings that they even boast of their blindness. And now I was at the top of the school of rhetoric, and I was proudly pleased with myself and swollen with arrogance. Yet I was far calmer, Lord, as You know, and had nothing at all to do with the subversions carried out by the "Subverters." That ill-omened and devilish name was worn as a badge of sophistication. I lived among them with a shameless shame, because I was not like them. I lived with them, and sometimes I enjoyed their friendship, though I always hated what they did, that is, their "subversions," in which they insolently attacked the shyness of newcomers, harassing them with unprovoked mockery and feeding their own malicious mirth on it. Nothing could be more like the actions of demons than this. So what could they be more truly called than "Subverters"? They were themselves subverted and wholly perverted first, while deceiving spirits secretly mocked and led them astray in the very thing they loved to do, mocking and deceiving others.

It was among people like these, at that unsteady age, that I was studying the books of eloquence, in which I wanted to shine, for a damnable and empty purpose: the joys of human vanity. Following the usual course of study, I came upon a certain book by Cicero, whose language almost everyone admires, though not his heart. This book of his contains an exhortation to philosophy and is called "Hortensius." But this book changed my feelings. It turned my prayers toward You Yourself, O Lord, and gave me different aims and desires. Every empty hope suddenly lost its worth for me, and with an unbelievable burning of heart I longed for the immortality of wisdom, and I began to rise, so that I might return to You. For I did not use that book to sharpen my tongue, which was what I seemed to be buying with my mother's money in my nineteenth year, my father having died two years before. No, I did not use that book to sharpen my tongue; what won me over was not its style but what it said.

How I burned then, my God, how I burned to fly back from earthly things to You, and I did not know what You were doing with me! For with You is wisdom. Now the love of wisdom has a Greek name, "philosophy," and it was with this love that that book set me on fire. There are some who lead people astray through philosophy, painting over and disguising their own errors with that great, attractive and honorable name; and nearly all who were like this, in that author's own age and before it, are criticized and exposed in that book. There, too, is made plain that saving warning of Your Spirit through Your good and devout servant: Beware lest anyone spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily. At that time, as You know, O light of my heart, these words of the Apostle were not yet known to me. Even so, the one thing that delighted me in that exhortation was that it stirred me up strongly and kindled and inflamed me to love and seek and win and hold and embrace, not this sect or that, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be. And the only thing that held me back in all this blaze was that the name of Christ was not in it. For this name, by Your mercy, O Lord, this name of my Savior, Your Son, my tender heart had devoutly drunk in with my mother's milk and kept deep within it; and whatever lacked that name, however learned, polished or true, did not take complete hold of me.

So I made up my mind to turn my attention to the holy Scriptures and see what they were like. And look, what I see is something not discovered by the proud, nor laid bare to children, humble at the entrance but lofty further in, and veiled in mysteries; and I was not the kind of person who could enter it, or bend my neck to follow its steps. For when I first turned to those Scriptures, I did not feel as I speak about them now. Instead they seemed to me unworthy to be compared with the dignity of Tully. My swollen pride recoiled from their plainness, and my sharp mind could not get through to what lay inside them. Yet they were the kind of thing that grows up along with little ones. But I scorned to be a little one, and, puffed up with pride, I thought myself a great one.

And so I fell in with men who were proud and raving, far too carnal and far too talkative, in whose mouths were the snares of the Devil, a birdlime made from a mixture of the syllables of Your name, and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, our Comforter. These names never left their lips, but only as sound and the clatter of the tongue; their hearts were empty of truth. Still, they kept crying "Truth, Truth," and talked to me about it a great deal, yet it was nowhere in them. They spoke falsehoods, not only about You, who truly are Truth, but even about the elements of this world, Your creatures. And yet for love of You, my Father, supremely good, Beauty of all things beautiful, I should have passed beyond even the philosophers who spoke truly about those things. O Truth, Truth, how deeply even then did the very marrow of my soul sigh for You, while those men sounded Your name at me often and in many ways, with the voice alone and in many huge books, though it was only an echo! These were the dishes on which, when I was hungry for You, they served me, instead of You, the sun and the moon, beautiful works of Yours, but still Your works, not You Yourself, and not even Your first works. For Your spiritual works come before these bodily works, bright and heavenly as they are. But it was not even those first works of Yours that I hungered and thirsted for, but You Yourself, the Truth, in whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. Yet they still kept setting before me on those dishes glittering fantasies. It would have been better to love this real sun, which is at least true to our eyes, than those falsehoods, which deceive the mind through the eyes. Still, because I thought they were You, I fed on them. I did not eat eagerly, for You did not taste in my mouth as You really are, since You were not those empty inventions; and I was not nourished by them, but rather drained. Food in dreams is very like the food of people who are awake, yet sleepers are not nourished by it, because they are asleep. But those fantasies were not like You in any way at all, as You have now told me, for they were bodily fantasies, false bodies. These true bodies that we see with our fleshly sight, whether in the heavens or on earth, are far more certain than they are. The beasts and birds see these things as well as we do, and they are more certain than when we imagine them. And again, we imagine them with more certainty than we use them to guess at other, larger and infinite bodies that do not exist at all. Such empty husks were what I was fed on then, and I was not fed. But You, my soul's Love, for whom I faint so that I may become strong, are neither those bodies we see, even in heaven, nor those we do not see there; for You created them, and You do not count them among Your highest works. How far, then, You are from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies that do not exist at all! The images of bodies that do exist are far more certain than they are, and the bodies themselves more certain still; yet You are not those bodies. Nor are You the soul, which is the life of bodies, and so the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies are. But You are the life of souls, the life of lives, living by Yourself, and You do not change, O life of my soul.

Where were You for me then, and how far away? I was indeed wandering far from You, shut out even from the husks of the swine that I was feeding with husks. For how much better are the tales of the poets and grammarians than these traps! Verses and poems and "Medea flying" are certainly more useful than these men's five elements, dressed up in various colors to match the five caves of darkness, which do not exist at all and yet kill the one who believes in them. For verses and poems I can turn into real nourishment; and as for "Medea flying," though I sang about it, I did not claim it was true, and though I heard it sung, I did not believe it. But those other things I did believe. Woe, woe! By what steps I was led down into the depths of hell, toiling and feverish for lack of truth, because I was seeking You, my God (I confess it to You, who had mercy on me before I was yet confessing), not by the understanding of the mind, by which You willed me to be above the beasts, but by the sense of the flesh. But You were more inward to me than my innermost self, and higher than my highest. I stumbled upon that bold woman who has no sense, the one pictured in Solomon's riddle, sitting at her door and saying, Eat gladly the bread of secrecy, and drink the stolen waters, which are sweet. She seduced me, because she found my soul living outside itself, in the eye of my flesh, and chewing over the kind of food I had swallowed through that eye.

For I knew nothing else, nothing that truly is; and I was pushed, as if by some cleverness of mind, into siding with foolish deceivers when they asked me, "Where does evil come from?" and "Is God confined within a bodily shape, and does He have hair and nails?" and "Should those be considered righteous who had many wives at the same time, and killed people, and sacrificed animals?" In my ignorance these questions greatly troubled me, and while I was moving away from the truth I thought I was heading toward it. For I did not yet know that evil is nothing but a privation of good, until finally a thing ceases to exist altogether. How could I have seen that, when the sight of my eyes reached no further than bodies, and the sight of my mind no further than a phantasm? I did not know that God is a Spirit, not something with limbs stretched out in length and breadth, or whose being is bulk. For every bulk is smaller in a part than in its whole; and if it is infinite, it is smaller in any part marked out by a certain space than in its infinity, and so it is not wholly present everywhere, as a Spirit is, as God is. And what it is in us by which we are like God, and by which we are rightly said to be made in the image of God, I did not know at all.

Nor did I know that true inner righteousness which does not judge by custom but by the perfectly right law of Almighty God. By that law the customs of places and times were shaped to suit those places and times, while the law itself remains the same always and everywhere, not one thing in one place and another in another. By it Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, and Moses, and David, and all those praised by the mouth of God, were righteous. Yet they were judged unrighteous by foolish people who judge by merely human standards and measure the morals of the whole human race by the small measure of their own habits. It is as if someone in an armory, not knowing what was made for which part of the body, tried to cover his head with leg armor, or to put a helmet on his foot, and then complained that they did not fit. Or as if, on a day when public business was suspended from noon onward, someone grew angry at not being allowed to keep his shop open in the afternoon, because he had been allowed to in the morning.
