Or as if, in a single house, he saw some servant handling something that the one who serves the cups was not permitted to touch, or something being done out of doors that was forbidden in the dining room, and was indignant that in one house and one household the same thing was not allowed everywhere and to everyone. Such are those who are upset to hear that something was once permitted to righteous men that is not permitted now; or that God, for reasons belonging to particular times, commanded one thing to those people and another to these, though both obeyed the same righteousness. And all the while they can see, in one man, and one day, and one house, that different things suit different parts, that something permitted a moment ago is not permitted an hour later, and that what is allowed or ordered in one corner is rightly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice, then, changeable or inconsistent? No; but the times over which it presides do not run evenly, because they are times. People, whose days on earth are few, cannot use their senses to connect the causes of earlier ages and other nations, which they have not experienced, with those they have experienced. Yet in one and the same body, or day, or household, they easily see what fits each part, each moment, each section and each person. So they take offense at the one and submit to the other.

These things I did not know then, nor did I notice them. They struck my eyes on every side, and I did not see them. I wrote verses, in which I was not free to put any foot anywhere I liked, but had to place them differently in different meters, and even within a single line could not use the same foot in every position. Yet the art by which I wrote did not have one principle here and another there; it held them all together at once. Even so, I did not see that the righteousness which good and holy men obeyed holds together at once, far more excellently and sublimely, all the things God commands, and varies in no part, even though at different times it does not prescribe everything at once but assigns and commands what is proper to each. And in my blindness I found fault with the holy Fathers, not only for the way they used present things as God commanded and inspired them, but also for the way they foretold things to come as God revealed them.

Can it ever, at any time or in any place, be unjust to love God with all one's heart, with all one's soul, and with all one's mind, and to love one's neighbor as oneself? So the shameful acts that are against nature must be hated and punished everywhere and always, such as those of the men of Sodom. If every nation committed them, all would be held guilty of the same crime under the law of God, which did not make human beings to use one another in that way. For the very fellowship that ought to exist between God and us is violated when that same nature of which He is the Author is polluted by perverted lust. But acts that offend against human customs are to be avoided according to the variety of those customs, so that an agreement a city or nation has made among its members, confirmed by custom or by law, may not be broken at the whim of anyone, whether citizen or foreigner. For any part that does not fit with its whole is ugly. But when God commands something against the custom or agreement of any people, even if it has never been done there before, it must be done; if it has been dropped, it must be restored; and if it was never established, it must now be established. For if a king may lawfully command, in the city he rules, something that no one before him, nor he himself, had ever commanded, and if obeying him is not against the good of that city (in fact, it would be against it not to obey, since it is a general agreement of human society to obey its rulers), how much more must we obey God without hesitation in everything He commands, the Ruler of all His creatures! For just as, among the authorities of human society, the greater authority is obeyed before the lesser, so God is obeyed above all.

It is the same with crimes of violence, where there is a desire to hurt, whether by insult or by injury. These are done either for revenge, as one enemy against another; or to gain some advantage that belongs to someone else, as the robber against the traveler; or to escape some evil, as against someone who is feared; or out of envy, as the less fortunate against the more fortunate, or as someone who has done well in some matter against a person he fears may become his equal, or resents already being his equal; or simply for the pleasure of another's pain, as with those who watch gladiators, or who laugh at and mock others. These are the heads of wickedness that sprout from the lust of the flesh, of the eye, or of power, whether one of them alone, or two together, or all three at once. And so people live badly, against the three and the seven, that psaltery of ten strings, Your Ten Commandments, O God most high and most sweet. But what shameful acts can there be against You, who cannot be defiled? Or what acts of violence against You, who cannot be harmed? Yet You punish what people commit against themselves, because even when they sin against You, they act wickedly against their own souls, and iniquity lies to itself. It does this by corrupting and perverting their nature, which You made and ordered, or by using permitted things without restraint, or by burning for forbidden things, for that use which is against nature. Or they are found guilty of raging against You in heart and word, kicking against the goads. Or they break through the boundaries of human society and boldly delight in private alliances or divisions, depending on what has pleased or offended them. These things happen when You are abandoned, O Fountain of Life, who are the one and true Creator and Ruler of the universe, and when, out of self-willed pride, some single false thing is picked out from the whole and loved. So it is by humble devotion that we return to You. And You cleanse us of our evil habits, and are merciful to the sins of those who confess, and hear the groaning of the prisoners, and free us from the chains we have made for ourselves, provided that we no longer raise against You the horns of a false freedom, losing everything through greed for more, by loving our own private good more than You, the Good of all.

Among these shameful acts, these crimes of violence and all these many sins, there are also the sins of people who are, on the whole, making progress. Those who judge rightly condemn these sins by the standard of perfection, yet praise the people themselves in hope of the harvest to come, as with the green blade of growing corn. And there are some acts that look like shameful acts or crimes of violence and yet are not sins, because they offend neither You, our Lord God, nor human society. This happens, for example, when things suited to a particular time are acquired for the needs of life, and we cannot tell whether it was done out of a lust for possessing; or when wrongs are punished by lawful authority for the sake of correction, and we cannot tell whether it was done out of a lust for hurting. So many actions that people disapprove of are approved by Your testimony, and many that people praise are condemned with You as witness, because the outward look of the deed, the mind of the one who does it, and the hidden needs of the moment often differ. But when You suddenly command something unusual and unforeseen, even something You once forbade, and for the time being keep the reason for Your command hidden, and even if it goes against the agreement of some human society, who can doubt that it must be done, since only that human society is just which serves You? But blessed are those who know that You have commanded it! For all things were done by Your servants either to show something needed for the present, or to foretell things to come.

Knowing nothing of this, I mocked those holy servants and prophets of Yours. And what did I achieve by mocking them, except to be mocked by You? Little by little, without noticing, I was led on into such nonsense as believing that a fig weeps when it is picked, and that the tree, its mother, sheds milky tears. Yet if some Manichaean saint ate that fig (picked, of course, by someone else's guilt, not his own), it would be mixed into his insides, and he would breathe angels out of it; indeed, particles of God would burst out of him with every sigh and belch as he prayed. Those particles of the most high and true God would have stayed bound up in that fig, unless they had been set free by the teeth and belly of some "Elect" saint! And I, wretched as I was, believed that more mercy should be shown to the fruits of the earth than to human beings, for whose sake they were made. For if someone who was hungry, and not a Manichaean, asked for some, the mouthful given to him would seem, as it were, condemned to capital punishment.

And You reached out Your hand from above and drew my soul out of that deep darkness, while my mother, Your faithful one, wept to You for me more than mothers weep over the bodily deaths of their children. For by the faith and the spirit she had from You, she saw the death in which I lay; and You heard her, O Lord. You heard her and did not despise her tears when they poured down and watered the ground beneath her eyes in every place where she prayed; yes, You heard her. For where else did that dream come from by which You comforted her, so that she agreed to live with me and eat at the same table in the house? She had begun to refuse this, turning away from and detesting the blasphemies of my error. For she saw herself standing on a kind of wooden rule, and a radiant young man coming toward her, cheerful and smiling at her, while she was grieving and worn out with grief. He asked her the reasons for her sorrow and her daily tears (in order to teach, as such beings usually do, not to learn), and she answered that she was mourning my ruin. Then he told her to set her mind at rest, and urged her to look closely and see "that where she was, there I was too." And when she looked, she saw me standing beside her on the same rule. Where did this come from, if not from the fact that Your ears were turned toward her heart? O You, the Good and all-powerful, who care for each one of us as though You cared for that one alone, and for all as though each were the only one!

And where did this come from too? When she had told me about this vision, and I tried to twist it to mean "that she should rather not despair of one day being what I was," she replied at once, without any hesitation: "No. I was not told, 'Where he is, there you are too,' but, 'Where you are, there he is too.'" I confess to You, O Lord, as far as I can remember (and I have often spoken of this), that Your answer through my mother when she was awake moved me even then more than the dream itself. She was not thrown off by the plausibility of my false interpretation, and she saw so quickly what there was to see, which I certainly had not seen before she said it. And it was by that dream that a joy for this holy woman, to be fulfilled so long afterward, was foretold so long beforehand, to console her in her present distress. For almost nine years followed, in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and in the darkness of falsehood, often trying to rise but being dashed down all the harder. All that time that chaste, devout and sober widow, the kind You love, now more cheerful in hope but no less earnest in her weeping and mourning, never stopped, at every hour of her prayers, lamenting over me to You. And her prayers entered Your presence; yet You still let me be tangled and tangled again in that darkness.

Meanwhile You gave her another answer, which I remember. For I pass over much, hurrying on to the things that press me more urgently to confess to You, and much I do not remember. You gave her, then, another answer through a priest of Yours, a certain bishop brought up in Your Church and well trained in Your books. When this woman begged him to be so kind as to talk with me, refute my errors, unteach me what was bad and teach me what was good (for he used to do this when he happened to find people suited to receive it), he refused. That was wise of him, as I later came to see. For he answered that I was still unteachable, being puffed up with the novelty of that heresy, and that I had already unsettled a number of untrained people with tricky little questions, as she herself had told him. "But leave him alone for a while," he said. "Just pray to God for him. By reading he will find out for himself what that error is, and how great its impiety." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a little boy, had been handed over to the Manichees by his misled mother, and had not only read almost all their books but had even copied them out many times; and how it had become clear to him, without anyone arguing with him or convincing him, how much that sect ought to be avoided; and so he had avoided it. When he had said this and she still would not be satisfied, but pressed him harder, pleading with him and weeping many tears that he would see me and talk with me, he became a little irritated with her persistence and said, "Go now, and God bless you; it is impossible that the son of these tears should perish." She often recalled in her conversations with me that she had taken this answer as if it had sounded from heaven.

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: For this stretch of nine years, from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth, we lived led astray and leading others astray, deceived and deceiving, in all kinds of desires: openly, through the studies they call liberal; secretly, under the false name of religion; proud in one place, superstitious in another, empty everywhere. On one side we chased the hollowness of popular fame, all the way down to applause in the theater, prizes for poems, contests for garlands of grass, the nonsense of public shows, and unbridled desires. On the other side, wanting to be cleansed of these filthy things, we carried food to those who were called "elect" and "holy," so that out of it, in the workshop of their stomachs, they might forge for us angels and gods through whom we would be cleansed. These were the things I pursued and practiced with my friends, who were deceived through me and along with me. Let the arrogant mock me, and those who have not yet been struck down and crushed by You, O my God, for their soul's health; but I will still confess my own shame to You, in Your praise. Bear with me, I beg You, and give me grace to go back over, in my present memory, the winding paths of my past wanderings, and to offer You the sacrifice of thanksgiving. For what am I to myself without You, but a guide leading myself over a cliff? Or what am I, even at my best, but an infant sucking the milk You give, and feeding on You, the food that does not perish? And what kind of man is any man, since he is only a man? Let the strong and the mighty laugh at us now; but let us, the poor and needy, confess to You.

In those years I taught rhetoric, and, overcome by greed, I sold a talking skill designed to overcome others. Yet I preferred, Lord, as You know, to have good students, as they are usually reckoned, and without any trickery I taught them tricks: not to be used against the life of an innocent person, though sometimes to save the life of a guilty one. And You, O God, saw me from far off, stumbling on that slippery path, and through all the smoke giving off a few sparks of good faith, which I showed in my teaching of those who loved vanity and sought after lies, while I was their companion. In those years I had one woman, not joined to me in what is called lawful marriage, but one whom my restless passion, lacking all good sense, had tracked down; yet she was only one, and I kept faith with her bed. With her I learned from my own experience what a difference there is between the self-restraint of the marriage covenant, entered into for the sake of having children, and the bargain of a lustful love, in which children are born against their parents' wishes, although once they are born they compel their parents to love them.

I also remember that when I had decided to compete for a prize for theatrical verse, some soothsayer sent to ask me what fee I would pay him to make me win. But I, loathing and detesting those foul rites, answered that even if the garland were made of undying gold, I would not allow a fly to be killed to win it for me. For he was going to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and with those offerings he seemed about to invite the demons to take my side. But I rejected this evil, too, not out of any pure love for You, O God of my heart; for I did not know how to love You, since I did not know how to think of anything beyond bodily brightness. And does not a soul that sighs after such fictions commit fornication against You, put its trust in false things, and feed the wind? Yet, of course, I would not have sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf, while I myself was offering myself to them through that superstition. For what else is feeding the wind but feeding them, that is, by going astray, becoming their delight and their laughingstock?

So I kept consulting, without any hesitation, those impostors called mathematicians, because they seemed to use no sacrifice and to direct no prayers to any spirit for the sake of their divinations. Even so, true Christian piety consistently rejects and condemns that art. For it is good to confess to You and to say, Have mercy on me, heal my soul, for I have sinned against You; and not to abuse Your mercy as license to sin, but to remember the Lord's words: Behold, you are made whole; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you. They try to destroy all this healthy counsel when they say, "The cause of your sin is fixed in the heavens and cannot be avoided," and "Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars." The point, of course, is that man, who is flesh and blood and proud corruption, should be blameless, while the Creator and Ordainer of heaven and the stars should bear the blame. And who is He but our God, the very sweetness and source of righteousness, You who will render to every man according to his works, and who will not despise a broken and contrite heart?

There was at that time a shrewd man, highly skilled in medicine and famous for it, who as proconsul had placed that contest garland with his own hand on my unhealthy head, though not as a physician. For that disease You alone cure, You who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. But did You fail me even through that old man, or stop healing my soul? I had become better acquainted with him, and I hung constantly and intently on his conversation, for though it was plain in its words, it was lively, pleasant and serious in its thought. When he learned from our talks that I was devoted to the books of the horoscope-casters, he advised me, kindly and like a father, to throw them away and not to waste on such empty things the care and effort that useful matters require. He told me that in his early years he had studied that art with the intention of making it the profession he would live by, and that since he understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood these writings too. Yet he had later given them up and taken to medicine for no other reason than that he had found them utterly false, and as a serious man he would not earn his living by deceiving people. "But you," he said, "have rhetoric to support yourself by in the world, so you pursue this fraud out of free choice, not out of need. All the more reason, then, for you to believe me about it, since I worked to learn it so thoroughly that I meant to live by it alone." When I asked him what, then, caused many true things to be foretold by it, he answered as best he could that it was the force of chance, spread everywhere throughout the order of nature. For, he said, if someone happens to consult the pages of a poet who was singing and thinking about something entirely different, a verse often comes out that fits the matter at hand astonishingly well. So it was no wonder if, from a human soul unaware of what was happening within it, some higher impulse drew out an answer, by chance and not by art, that matched the affairs and actions of the person asking.

This much, then, You provided for me, either from him or through him, and You traced in my memory what I would later investigate for myself. But at that time neither he nor my dearest Nebridius, a young man truly good and truly chaste, who laughed at the whole business of divination, could persuade me to throw these things aside. The authority of the writers carried more weight with me, and I had not yet found the kind of sure proof I was looking for, one that would show me beyond all doubt that the true things said by those who were consulted came from luck or chance, and not from the art of reading the stars.

In those years, when I first began to teach in the town where I was born, I had gained a friend who, through our shared studies, became far too dear to me. He was my own age, and like me he was in the first bloom of youth. He had grown up with me as a boy, and we had gone to school together and played together. But he was not yet my friend in the way he later became, and even then not in the way true friendship is; for friendship cannot be true unless You bind it together between those who cling to You, through that love which is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit who is given to us. Still, it was all too sweet, ripened by the heat of our common studies. For I had also turned him away from the true faith, which as a young man he did not hold genuinely or deeply, toward those superstitious and destructive fables for which my mother wept over me. Now this man went astray in mind along with me, and my soul could not be without him. But look: You were close behind Your runaways, at once God of vengeance and Fountain of mercies, turning us to Yourself in wonderful ways. You took that man out of this life when he had barely completed one year of friendship with me, a friendship sweeter to me than all the sweetness of that life of mine.

Who can list all Your praises, even those he has experienced in his own single self? What did You do then, my God, and how unsearchable is the abyss of Your judgments? For he was struggling with a fever and lay for a long time unconscious in a deathly sweat; and when his recovery was despaired of, he was baptized without knowing it. I paid little attention to this, assuming that his soul would keep what it had received from me rather than what was being done to his unconscious body. But it turned out quite otherwise, for he revived and was restored to health. At once, as soon as I could speak with him (and I could as soon as he could, since I never left his side and we depended on each other far too much), I tried to make fun of that baptism in front of him, expecting him to laugh at it with me, since he had received it when he was completely absent in mind and senses; but he had by now learned that he had received it. Yet he recoiled from me as if I were an enemy, and with a startling and sudden frankness he warned me that if I wanted to remain his friend, I must stop saying such things to him. I was stunned and shaken, and I held back all my feelings until he should get well and be strong enough in health for me to deal with him as I wished. But he was snatched away from my madness, so that he might be kept safe with You for my comfort. A few days later, while I was away, the fever returned and he died.

With this grief my heart was plunged into darkness, and whatever I looked at was death. My home town became a torment to me, and my father's house a strange misery; and everything I had shared with him turned, without him, into a savage torture. My eyes looked for him everywhere, and he was not given back to them. I hated every place because he was not in it, and no place could say to me any longer, "Look, he is coming," as it could when he was alive but away. I had become a great puzzle to myself, and I kept asking my soul why she was so sad and why she troubled me so deeply; but she did not know how to answer me. And if I said, Hope in God, she quite rightly did not obey me, because the dearest friend she had lost was, as a man, both more real and better than the phantom she was told to hope in. Only weeping was sweet to me, and it had taken my friend's place in my heart's delight.

And now, Lord, those things have passed, and time has softened my wound. May I hear from You, who are Truth, and bring the ear of my heart close to Your mouth, so that You may tell me why weeping is sweet to the wretched? Or have You, though You are present everywhere, cast our misery far away from You? You remain in Yourself, while we are tossed about in one trial after another. And yet, unless we wept into Your ears, nothing would be left of our hope. Where, then, does it come from, this sweet fruit plucked from the bitterness of life: groaning, weeping, sighing and lamenting? Is it sweet because we hope that You hear us? That is true of prayers, because in them there is a longing to reach You. But is it true of grief for something lost, and of the mourning that covered me then? For I did not hope that he would come back to life, nor did I ask for this with my tears; I simply grieved and wept. I was wretched, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping in fact a bitter thing, which delights us because we are sick of the things we used to enjoy and now shrink from them?

But why am I saying these things? This is not the time for asking questions, but for confessing to You. I was wretched, and every mind is wretched that is chained by love to mortal things. It is torn apart when it loses them, and then it feels the wretchedness it was already in even before it lost them. That is how I was at that time. I wept most bitterly, and I found rest in bitterness. I was so wretched that I held that wretched life itself dearer than my friend. For although I wanted to change it, I would have been even less willing to lose it than to lose him. Indeed, I do not know whether I would have given it up even for him, as the story goes (if it is not invented) of Orestes and Pylades, who were willing to die for each other or together, since not living together was worse to them than death. But in me some feeling had arisen that was quite the opposite of this: I was heavily weary of living, and at the same time afraid of dying. I believe that the more I loved him, the more I hated and feared death, which had taken him from me, as though it were my cruelest enemy; and I thought it would suddenly devour all people, since it had been able to take him. That is exactly how I was, I remember. Look at my heart, O my God, look inside it; see, for I remember, O my Hope, You who cleanse me from the uncleanness of such feelings, directing my eyes toward You and pulling my feet out of the snare. For I was amazed that other mortals were alive, since he whom I had loved as if he would never die was dead; and I was more amazed still that I, who was his second self, could be alive when he was dead. Someone put it well when he called his friend "half of my soul." For I felt that my soul and his soul had been "one soul in two bodies," and so life was a horror to me, because I did not want to live as half a person. And that, perhaps, is why I was afraid to die: so that he whom I had loved so much would not die completely.

What madness, not to know how to love human beings as human beings! What a foolish man, to bear the human lot with so little restraint! That is what I was then. So I raged, sighed, wept and was thrown into turmoil, with no rest and no counsel. I was carrying around a soul cut to pieces and bleeding, a soul that could not bear being carried by me, and I could find nowhere to set it down. It found no rest in pleasant groves, not in games and songs, not in sweet-scented places, not in lavish banquets, not in the pleasures of the bedroom and the bed, and finally not in books and poetry either. Everything filled me with horror, even the light itself; whatever was not what he was seemed vile and hateful to me, except groaning and tears, for in those alone I found a little rest. But whenever my soul was drawn away from them, a huge burden of misery weighed me down. I knew it ought to have been lifted up to You, Lord, to be lightened and healed; but I neither wanted to nor was able to, all the more because, when I thought of You, You were not anything solid or firm to me. For it was not You, but an empty phantom, and my error was my God. If I tried to set my soul down there to rest, it slipped through the emptiness and came crashing down on me again, and I remained to myself an unhappy place where I could neither stay nor get away. For where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I flee from myself? Where would I not follow myself? And yet I fled from my home town, since my eyes would look for him less in places where they were not used to seeing him. And so from the town of Thagaste I came to Carthage.

Time does not stand idle, nor does it roll uselessly past our senses; it works wonders in the mind. Look how the days came and went, one after another, and by coming and going they planted in me new hopes and new memories, and little by little they patched me up again with the old kinds of pleasure, before which that grief of mine gave way. And yet in its place came, not other griefs exactly, but the causes of other griefs. For why had that grief pierced me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand by loving a man who would die as though he would never die? What mainly restored and revived me was the comfort of other friends, with whom I loved what I loved instead of You; and this was one enormous fable and one long lie, and by its adulterous rubbing our minds, which had itching ears, were being corrupted. But that fable did not die for me whenever one of my friends died. There were other things in them that captured my mind more: talking and laughing together, doing each other kindnesses in turn, reading sweetly written books together, joking together and being serious together, disagreeing now and then without bad feeling, as a man might with himself, and by those very rare disagreements seasoning our far more frequent agreements; teaching each other something or learning from each other; missing the absent with an ache and welcoming them back with joy. These signs and others like them, coming from the hearts of those who love and are loved in return, and showing through the face, the tongue, the eyes and a thousand delightful gestures, were like kindling that set our souls ablaze together and made one out of many.

This is what we love in friends, and we love it so much that a person's conscience accuses itself if he does not love the one who loves him, or does not return the love of the one who loves him, seeking nothing from the other's person except signs of goodwill. This is where that mourning comes from when someone dies, the darkness of sorrows, the heart soaked in tears, all sweetness turned into bitterness; and, from the lost life of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves You, and his friend in You, and his enemy for Your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, to whom all are dear in the One who cannot be lost. And who is this but our God, the God who made heaven and earth and fills them, because by filling them He made them? No one loses You except the one who leaves You. And the one who leaves You, where does he go, or where does he flee, except from You at peace to You angered? For where does he not find Your law in his own punishment? And Your law is truth, and truth is You.

Turn us, O God of hosts, show us Your face, and we shall be saved. For wherever the soul of man turns, except toward You, it is pinned fast to sorrows, even if it is pinned to beautiful things outside You and outside itself. And yet those things would be nothing at all if they were not from You. They rise and they set. By rising they begin, as it were, to exist; they grow in order to be made complete; and once complete, they grow old and die. Not all of them grow old, but all of them die. So when they rise and strive to exist, the faster they grow toward being, the more they hurry toward not being. That is the measure set for them. This much You have given them, because they are parts of things that do not all exist at once, but by passing away and following one another they together make up the whole of which they are parts. Our speech, too, is completed in just this way, through sounding signs; for a sentence will not be whole unless each word, once it has sounded its part, passes away so that another can follow. Out of all these things let my soul praise You, O God, Creator of all; but let it not be stuck fast to them by the glue of love through the senses of the body. For they go where they were going, toward not being, and they tear the soul apart with deadly longings, because the soul itself wants to exist and loves to rest in the things it loves. But in these things there is no place to rest, because they do not stay; they run away. And who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? Who can grasp them even when they are right at hand? For the sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh; that is its limit. It is enough for the other purpose it was made for, but it is not enough to hold things fast as they run their course from their appointed beginning to their appointed end. For in Your Word, by whom they are created, they hear their sentence: "From here, and this far."

Do not be foolish, my soul, and do not let the ear of your heart go deaf with the uproar of your foolishness. You too, listen. The Word Himself calls you to come back, and there is the place of undisturbed rest, where love is not abandoned unless it abandons first. See how these things pass away so that others may take their place, and so this lower universe is made complete in all its parts. But do I go away anywhere? says the Word of God. Make your dwelling there; entrust to it whatever you have from there, my soul, at least now that you are worn out with deceptions. Entrust to Truth whatever you have from the Truth, and you will lose nothing. What has decayed in you will flower again, all your sicknesses will be healed, and your perishing parts will be reshaped, renewed and bound closely to you. They will not drag you down to where they themselves are sinking, but will stand firm with you and remain forever before God, who stands firm and remains forever.

Why, then, turned the wrong way, do you follow your flesh? Let it follow you instead, once you have turned back. Whatever you perceive through it is only a part, and you do not know the whole of which these are parts; and yet they delight you. But if the sense of your flesh were capable of grasping the whole, and had not itself, as your punishment, been justly limited to a part of the universe, you would want whatever exists in the present moment to pass on, so that the whole might please you more. For you hear what we say through that same sense of the flesh, and you certainly do not want the syllables to stand still; you want them to fly past, so that others may come and you may hear the whole. So it always is when any single thing is made up of many parts, not all of which exist at the same time: all of them together would delight us more than each one alone, if all of them could be perceived together. But far better than these is He who made all things, and He is our God; and He does not pass away, because nothing takes His place.

If bodies please you, praise God for them, and turn your love back toward their Maker, so that in the things that please you, you do not displease Him. If souls please you, let them be loved in God; for they too are changeable, but in Him they are made firm and steady; otherwise they would pass on and pass away. So let them be loved in Him. Carry with you to Him as many souls as you can, and say to them: "Let us love Him, let us love Him. He made these things, and He is not far away. For He did not make them and then leave; they are from Him and in Him. Look, there He is, wherever truth is savored. He is within the very heart, but the heart has wandered away from Him. Return to your heart, you transgressors, and cling to Him who made you. Stand with Him, and you will stand firm. Rest in Him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, along these rough roads? Where are you going? The good you love comes from Him; but it is good and pleasant only as it relates to Him, and it will rightly become bitter, because whatever comes from Him is wrongly loved if He is abandoned for it. Why do you still keep on walking these hard and wearisome roads? There is no rest where you are looking for it. Seek what you are seeking, but it is not where you are seeking it. You are seeking a blessed life in the land of death; it is not there. For how can there be a blessed life where there is not even life?

"But our Life Himself came down here, and carried our death, and killed it out of the abundance of His own life. And He thundered, calling out to us to return from here to Him, into that hidden place from which He came out to us: first into the Virgin's womb, where the human creation, mortal flesh, was wedded to Him, so that it would not be mortal forever; and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of His chamber, He rejoiced like a giant to run His course. For He did not delay, but ran, calling out by His words, deeds, death, life, descent and ascension, crying out to us to return to Him. And He withdrew from our eyes, so that we might return to our heart and find Him there. For He went away, and look, He is here. He did not want to stay with us long, and yet He did not leave us; for He went back to the place He never left, because the world was made by Him. And He was in this world, and He came into this world to save sinners. To Him my soul confesses, and He heals it, for it has sinned against Him. O sons of men, how long will you be so heavy of heart? Even now, after Life has come down to you, will you not rise up and live? But where can you rise to, when you are already on high and have set your mouth against the heavens? Come down, so that you may rise, and rise to God. For you fell by rising up against Him." Tell them this, so that they may weep in the valley of tears, and so carry them with you to God; for you are saying these things to them from His Spirit, if you say them burning with the fire of love.

I did not know these things then. I loved these lower beauties and was sinking into the depths, and I used to say to my friends: "Do we love anything except what is beautiful? What, then, is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it that draws us and attaches us to the things we love? For unless there were grace and beauty in them, they could never attract us to themselves." And I noticed and saw that in bodies themselves there is one kind of beauty that comes from their being a kind of whole, and another that comes from fitting well with something else, as a part of the body fits its whole, or a shoe fits a foot, and so on. This reflection welled up in my mind from my inmost heart, and I wrote books "On the Beautiful and the Fitting," two or three, I think. You know, O Lord, for it has slipped my memory. I no longer have them; they have strayed away from me somehow.

But what moved me, O Lord my God, to dedicate those books to Hierius, an orator in the city of Rome? I did not know him by sight, but I loved the man for his reputation for learning, which was brilliant, and I had heard some of his words, and they pleased me. But he pleased me more because he pleased others, who praised him to the skies, astonished that a Syrian, first trained in Greek eloquence, had afterward become a marvelous speaker in Latin as well, and was deeply learned in everything that belongs to the pursuit of wisdom. A man is praised, and though absent, he is loved. Does that love pass from the mouth of the one who praises into the heart of the one who hears? Not at all. Rather, one person is set on fire by another who loves. For this is why the one who is praised comes to be loved: when we believe he is being extolled by someone whose heart is not deceitful, that is, when the one praising him loves him.

That was how I loved people then: by human judgment, not by Yours, O my God, in whom no one is deceived. But still, why did I not love him the way people love a famous charioteer, or a fighter of wild beasts known far and wide through the crowd's enthusiasm, but in a very different and more serious way, the way I would have wanted to be praised myself? For I would not have wanted to be praised and loved as actors are, although I myself praised and loved them; I would rather have stayed unknown than be known in that way, and even be hated rather than loved in that way. Where in one soul are these weights of such various and different loves distributed? What is it that I love in another person, which, unless I hated it, I would not reject and push away from myself, since each of us is equally a man? For it does not follow that, just as a good horse is loved by someone who would not want to be that horse even if he could, the same can be said of an actor, who shares our nature. Do I then love in a man what I hate to be, though I am a man? Man himself is a great deep, whose very hairs You number, O Lord, and they do not fall to the ground without You. And yet the hairs of his head are easier to count than his feelings and the stirrings of his heart.

But that orator was the kind of man I loved in such a way that I wanted to be like him myself. I was wandering astray, puffed up with pride, and tossed about by every wind, and yet, very secretly, I was being steered by You. And how do I know, and how can I confess to You with certainty, that I had loved him more because of the love of those who praised him than because of the things for which he was praised? Because if those very same people had not praised him but had found fault with him, and had told the very same things about him with blame and contempt, I would never have been set on fire and stirred up about him. Yet the things themselves would not have been different, nor would the man himself; only the feelings of those telling about him. See where the weak soul lies, when it does not yet cling to the solidity of truth! As the breezes of tongues blow from the chests of those who hold opinions, so it is carried along and turned about, twisted this way and back again; the light is clouded over for it, and the truth is not seen. And yet, look, it is right in front of us. It mattered a great deal to me that my writing and my studies should become known to that man. If he approved of them, I would be all the more on fire; but if he disapproved, my vain heart, empty of Your solidity, would have been wounded. And yet that "beautiful and fitting," on which I had written to him, I gladly turned over in my mind and held before my eyes to contemplate, and I admired it even with no one to join me in praising it.

But I did not yet see the hinge on which so great a matter turns in Your wisdom, O Almighty, who alone do wonders. My mind moved among bodily forms. I defined and distinguished the "beautiful" as what is so in itself, and the "fitting" as what is becoming because it suits something else, and I supported this with bodily examples. Then I turned to the nature of the mind, but the false idea I held about spiritual things would not let me see the truth. The very force of truth flashed into my eyes, and yet I turned my trembling mind away from what is incorporeal toward outlines, colors and swelling sizes; and because I could not see these in the mind, I thought I could not see my mind. And since in virtue I loved peace, and in vice I hated discord, I noticed a kind of unity in the first and a kind of division in the second. In that unity I thought the rational mind, and the nature of truth and of the highest good, consisted. But in this division, wretched as I was, I imagined there was some unknown substance of irrational life, and the nature of the highest evil, which was not only a substance but truly a life, and yet did not come from You, O my God, from whom all things come. The first I called a Monad, as though it were a mind without sex; the second a Dyad: anger in deeds of violence, lust in shameful acts. I did not know what I was talking about. For I had not known or learned that evil is not a substance at all, and that our own mind is not the highest and unchangeable good.

For just as deeds of violence arise when that movement of the soul from which impulse springs is corrupted, and throws itself about insolently and wildly; and acts of lust arise when that affection of the soul by which fleshly pleasures are drunk in is out of control; so errors and false opinions defile one's life when the rational mind itself is corrupted. That was how it was in me then, for I did not know that the mind must be lit by another light in order to share in truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For You will light my lamp, O Lord my God; You will lighten my darkness; and of Your fullness we have all received. For You are the true light that lights every man who comes into the world, for in You there is no variableness, nor shadow of change.

But I strained toward You and was pushed back from You, so that I might taste death; for You resist the proud. And what could be prouder than for me, in a strange madness, to claim that I was by nature what You are? For although I was changeable, and this much was plain to me, since my very desire to become wise was a wish to go from worse to better, I still preferred to think that You were changeable rather than that I was not what You are. So I was pushed back, and You resisted my puffed-up, stiff neck. I kept picturing bodily forms; flesh myself, I accused the flesh; and, a wind that passes away, I did not return to You, but went on and on toward things that have no being, not in You, not in me, and not in the body. Nor were they created for me by Your truth; they were made up by my vanity out of bodily things. And I used to say to Your faithful little ones, my fellow citizens, from whom I was exiled without knowing it, I used to say to them, chattering and foolish, "Why, then, does the soul that God made go wrong?" But I would not let anyone ask me, "Why, then, does God go wrong?" And I argued that Your unchangeable substance went wrong under compulsion, rather than admit that my changeable substance had strayed of its own accord and was now in error as its punishment.

I was about twenty-six or twenty-seven years old when I wrote those volumes, turning over within me bodily fictions that clattered in the ears of my heart. Those ears I was straining, O sweet Truth, toward Your inward melody, as I thought about the "beautiful and fitting." I longed to stand and listen to You and to rejoice greatly at the Bridegroom's voice, but I could not, because I was dragged outside by the voices of my own errors, and by the weight of my own pride I was sinking into the lowest pit. For You did not make me hear joy and gladness, nor did the bones rejoice, since they had not yet been humbled.

And what good did it do me that, when I was barely twenty years old, a work of Aristotle that they call the Ten Categories came into my hands, and I read it and understood it on my own? I used to hang on its very name, as on something great and divine, whenever my teacher of rhetoric at Carthage, and others who were thought learned, mouthed it with cheeks puffed out in pride. When I compared notes with others who said they had barely understood it with the help of very learned teachers, who not only explained it aloud but drew many diagrams in the sand, they could tell me nothing about it beyond what I had already learned by reading it alone. And the book seemed to me to speak quite clearly about substances, such as "man," and about what belongs to them: a man's shape, what sort it is; his height, how many feet tall; his relationships, whose brother he is; where he is placed, or when he was born; whether he is standing or sitting, whether he has shoes on or is armed; whether he is doing something or having something done to him; and all the countless things that can be found under these nine categories, of which I have given some examples, or under the chief category of substance itself.

What good did this do me, when it actually harmed me? For I thought that absolutely everything that exists was contained in those ten categories, and so I tried to understand even Your wonderful and unchangeable Unity, O my God, as though You were also a subject of Your own greatness or beauty, so that these existed in You as in a subject, the way they do in a body. But You Yourself are Your greatness and Your beauty, whereas a body is not great or beautiful by the fact that it is a body, since even if it were less great or less beautiful, it would still be a body. What I thought about You was falsehood, not truth; it was the fictions of my misery, not the firm realities of Your blessedness. For You had commanded, and so it was being done in me, that the earth should bring forth briars and thorns for me, and that I should eat my bread in the sweat of my brow.

And what good did it do me that I, at that time the worthless slave of evil desires, read on my own and understood every book I could get hold of on the arts they call liberal? I took pleasure in them, but I did not know where whatever was true and certain in them came from. For I had my back to the light and my face toward the things that are lit up, so that my face, with which I saw the things lit up, was not itself lit. Whatever there was on the art of speaking and the art of reasoning, on the measurements of figures, on music and on numbers, I understood without much difficulty and with no one to teach me. You know this, O Lord my God, because both quickness of understanding and sharpness of discernment are Your gift. Yet I did not offer sacrifice to You from them. So they served not for my good use but rather for my ruin, because I worked so hard to keep so good a portion of my substance under my own control. I did not keep my strength for You, but went away from You into a far country, to squander it on harlot desires. For what good did a good thing do me when I did not use it well? I did not realize that those arts are very hard to understand even for studious and gifted people, until I tried to explain them to such people; and the one who excelled most among them was the one who followed my explanations not too slowly.

But what good did this do me, when I thought that You, O Lord God, the Truth, were a vast, bright body, and that I was a chip of that body? What utter perversity! But that is what I was. Nor do I blush, O my God, to confess to You Your mercies toward me and to call on You, I who did not blush then to proclaim my blasphemies to people and to bark against You. What good, then, did my agile mind do me in those studies, and all those knotty books I untangled without the help of any human teacher, when I was going so hideously wrong, with such sacrilegious shamefulness, in the teaching of piety? Or what great harm did a much slower mind do to Your little ones, since they did not go far away from You, so that in the nest of Your Church they could safely grow their feathers and strengthen the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? O Lord our God, let us hope in the shelter of Your wings; protect us and carry us. You will carry us when we are little, and You will carry us even to gray hairs; for our firmness is firmness only when it is You, but when it is our own, it is weakness. Our good lives always with You, and because we turned away from it, we are turned awry. Let us now return, O Lord, so that we may not be overturned, for our good lives with You without any flaw, and that good is You Yourself. Nor are we afraid that there will be no place to return to because we fell from it; for while we were away, our home did not fall: Your eternity.

chapters.title: Book 5
paragraphs: Accept the sacrifice of my confessions, offered by the hand of my tongue, which You formed and roused to confess Your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say, O Lord, who is like You? For a person who confesses to You does not inform You of what is going on inside him. A closed heart does not shut out Your eye, and human hardness of heart cannot push back Your hand: You melt it whenever You will, either in pity or in punishment, and there is nothing that can hide itself from Your heat. But let my soul praise You so that it may love You, and let it confess Your own mercies to You so that it may praise You. Your whole creation never ceases and is never silent in praising You: every spirit praises You with a voice turned toward You, and living things and material things praise You through the voice of those who contemplate them, so that our souls may rise out of their weariness toward You, leaning on the things You have made and passing beyond them to You, who made them so wonderfully; and there is refreshment and true strength.

Let the restless and the wicked go their way and run from You; You still see them, and You mark off the shadows. And look: the whole universe, with them in it, is beautiful, though they themselves are ugly. What harm have they done You? How have they brought disgrace on Your rule, which is just and whole from the heavens down to the lowest things of earth? Where did they run to when they ran from Your face? Or where is there a place You do not find them? No, they ran away so as not to see You seeing them, so that in their blindness they might stumble against You (for You abandon nothing You have made). They ran so that the unjust might stumble against You, I say, and be justly hurt, pulling away from Your gentleness, colliding with Your uprightness and falling onto their own roughness. The truth is, they do not know that You are everywhere, You whom no place contains, and that You alone are present even to those who go far away from You. So let them turn back and seek You, because You have not deserted Your creation the way they deserted their Creator. Let them turn back and seek You, and look: You are there, in their heart, in the heart of those who confess to You, who throw themselves on You and weep in Your lap after all their hard roads. Then You gently wipe away their tears, and they weep all the more and find joy in their weeping, because it is You, Lord, and not some human being of flesh and blood, but You, Lord, who made them, who now remake and comfort them. But where was I when I was looking for You? You were right in front of me, but I had gone away even from myself. I could not find myself, so how much less could I find You!

I want to set out in the sight of my God that twenty-ninth year of my life. At that time a certain bishop of the Manichees had come to Carthage, Faustus by name, a great snare of the Devil, and many people were entangled in him by the lure of his smooth speech. I did praise that smoothness, but I could still tell it apart from the truth of the things I was eager to learn. I was not so much looking at the dish his words were served in as at the knowledge this Faustus, so famous among them, was setting before me to eat. His reputation had already told me that he was highly expert in every respectable branch of learning and especially accomplished in the liberal arts. And since I had read a good deal of the philosophers and still held it in my memory, I compared some of their teachings with the long fables of the Manichees, and the philosophers' account seemed to me the more probable. Yet they were only able to go so far as to form a judgment about this lower world; its Lord they could by no means find. For You are great, O Lord, and You look upon the humble, but the proud You know from far away. You draw near only to the contrite in heart, and You are not found by the proud, not even if with their curious skill they could count the stars and the grains of sand, measure the regions of the sky and trace the paths of the planets.

For they investigate these things with the understanding and ingenuity You gave them, and they have discovered a great deal. Many years in advance they have predicted eclipses of those great lights, the sun and the moon: on what day, at what hour and to what extent they would happen. Their calculation did not fail them; it happened just as they predicted. They wrote down the rules they had worked out, and these are read to this day. From them others predict in what year, in what month of the year, on what day of the month, at what hour of the day and in what portion of its light the moon or the sun is to be eclipsed, and it will happen just as it is foretold. People who do not know this science marvel at these things and are amazed, and those who do know it exult and are puffed up. Through an ungodly pride they draw away from You and fall short of Your light; they foresee an eclipse of the sun that will come so long afterward, yet they do not see their own eclipse, which is happening now. For they do not ask in a religious spirit where they got the ingenuity with which they investigate these things. And when they find that You made them, they do not give themselves up to You so that You may preserve what You made. They do not sacrifice to You what they have made of themselves. They do not slaughter their own soaring thoughts, like the birds of the air, or their own diving curiosities, with which, like the fish of the sea, they roam the hidden paths of the deep, or their own self-indulgence, like the beasts of the field, so that You, Lord, a consuming fire, might burn up their dead cares and re-create them to live forever.

But they did not know the way, Your Word, through whom You made these things that they count, and the people who do the counting, and the sense by which they perceive what they count, and the mind from which they count; nor did they know that of Your wisdom there is no number. But the Only Begotten Himself has been made for us wisdom and righteousness and sanctification, and He was counted among us and paid tribute to Caesar. They did not know this way, by which they could come down from themselves to Him and through Him go up to Him. They did not know this way, and they thought themselves raised on high among the stars and shining; and look, they fell to the earth, and their foolish heart was darkened. They say many true things about the creature, but they do not seek the Truth, the Maker of the creature, in a spirit of piety, and so they do not find Him. Or if they do find Him, though they know Him to be God, they do not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but become futile in their thinking and declare themselves wise, claiming for themselves what is Yours. And through this, with the most perverse blindness, they go on to attribute to You what is their own, heaping lies on You who are the Truth, changing the glory of the incorruptible God into an image made like corruptible man, and birds, and four-footed beasts, and creeping things. They change Your truth into a lie, and they worship and serve the creature rather than the Creator.

Still, I kept hold of many true things these men had said about the creature itself, and I could see the reasoning behind them in their calculations, in the orderly succession of the seasons and in the visible evidence of the stars. I compared them with the sayings of Manichaeus, who in his raving had written at enormous length on these subjects. But I found in him no account of the solstices or the equinoxes or the eclipses of the great lights, nor of anything else of this kind that I had learned in the books of worldly philosophy. There, though, I was ordered to believe; and what I was told did not agree with what had been established by calculation and by my own eyes. It was quite the opposite.

O Lord God of truth, does anyone who knows these things please You simply because of that? Surely the person who knows all these things and does not know You is unhappy, while the person who knows You is happy, even if he does not know these things. And the one who knows both You and them is not happier because of them, but happy because of You alone, provided that, knowing You, he glorifies You as God and gives thanks, and does not become futile in his thinking. Think of a man who knows how to own a tree and thanks You for the use of it, even though he does not know how many cubits tall it is or how wide it spreads. He is better off than someone who can measure it and count all its branches, but neither owns it nor knows or loves its Creator. In the same way, a believer to whom this whole world of riches belongs, and who, as having nothing, yet possesses all things by clinging to You whom all things serve, is certainly in a better state, even if he does not know so much as the circuits of the Great Bear. It would be foolish to doubt that he is better off than one who can measure the heavens, count the stars and weigh the elements, yet neglects You, who have ordered all things in number, weight and measure.

But then, who asked this Manichaeus to write about these things too, when skill in them was no part of piety? For You have said to man, Behold, piety is wisdom. He might have been ignorant of that even if he had a perfect knowledge of these things; but since he did not know these things and yet had the utter impudence to teach them, he plainly could not have known piety. It is vanity to make a show of knowing these worldly things, even when one does know them; but to confess to You is piety. So this wanderer talked a great deal about these things for this very purpose: that when he was refuted by people who had truly learned them, it would become obvious what kind of understanding he had in other, more hidden matters. For he did not want to be thought little of; he tried to persuade people "that the Holy Spirit, the Comforter and Enricher of Your faithful, was personally present in him with full authority." So when he was caught teaching falsehoods about the sky and the stars and the movements of the sun and moon, even though these things have nothing to do with the teaching of religion, his sacrilegious presumption became plain enough. He was putting forward things he not only did not know but that were actually false, and doing it with such insane, prideful vanity that he tried to attribute them to himself as to a divine person.

When I hear some Christian brother who is ignorant of these things and mistaken about them, I can patiently watch such a man holding his opinion. I do not see how any ignorance about the position or nature of the bodily creation can harm him, as long as he does not believe anything unworthy of You, O Lord, Creator of all. But it does harm him if he imagines that it belongs to the very shape of the teaching of piety, and still insists too stubbornly on something he does not know. Yet even that kind of weakness, in the cradle of faith, is borne by our mother Charity, until the newborn grows up into a perfect man and can no longer be carried about by every wind of doctrine. But what about a man who dared to set himself up as teacher, source, guide and leader of all whom he could persuade, so that his followers thought they were following not an ordinary human being but Your Holy Spirit? Once he was proved to have taught anything false, who would not judge that such madness should be detested and utterly thrown out? But I had not yet clearly worked out whether the changes of longer and shorter days and nights, and of day and night itself, along with the eclipses of the great lights and whatever else of the sort I had read in other books, could be explained in a way consistent with his sayings. If somehow they could, it would still remain an open question for me whether it was so or not; but I could, because of his reputed holiness, rest my belief on his authority.

For nearly the whole of those nine years in which I had listened to the Manichees as a disciple, with a restless mind, I had been waiting for this Faustus to arrive, with a longing that was far too intense. The other members of the sect I happened to come across, when they could not answer the objections I raised about these matters, kept holding out to me the prospect of this Faustus's coming. Once he came and I could talk with him, they said, these difficulties, and any greater ones I might have, would be cleared up very easily and very fully. So when he did come, I found him a man of pleasant speech, who could talk fluently and in better language, but he was still saying exactly the same things they usually said. What good was the most elegant cup-bearer to my thirst for a more precious drink? My ears had already had their fill of such things. They did not seem any better to me because they were better said, nor true because they were eloquent, nor did the soul seem wise because the face was attractive and the language graceful. The people who had held him out to me were not good judges of things; so he seemed to them intelligent and wise simply because his speaking pleased them. I was aware, however, of another kind of people who are suspicious even of the truth and refuse to accept it if it is presented in polished and abundant speech. But You, my God, had already taught me in wonderful and hidden ways. I believe it was You who taught me, because it is the truth, and there is no other teacher of truth besides You, wherever and from whatever source it may shine on us. So I had already learned from You that nothing should seem true just because it is said eloquently, or false because the sounds coming from the lips are clumsy; and again, that nothing is true because it is expressed roughly, or false because the language is splendid. Rather, wisdom and folly are like wholesome and unwholesome food, and elaborate or plain words are like fine city dishes or rustic ones: either kind of food can be served on either kind of dish.

So the eagerness with which I had waited so long for that man was certainly delighted by his energy and feeling in debate, and by the fitting words that came so readily to him to clothe his ideas. I was delighted, and along with many others, and even more than they did, I praised him and spoke highly of him. It bothered me, though, that in the gathering of his listeners I was not allowed to put forward the questions that were troubling me and share them with him in a friendly exchange, giving and taking in conversation. When at last I could do so, I began, together with my friends, to claim his attention at a time when it was not unfitting for him to discuss things back and forth with me. I brought up some of the things that troubled me, and I discovered first of all that he was a man with no knowledge of the liberal arts except grammar, and even that only in an ordinary way. But he had read some of Tully's speeches, a very few books of Seneca, some of the poets, and whatever volumes of his own sect were written in Latin and in good style; and he had daily practice in speaking. From all this he had acquired a certain eloquence, which became all the more pleasing and seductive because it was controlled by a good mind and had a kind of natural charm. Is it not so, as I remember it, O Lord my God, judge of my conscience? My heart and my memory lie open before You, who were guiding me even then by the hidden secret of Your providence, and were already turning my shameful errors around to face me, so that I might see them and hate them.

For once it was clear enough that he was untrained in the arts in which I had thought he excelled, I began to lose hope that he could open up and resolve the problems that troubled me. He could, of course, have been ignorant of them and still hold the truth of piety, but only if he had not been a Manichee. Their books are full of endless fables about the sky and the stars and the sun and moon, and I no longer thought he could do what I very much wanted: to compare these things with the calculations I had read elsewhere and explain precisely whether the account given in the books of Manichaeus was the better one, or at least an equally good one. But when I put these things forward to be considered and discussed, he was modest enough not to dare to take up the burden. He knew that he did not know these things, and he was not ashamed to admit it. He was not one of those talkers, many of whom I had put up with, who tried to teach me these things and said nothing. This man had a heart which, though not right toward You, was still not altogether careless of itself. He was not wholly unaware of his own ignorance, and he did not want to rush into an argument and get himself trapped in a position from which he could neither get out nor easily retreat. Even for this I liked him more. For the moderation of a mind that admits the truth is more beautiful than the knowledge I was longing for; and that is how I found him in all the harder and subtler questions.

So my enthusiasm for the writings of Manichaeus was broken, and I lost hope even more in their other teachers, since the famous Faustus had turned out as he did on so many of the points that troubled me. I began instead to spend time with him on account of his own enthusiasm for literature, which he was keen on and which I was by then teaching to young men at Carthage as a teacher of rhetoric. I read with him either books he wanted to hear or ones I judged suited to a mind like his. But all the efforts by which I had meant to advance in that sect came completely to an end once I got to know that man. It was not that I cut myself off from them altogether; rather, finding nothing better, I had decided to be content for the time being with what I had somehow stumbled into, unless something more worth choosing should happen to dawn on me. So that Faustus, who was a snare of death to so many, had now begun, without wanting it or knowing it, to loosen the snare in which I was caught. For Your hands, my God, in the hidden depths of Your providence, did not abandon my soul. Out of my mother's heart's blood, through the tears she poured out day and night, a sacrifice was offered to You for me, and You dealt with me in wonderful ways. You did it, my God: for the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and He shall choose his way. Or how are we to obtain salvation except from Your hand, remaking what it made?

You were at work in me so that I would be persuaded to go to Rome and teach there instead the same subjects I was teaching at Carthage. I will not fail to confess to You how I was persuaded to do this, because here too the deepest recesses of Your wisdom and Your mercy, so very present to us, must be thought about and acknowledged. My reason for wanting to go to Rome was not that the friends who urged me to go promised me larger earnings and higher rank, although at that time even these things had a hold on my mind. My chief and almost only reason was that I had heard that young men studied more peacefully there and were kept in order by the restraint of a better-regulated discipline. They did not rush wildly and rudely whenever they liked into the classroom of a teacher whose students they were not, and they were not admitted at all unless he gave them permission. At Carthage, by contrast, the students have a disgraceful and uncontrolled license. They burst in shamelessly and, with an almost crazed look, throw into confusion the order that each teacher has set up for his pupils' progress. They commit many outrages with an astonishing dullness of mind, things that would be punished by law if custom did not protect them. That very custom shows them to be all the more wretched, since they now do as though it were allowed what by Your eternal law will never be allowed. And they think they do it without punishment, when in fact they are punished by the very blindness with which they do it, and suffer incomparably worse than what they inflict. So the behavior I refused to make my own when I was a student I was forced to put up with in others when I was a teacher; and that is why I was glad to go to a place where, as everyone who knew it told me, such things did not happen. But it was You, my refuge and my portion in the land of the living, who, so that I would change my earthly home for the salvation of my soul, applied goads to me at Carthage to tear me away from it, and held out attractions to me at Rome to draw me there. You did it through people who love a life that is really death, some of them doing insane things, the others promising empty ones; and to correct my steps You secretly made use of their perversity and my own. For those who disturbed my peace were blinded by a disgraceful frenzy, and those who invited me elsewhere had a taste only for earthly things. And I, who here hated a real misery, was there seeking a false happiness.

But why I was leaving one place and going to the other, You knew, O God, yet You did not reveal it either to me or to my mother. She bitterly grieved over my going and followed me all the way to the sea. But she clung to me with all her strength, determined either to call me back or to go with me, and I deceived her. I pretended that I had a friend I did not want to leave until he had a good wind to sail. So I lied to my mother, and such a mother, and got away. This too You have mercifully forgiven me, saving me, full as I was of detestable filth, from the waters of the sea to bring me to the water of Your grace. Once I was washed in it, the rivers flowing from my mother's eyes would be dried, the tears with which she watered the ground beneath her face every day for my sake. Still, since she refused to go back home without me, I barely managed to persuade her to stay that night in a place close to our ship, a shrine in memory of the blessed Cyprian. But that night I secretly set out, while she stayed behind, praying and weeping. And what was she asking of You, O Lord, with so many tears, except that You would not let me sail? But You, taking a deeper counsel and hearing the heart of her desire, did not grant what she was asking for then, so that You might make me what she was always asking for. The wind blew and filled our sails and took the shore out of our sight. The next morning she was there on that shore, wild with grief, filling Your ears with complaints and groans, which You then disregarded. For You were sweeping me along through my own desires to put an end to those very desires, and the earthly part of her love for me was being chastened by the just scourge of grief. She loved to have me with her, as mothers do, but far more than many mothers; and she did not know what great joy You were going to bring her out of my absence. She did not know, so she wept and wailed, and in that agony the inheritance of Eve showed itself in her, as she sought in sorrow the child she had brought forth in sorrow. And yet, after accusing me of treachery and cruelty, she turned again to praying to You for me and went back to her usual life, and I went on to Rome.

And look: there in Rome I was greeted by the scourge of bodily illness, and I was already on my way down to hell, carrying all the sins I had committed against You, against myself and against others, many and grievous sins, on top of that bond of original sin by which we all die in Adam. For You had not yet forgiven me any of these things in Christ, and He had not yet abolished on His Cross the enmity I had brought on myself with You by my sins. How could He have abolished it by the crucifixion of a phantom, which is what I believed Him to be? So the death of my soul was as real as the death of His flesh seemed to me unreal; and as real as the death of His body was, so unreal was the life of my soul, which did not believe it. And as the fever grew worse I was already going, already perishing. For if I had left this world then, where would I have gone except into the fire and the torments my deeds deserved, in the truth of the order You have established? She did not know about this, yet she was praying for me from far away. But You, present everywhere, heard her where she was and had pity on me where I was, so that I recovered the health of my body, though my heart was still sick and sacrilegious. For in all that danger I did not ask for Your baptism. I had been better as a boy, when I begged for it from my mother's devotion, as I have already recalled and confessed. But I had grown up to my own disgrace, and in my madness I laughed at the counsels of Your medicine, You who would not let me die a double death in the state I was in. If my mother's heart had been struck by that wound, it could never have been healed. For I cannot adequately express the love she had for me, and how much greater was the anguish with which she was now in labor with me in the spirit than when she had given birth to me in the flesh.

So I do not see how she could have been healed if a death like that had pierced the very depths of her love. And what would have become of all those prayers of hers, so intense and so frequent, offered without ceasing to You alone? Would You, God of mercies, despise the contrite and humbled heart of that chaste and sober widow? She gave alms so often; she was so dutiful and so ready to serve Your saints; she never let a day pass without making her offering at Your altar. Twice a day, morning and evening, without fail, she came to Your church, not for idle gossip and old wives' tales, but so that she might hear You in Your sermons and You might hear her in her prayers. Could You despise such a woman's tears and turn them away from Your help, when with them she was asking You not for gold or silver or any changeable, passing good, but for the salvation of her son's soul? Could You, by whose gift she was what she was? Never, Lord. No, You were there, hearing and acting, in the order You had determined beforehand that it should be done. Far be it from You to deceive her in those visions and answers of Yours, some of which I have mentioned and some not. She kept them in her faithful heart and, always praying, pressed them on You as though they were Your own signed pledges. For since Your mercy endures forever, You graciously consent to become a debtor through Your promises to those whose debts You forgive entirely.

So You brought me through that illness and made the son of Your handmaid well, for the time being in body, so that he might live for You to give him a better and more lasting health. And even then, in Rome, I was joining up with those deceived and deceiving "holy ones." I associated not only with their hearers (the man in whose house I had fallen ill and recovered was one of them) but also with those they call "the Elect." For it still seemed to me "that it is not we who sin, but some other nature, I do not know what, that sins in us." It pleased my pride to stand outside all blame, and when I had done something wrong, not to confess that I had done it, so that You might heal my soul, since it had sinned against You.
