Instead I loved to excuse myself and to accuse some other thing, I did not know what, that was with me but was not I. But in truth it was all I, and my own ungodliness had divided me against myself. And that sin was all the more incurable because I did not think I was a sinner. It was a detestable wickedness that I would rather have You, You, almighty God, be overcome in me to my ruin than have myself be overcome by You to my salvation. So You had not yet set a watch before my mouth, and a door of safe keeping around my lips, so that my heart would not turn aside to wicked words, to make excuses for sins with men who work iniquity. And that is why I was still united with their Elect.

But by now I had given up hope of making any progress in that false teaching, and even the things I had decided to be content with if I found nothing better I now held more loosely and carelessly. For a thought had half arisen in me that the philosophers they call Academics were wiser than the rest, because they held that people ought to doubt everything and had laid it down that no truth can be grasped by a human being. That is what I, too, was plainly convinced they thought, as they are commonly reported to, since I did not yet understand even what they really meant. Yet I did not hesitate to warn my host, freely and openly, against the excessive confidence I could see he had in the fables that fill the books of Manichaeus. Still, I lived on closer terms of friendship with them than with others who did not belong to that heresy. I no longer defended it with my old eagerness; but my intimacy with that sect (Rome hides a good many of them) made me slower to look for any other way. This was especially so because I had given up hope of finding the truth in Your Church, O Lord of heaven and earth, Creator of all things visible and invisible, for they had turned me away from it. It seemed to me very degrading to believe that You had the shape of human flesh and were bounded by the bodily outlines of our limbs. And because, whenever I wanted to think about my God, I did not know how to think of anything except a mass of bodies (for whatever was not like that did not seem to me to exist at all), this was the greatest and almost the only cause of the error I could not escape.

For this is why I believed that evil, too, was some such kind of substance, with its own foul and hideous bulk. It might be dense, which they called earth, or thin and fine, like the body of the air, which they imagine as a malignant mind creeping through that earth. And because some kind of piety, such as it was, forced me to believe that the good God never created any evil nature, I pictured two masses opposed to each other, both of them infinite, but the evil one narrower and the good one larger. From this poisonous starting point all my other sacrilegious notions followed. For whenever my mind tried to go back to the Catholic faith, I was thrown back, because what I took to be the Catholic faith was not the Catholic faith. I thought myself more reverent if I believed that You, my God (to whom Your mercies make confession through my mouth), were infinite at least on the other sides, even though on the one side where the mass of evil stood against You I was forced to admit that You were bounded, than if I imagined You bounded on every side by the shape of a human body. And it seemed better to me to believe that You had created no evil than to believe that the nature of evil, as I pictured it, came from You. In my ignorance, evil seemed to me not merely a substance of some kind but a bodily one, because I could not think of mind except as a fine body, spread out through the spaces of place. I even believed that our Savior Himself, Your Only Begotten, had been stretched out, as it were, for our salvation from the mass of Your most shining substance, so that I believed nothing about Him except what I could imagine in my emptiness. I thought, then, that a nature like His could not be born of the Virgin Mary without being mixed with the flesh; and I could not see how something like what I had pictured could be mixed with the flesh and not be defiled. So I was afraid to believe that He was born in the flesh, in case I should be forced to believe that He was defiled by the flesh. Your spiritual ones will smile at me gently and lovingly if they read these confessions of mine. But that is what I was.

Moreover, I thought that the things the Manichees had attacked in Your Scriptures could not be defended. Yet at times I really did want to talk over these points one by one with someone very learned in those books and find out what he thought about them. For even at Carthage I had begun to be stirred by the words of a certain Helpidius, who spoke and argued face to face against these same Manichees. He brought forward things from the Scriptures that could not easily be resisted, and the Manichees' answer to him seemed weak to me. They did not like to give this answer publicly, only to us in private. It was that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been corrupted by someone or other who wanted to graft the law of the Jews onto the Christian faith; yet they themselves never produced any uncorrupted copies. But since I could think only of bodily things, I was held down above all, crushed and in a way suffocated, by those "masses." Gasping under them for the breath of Your truth, I could not breathe it in its pure and simple air.

So I began to work hard at what I had come to Rome to do, teaching rhetoric. First I gathered a few students at my house, people through whom, and to whom, I had begun to become known. And then I discovered that other offenses were committed at Rome which I had not had to put up with in Africa. It was true, as I had been told, that those "wreckings" by dissolute young men did not go on there. But suddenly, they told me, to avoid paying their teacher's fee, a group of young men conspire together and move to another teacher: breakers of their word, who for love of money think nothing of justice. My heart hated these people too, though not with a perfect hatred. For perhaps I hated them more because I was going to suffer at their hands than because they were doing things that were wrong in themselves. Certainly such people are base, and they go whoring away from You, loving the fleeting mockeries of temporal things and filthy gain, which dirties the hand that grasps it. They embrace a world that is running away and despise You, who remain, who call back the adulterous human soul and forgive her when she returns to You. And now I hate such twisted and crooked people, though I love them as people who can be corrected, so that they may come to prefer the learning they acquire to money, and to learning prefer You, O God, the truth and abundance of sure good and the purest peace. But back then I was more unwilling to put up with their wickedness for my own sake than I was wishing them to become good for Yours.

So when the people of Milan sent to the prefect of the city of Rome asking him to provide their city with a teacher of rhetoric, and to send him with travel at public expense, I put myself forward. I did it through those very people who were drunk on Manichaean foolishness, the very people I was going away to be rid of, though neither they nor I knew it. I asked that Symmachus, who was then prefect of the city, should test me by setting me a speech to deliver, and so send me. And I came to Milan, to Ambrose the bishop, known throughout the world as one of the best of men, Your devout worshipper. In those days his eloquent sermons were vigorously giving out to Your people the finest flour of Your wheat, the gladness of Your oil and the sober intoxication of Your wine. I was being led to him by You without knowing it, so that through him I might be led to You knowing it. That man of God welcomed me like a father and, as a bishop should, was kind about my coming there as a stranger. And I began to love him, at first not as a teacher of the truth, for I had entirely given up hope of finding that in Your Church, but as a man who was kind to me. I listened carefully when he preached to the people, not with the intention I should have had, but as if I were testing his eloquence to see whether it lived up to its reputation or flowed more or less freely than people said. I hung intently on his words, but as for their content, I stood by uninterested and scornful. I was delighted by the charm of his speech, which was more learned than that of Faustus but, in its manner of delivery, less lively and soothing. As for the substance, though, there was no comparison: the one was wandering among Manichaean deceptions, while the other was teaching salvation in the soundest way. But salvation is far from sinners, and such was I as I stood there then. And yet I was drawing closer, little by little and without knowing it.

I did not take the trouble to learn what he was saying, only to hear how he said it, since that empty concern was all I had left, now that I had given up hope that any way to You lay open to human beings. Yet along with the words I enjoyed, the things I did not care about also came into my mind, for I could not separate them. And while I opened my heart to take in "how eloquently he spoke," there also came in "how truly he spoke," though only by degrees. For first, these things too began to seem to me capable of being defended. The Catholic faith, for which I had thought nothing could be said against the attacks of the Manichees, I now thought could be upheld without shame. This was especially so after I had heard one or two passages of the Old Testament explained, and often "in a figure," passages which had been killing me when I took them literally. So when many passages of those books had been explained in a spiritual sense, I now began to blame my despair, at least the despair in which I had believed that no answer at all could be given to those who hated and mocked the Law and the Prophets. But I did not yet feel that the Catholic way was the one I must hold just because it too could have its learned defenders, who could answer objections fully and not unreasonably. Nor did I feel that what I held should be condemned just because the two sides were equally matched in defense. For the Catholic cause seemed to me not defeated, but not yet victorious either.

Then I set my mind hard to work, to see whether I could somehow convict the Manichees of falsehood by some certain proofs. If I had been able to conceive of a spiritual substance, all their strongholds would at once have been broken down and thrown out of my mind; but I could not. Still, as I considered and compared things more and more, I judged that most of the philosophers had held far more probable views about the physical frame of this world and about the whole of nature that the senses of the flesh can reach. So, in the manner of the Academics as they are commonly understood, doubting everything and wavering among all views, I did at least decide that the Manichees must be abandoned. I judged that even during my time of doubt I should not remain in a sect to which I already preferred some of the philosophers. Yet I absolutely refused to entrust the cure of my sick soul to those philosophers, because they were without the saving Name of Christ. So I decided to be a catechumen in the Catholic Church, which my parents had commended to me, for as long as it took until something certain should dawn on me by which I could steer my course.

chapters.title: Book 6
paragraphs: You, my hope from my youth, where were You for me, and where had You gone? Had You not created me and set me apart from the beasts of the field and the birds of the air? You had made me wiser than they, and yet I walked in darkness and on slippery ground, searching for You outside myself, and I did not find the God of my heart. I had come down into the depths of the sea, and I lost confidence and despaired of ever finding the truth. By now my mother had come to me, strong in her devotion, following me over land and sea, and in every danger secure in You. When the sea was perilous she even comforted the sailors themselves (though it is usually they who comfort passengers new to the deep when they are frightened), promising them that they would arrive safely, because You had promised her this in a vision. She found me in grave danger through my despair of ever finding the truth. But when I told her that I was no longer a Manichee, though not yet a Catholic Christian either, she did not leap for joy as though she had heard something unexpected. Yet she was now reassured about that part of my misery for which she had been mourning me as one dead, though one You would raise again. She was carrying me out on the bier of her thoughts, so that You might say to the widow's son, Young man, I say to you, Arise; and he would come back to life and begin to speak, and You would give him back to his mother. So her heart was not shaken by any wild rejoicing when she heard that what she daily begged of You with tears had already been so largely accomplished: though I had not yet reached the truth, I had been rescued from falsehood. Rather, because she was sure that You, who had promised the whole, would one day give the rest, she answered me very calmly, with a heart full of confidence, "She believed in Christ that before she left this life she would see me a faithful Catholic." That much she said to me. But to You, Fountain of mercies, she poured out still more prayers and tears, that You would hurry Your help and light up my darkness. She hurried all the more eagerly to church and hung on the lips of Ambrose, longing for the fountain of that water which springs up to eternal life. She loved that man as an angel of God, because she knew that it was through him that I had been brought, for the time being, into that wavering state of faith I was now in. Through it she fully and confidently expected that I would pass from sickness to health, after going through, as it were, a sharper attack, the kind that physicians call "the crisis."

In Africa my mother had been in the habit of bringing cakes, bread and wine to the churches built in memory of the saints. Once, when she did this, the doorkeeper stopped her. As soon as she learned that the bishop had forbidden it, she accepted his wish so devoutly and obediently that I myself was amazed at how readily she found fault with her own custom rather than argue about his ban. For no craving for wine laid siege to her spirit, and no love of wine goaded her into hating the truth, as it does to a great many men and women, who are sickened by any call to sobriety the way drunkards are sickened by a drink mixed with water. When she brought her basket of the customary festival food, to be tasted first by herself and then given away, she never set out more than one small cup of wine, diluted to suit her own very sober palate, from which she would take a sip for courtesy's sake. And if there were many shrines of the departed saints that seemed to deserve this kind of honor, she carried the same single cup around to set down at each. By then it was not only thoroughly watered but also unpleasantly lukewarm, and she would share it in tiny sips with those around her, because what she sought there was devotion, not pleasure. So when she discovered that this famous preacher and most devout bishop had ordered that it should not be done, even by those who did it soberly, so that no opening for gorging might be given to drunkards, and because these quasi-memorial feasts for the dead closely resembled the superstition of the pagans, she gave it up most willingly. In place of a basket full of the fruits of the earth, she had learned to bring to the shrines of the martyrs a heart full of purer prayers, and to give what she could to the poor. In this way the communion of the Lord's Body could be rightly celebrated in the place where the martyrs, in imitation of His Passion, were sacrificed and crowned. And yet it seems to me, O Lord my God, and this is how my heart judges it in Your sight, that perhaps she would not so easily have given up this custom if it had been forbidden by someone else whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose. She loved him dearly for the sake of my salvation, and he loved her for her deeply religious way of life, so fervent in spirit, as she went constantly to church doing good works. Often when he saw me he would break out in praise of her, congratulating me on having such a mother. He did not know what kind of son she had in me, a son who doubted all these things and did not believe the way of life could ever be found.

I was not yet groaning in prayer for You to help me. My mind was wholly bent on inquiry and restless for argument. I regarded Ambrose himself as a fortunate man by the world's standards, since such important people held him in such honor; only his celibacy struck me as a hard burden. But what hope he carried within him, what struggles he had against the temptations that came with his very excellence, what comfort he found in hardship, and what delicious joys the hidden mouth of his heart tasted as it chewed over Your Bread, I could neither guess nor had I experienced. Nor did he know the surges of my feelings or the pit of my danger. For I could not ask him what I wanted, in the way I wanted, because crowds of people with business, whose weaknesses he served, shut me off from his ear and his speech. When he was not with them, which was only a very short time, he was either refreshing his body with the food it strictly needed or refreshing his mind with reading. When he read, his eyes moved over the pages and his heart probed the meaning, but his voice and tongue were still. We often came to him, for no one was forbidden to enter, and it was not his custom to have visitors announced, and we would see him reading like this, silently, and never any other way. After sitting a long while in silence (for who would dare to burden a man so absorbed?) we would leave. We guessed that in the little time he managed to get for restoring his mind, free from the noise of other people's affairs, he did not want to be drawn away to anything else. Perhaps, too, he was wary that if the author he was reading put something obscurely, some listener hanging on his words might need him to explain it, or to argue over some of the harder questions, and that with his time spent on this he would get through fewer books than he wanted. Then again, the need to save his voice, which became hoarse very easily, may have been the truer reason for his reading silently. But whatever his purpose in doing it, in such a man it was certainly a good one.

In any case, I was given no chance to ask what I wanted of that holy oracle of Yours, his heart, unless the matter could be heard briefly. But the surges within me that I needed to pour out to him required him to be wholly at leisure, and they never found him so. I did hear him every Lord's Day, rightly handling the word of truth before the people, and I became more and more convinced that all the knots of cunning slander that those deceivers of ours had tied against the divine Books could be untied. And when I also learned that "man, created by You in Your own image," was not understood by Your spiritual sons, whom You have given new birth through grace from the Catholic Mother, to mean that they believed and pictured You as bounded by the shape of a human body (although I had not even the faintest or dimmest idea of what a spiritual substance could be), I blushed, yet with joy, that for so many years I had been barking not at the Catholic faith but at the fictions of fleshly imaginings. I had been so rash and impious that I had condemned outright what I ought to have learned by asking. For You, Most High and most near, most hidden and most present, who do not have limbs, some larger and some smaller, but are everywhere whole and nowhere in space, are certainly not of such a bodily shape. And yet You have made man in Your own image, and look, from head to foot he is contained in space.

Since I did not know how this image of Yours could exist, I should have knocked and put forward the question of how it was to be believed, not mocked and opposed it as though it were believed in that way. So the question of what I could hold as certain gnawed at my heart all the more sharply the more ashamed I was that, having been deluded and deceived so long by the promise of certainties, I had babbled about so many uncertain things as if they were certain, with a child's error and passion. That they were actually false became clear to me only later. But I was certain that they were uncertain, and that I had once treated them as certain when I blindly and contentiously attacked Your Catholic Church. I had not yet found that she taught the truth, but I had found that she did not teach the things I had so harshly accused her of. So I was put to shame and turned around, and I rejoiced, my God, that the one only Church, the body of Your only Son, in which the name of Christ had been given to me as an infant, had no taste for infantile nonsense. Nor did her sound doctrine hold any teaching that would squeeze You, the Creator of all things, into a region of space, however lofty and vast, yet bounded on every side by the shape of human limbs.

I was glad, too, that the old writings of the Law and the Prophets were now set before me to be read no longer with the eye that had once found them absurd, when I used to attack Your holy ones for thinking things they did not in fact think. And I was glad to hear Ambrose in his sermons to the people often and very earnestly commend this text as a rule: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. Meanwhile he would draw aside the mystical veil and open up in a spiritual sense passages which, taken literally, seemed to teach something perverse. In this he taught nothing that offended me, though he did teach things whose truth I did not yet know. For I held my heart back from assenting to anything, afraid of falling headlong, but by hanging in suspense I was being killed all the more. I wanted to be as certain of the things I could not see as I was that seven and three make ten. I was not so mad as to think that even this could not be known; but I wanted other things to be just as clear, whether bodily things that were not present to my senses, or spiritual things, which I did not know how to conceive except in bodily terms. By believing I could have been cured, so that the eyesight of my soul, once cleared, might somehow be directed toward Your truth, which abides forever and fails in no part. But just as a person who has had a bad doctor is often afraid to trust himself even to a good one, so it was with the health of my soul. It could not be healed except by believing, and yet, for fear of believing falsehoods, it refused to be cured, resisting Your hands, You who have prepared the medicines of faith, applied them to the diseases of the whole world, and given them such great authority.

Even so, this led me to prefer the Catholic teaching. I felt that she acted more modestly and honestly in requiring belief in things that were not demonstrated (whether because they could be demonstrated in themselves, though not to certain people, or because they could not be demonstrated at all), whereas among the Manichees our credulity was mocked with a promise of certain knowledge, and then so many utterly fabulous and absurd things were imposed on us to be believed, precisely because they could not be demonstrated. Then, Lord, little by little, with a most gentle and merciful hand, You touched and settled my heart and persuaded me. I considered how countless were the things I believed that I had not seen, and had not been present for when they happened: so much in the history of nations, so many accounts of places and cities I had never seen, so much taken on trust from friends, so much from doctors, so much constantly from one person or another. Unless we believed these things, we would do nothing at all in this life. Last of all I considered how unshakably I believed who my parents were, something I could not know unless I had believed what I heard. Considering all this, You persuaded me that it was not those who believed Your Books, which You have established with such great authority among almost all nations, who deserved blame, but those who did not believe them. You persuaded me, too, that I should not listen to anyone who might say to me, "How do you know that those Scriptures were given to the human race by the Spirit of the one true and most truthful God?" For this was the very thing most to be believed. No combativeness in all the slanderous questions I had read among so many philosophers contradicting one another could ever wring from me the belief "that You are," whatever You might be (which I did not know), and "that the governing of human affairs belongs to You."

This I believed, sometimes more firmly, at other times more feebly. But I always believed both that You exist and that You care for us, even though I did not know what to think about Your substance, or what way led, or led back, to You. Since we were too weak to find the truth by clear reasoning, and for that very reason needed the authority of the holy Scriptures, I had now begun to believe that You would never have given that Scripture such outstanding authority throughout every land unless You had willed that through it You should be believed in, and through it sought. For now, having heard many of the passages that used to offend me by sounding absurd explained plausibly, I referred them to the depth of the mysteries. Its authority seemed to me all the more worthy of reverence and of holy faith because, while it lies open for everyone to read, it keeps the dignity of its secret within a deeper sense. It offers itself to all in the plainest words and the humblest style of speech, and yet it exercises the full attention of those who are not light-minded. In this way it welcomes everyone into its broad embrace, and through narrow openings carries a few across to You; yet these are many more than it would carry if it did not stand so high in authority, and did not draw the crowds into the lap of its holy humility. I was thinking these things over, and You were with me. I sighed, and You heard me. I wavered, and You steered me. I went along the broad road of the world, and You did not abandon me.

I gaped after honors, money and marriage, and You laughed at me. In these desires I suffered the bitterest hardships, and You were all the kinder to me the less You let anything that was not You grow sweet to me. Look at my heart, Lord, You who willed that I should remember this and confess it to You. Let my soul now cling to You, since You have freed it from the sticky birdlime of death that held it so fast. How wretched it was! And You kept prodding the sore of its wound, so that it might leave everything else and be turned to You, who are above all things and without whom all things would be nothing; so that it might be turned, and be healed. How miserable I was, then, and how You dealt with me to make me feel my misery on that day when I was preparing to deliver a speech in praise of the Emperor. In it I was to tell many lies, and my lying was to be applauded by people who knew I was lying. My heart was panting with these worries and seething with the fever of consuming thoughts. As I was passing through one of the streets of Milan, I noticed a poor beggar, already full, I suppose, joking and in high spirits. I sighed and spoke to the friends who were with me about the many sorrows that come from our madness. With all our strivings, like the ones I was then laboring at, dragging the burden of my own unhappiness under the goad of desire and making it heavier by dragging it, we were still aiming at nothing but to reach that carefree joy where that beggar had already arrived ahead of us, and where perhaps we would never arrive. What he had gained with a few coins he had begged, I was scheming for through so many miserable twists and turns: the joy of a passing happiness. He certainly did not have true joy; but with my ambitions I was seeking a joy far less true. And he was certainly glad while I was anxious; he was carefree, I was afraid. If anyone had asked me whether I would rather be merry or fearful, I would have answered that I would rather be merry. But if he had asked again whether I would rather be such a man as he was or such as I then was, I would have chosen myself, worn out with cares and fears as I was. But I would have chosen out of perversity; was it out of truth? For I had no business preferring myself to him because I was more learned, since my learning gave me no joy. I used it to seek to please people, not to teach them, but simply to please them. That is why You broke my bones with the rod of Your discipline.

Away from my soul, then, with those who say to her, "It makes a difference where a person's joy comes from. That beggar found his joy in drunkenness; you wanted to find yours in glory." What glory, Lord? A glory that is not in You. For just as his was not true joy, neither was mine true glory, and it overturned my mind all the more. That very night he would sleep off his drunkenness; but I had gone to sleep with mine and woken up with it, and I would go to sleep and wake up with it again, how many days You know, God. "But it does make a difference where a person's joy comes from." I know it, and the joy of faithful hope is incomparably beyond such vanity. Yet even then there was a difference between him and me, for he was without doubt the happier man. It was not only that he was soaked in cheerfulness while I was gutted by cares. It was also that he had got his wine by wishing people well, while I was seeking empty, puffed-up praise by lying. I said much to this effect to my friends at that time. I often noticed in them how things stood with me, and I found that things were bad with me, and I grieved, and so doubled that very badness. And if any good fortune smiled on me, I could not be bothered to reach for it, because it flew away almost before I could grasp it.

Those of us who lived together as friends lamented these things together, but I spoke of them most of all, and most intimately, with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius was born in the same town as I was, to a family of the leading rank there, but he was younger than me. He had studied under me, both when I first taught in our town and later at Carthage. He loved me very much because I seemed to him kind and learned, and I loved him for his great natural bent toward virtue, which stood out clearly enough in someone so young. But the whirlpool of Carthaginian habits, where those frivolous shows are followed with passion, had sucked him into the madness of the Circus. While he was wretchedly swirling around in it, I was teaching rhetoric there and had a public school, but he did not yet attend my classes, because of some ill feeling that had arisen between his father and me. I had found out how fatally he loved the Circus, and I was deeply distressed, because he seemed to me about to throw away, or even to have already thrown away, such great promise. Yet I had no way of warning him or of drawing him back by some kind of pressure, whether by the goodwill of a friend or by the authority of a teacher. For I supposed that he felt about me as his father did; but he did not. So, setting aside his father's wishes in this matter, he began to greet me, and sometimes came into my lecture room, listened a little, and left.

I, however, had forgotten to take the matter up with him, so that he would not ruin such a fine mind through a blind and headlong passion for empty games. But You, Lord, who guide the course of everything You have created, had not forgotten him, who was one day to be among Your children, a priest and dispenser of Your Sacrament. And so that his correction might plainly be credited to You, You brought it about through me, but without my knowing it. One day, as I sat in my usual place with my students before me, he came in, greeted me, sat down and turned his mind to what we were dealing with. I happened to have a passage in hand, and while I was explaining it, a comparison with the Circus races occurred to me as likely to make my point more pleasant and clearer, flavored with biting mockery of those whom that madness had enslaved. You know, our God, that I was not thinking at the time of curing Alypius of that disease. But he took it wholly to himself and believed that I had said it only because of him. What someone else would have taken as a reason to be angry with me, that honest young man took as a reason to be angry with himself and to love me more warmly. For You had said it long ago and woven it into Your book: Rebuke a wise man, and he will love you. But I had not rebuked him. It was You, who make use of everyone, whether they know it or not, in the order You know (and that order is just), who made burning coals out of my heart and tongue, to set on fire a mind of good promise that was wasting away, and so to cure it. Let anyone keep silent in Your praise who does not consider Your mercies, which confess to You from the depths of my being. For after those words he tore himself out of that deep pit into which he had been willingly plunging, blinded by its wretched pleasures. He shook his mind free with strong self-control, and all the filth of the Circus games dropped away from him, and he never went there again. After this he overcame his reluctant father's objections so that he might have me as his teacher. His father gave way and gave in. And when Alypius began to attend my lectures again, he became entangled with me in the same superstition, loving in the Manichees that display of continence which he supposed to be real and genuine. But it was a senseless and seductive continence, which ensnared precious souls that could not yet reach the depth of virtue and were easily deceived by the surface of what was only a shadowy and counterfeit virtue.

Not abandoning the worldly path that his parents had charmed him into following, he had gone ahead of me to Rome to study law. There he was seized, unbelievably, by an unbelievable craving for gladiatorial shows. He had loathed and detested such spectacles. But one day he happened to meet some of his acquaintances and fellow students coming back from dinner, and with the rough force of friends they dragged him, though he fiercely refused and resisted, into the amphitheater during the days of those cruel and deadly games. He protested, "You may drag my body to that place and set me down there, but can you make me turn my mind or my eyes to those shows? I will be absent though present, and so I will get the better of both you and them." When they heard this, they took him along all the same, perhaps wanting to test that very thing, whether he could do what he said. When they arrived and had taken what seats they could, the whole place was seething with that savage pleasure. But he shut the doors of his eyes and forbade his mind to go out after such evils. If only he had blocked his ears as well! For at some turn in the fight, when a man fell, a huge roar from the whole crowd struck him hard. Overcome by curiosity, and as if ready to despise and rise above whatever it was even once he had seen it, he opened his eyes. And he was struck by a deeper wound in his soul than the man he wanted to see had received in his body, and he fell more wretchedly than the man whose fall had raised that great roar. The roar came in through his ears and unlocked his eyes, opening the way for the striking and beating down of a soul that was bold rather than strong, and all the weaker for having relied on itself when it ought to have relied on You. As soon as he saw that blood, he drank in savagery along with it. He did not turn away but fixed his gaze, gulping down frenzy without knowing it, delighting in the wicked contest and getting drunk on the bloody pleasure. He was no longer the man who had come, but one of the crowd he had come into, and a true companion of those who had brought him there. What more is there to say? He watched, he shouted, he caught fire, and he carried away with him a madness that would goad him to come back, not only with those who had first dragged him there, but even ahead of them, and dragging others along too. Yet from there You rescued him with a most strong and most merciful hand, and taught him to put his confidence not in himself but in You. But that was long afterward.

Still, this was already being stored away in his memory as medicine for the future. So was another incident. When he was still studying under me at Carthage, he was going over at midday in the marketplace what he was to recite, as students usually practice, and You allowed him to be arrested by the marketplace officers as a thief. I think You allowed it, our God, for no other reason than that this man, who was one day to be so great, should begin to learn already that in hearing cases a person should not easily be condemned by another person through rash credulity. He was walking up and down alone in front of the judgment seat with his writing tablets and pen, when suddenly a young man, a lawyer, the real thief, secretly carrying a hatchet, slipped in without Alypius noticing, as far as the lead railings that stand above the silversmiths' street, and began to hack away the lead. But when the sound of the hatchet was heard, the silversmiths below started muttering and sent men to seize whoever they might find. The thief heard their voices and ran off, leaving his hatchet behind, afraid of being caught with it. Now Alypius, who had not seen him go in, noticed him leaving and saw how fast he was getting away. Wanting to know what was going on, he went into the place, found the hatchet, and was standing there looking at it in wonder when suddenly the men who had been sent found him alone, holding the very tool whose noise had alarmed them and brought them there. They grabbed him and dragged him off, and gathering the people who lived around the marketplace, they boasted of having caught a thief red-handed. And so he was being led away to be brought before the judge.

But this was as far as Alypius's lesson was to go. For at once, Lord, You came to the aid of his innocence, of which You alone were the witness. As he was being led off either to prison or to punishment, they were met by a certain architect who had chief charge of the public buildings. They were especially glad to meet him, because he usually suspected them of stealing the goods that went missing from the marketplace, and now at last, they thought, he would see who was committing these thefts. But this man had often seen Alypius at the house of a certain senator whom he regularly visited to pay his respects. He recognized him at once, took him by the hand and drew him aside, and asked the reason for such a disaster. He heard the whole story and ordered everyone present, who were in an uproar and making threats, to come with him. So they came to the house of the young man who had committed the crime. In front of the door was a boy, so young that he was likely to tell the whole story without fearing any harm to his master, for he had gone with his master to the marketplace as his attendant. As soon as Alypius remembered him, he told the architect, who showed the hatchet to the boy and asked him, "Whose is this?" "Ours," he said at once, and when he was questioned further he revealed everything. So the charge was shifted to that house, and the crowd that had begun to gloat over Alypius was put to shame. And he who was to be a dispenser of Your Word and a judge of many cases in Your Church went away more experienced and better taught.

I had found him, then, at Rome, and he clung to me with the strongest bond and went with me to Milan, both so as not to leave me and so as to practice something of the law he had studied, more to satisfy his parents' wishes than his own. There he had already sat three times as an assessor, with an integrity that others found astonishing, while he was more astonished at those who could prefer gold to honesty. His character was also tested, not only by the lure of greed but by the goad of fear. At Rome he served as assessor to the Count of the Italian Treasury. At that time there was a very powerful senator, to whom many were bound by favors and of whom many stood in fear. As his power allowed, he wanted to be permitted something that the laws did not permit. Alypius resisted. A bribe was promised; he scorned it with all his heart. Threats were made; he trampled on them. Everyone marveled at such an unusual spirit, which neither wanted the friendship nor feared the enmity of a man so great and so widely famed for his countless ways of doing good or harm. Even the judge whose counselor Alypius was, though he too did not want it done, did not openly refuse. Instead he shifted the matter onto Alypius, claiming that Alypius would not let him do it; and in truth, if the judge had done it, Alypius would have left. The one thing that very nearly tempted him was his love of learning: he could have had books copied for himself at Praetorian rates. But he consulted justice and changed his mind for the better, judging the fairness that forbade him more profitable than the power that would have allowed him. These are small things, but whoever is faithful in little is faithful also in much. And what came from the mouth of Your Truth can in no way be empty: If you have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will entrust to you the true riches? And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own? Such was the man who clung to me at that time and wavered with me over what way of life we should take.

Nebridius, too, had come to Milan. He had left his native place near Carthage, and Carthage itself, where he had spent much of his time; he had left his excellent family estate and his house, and a mother who was not going to follow him. He had come for no other reason than to live with me in a most ardent search for truth and wisdom. Like me he sighed, like me he wavered, an eager seeker of the happy life and a very sharp investigator of the hardest questions. So there were the mouths of three needy people, sighing out their wants to one another and waiting on You, that You might give them their food in due season. And in all the bitterness that, by Your mercy, followed our worldly dealings, when we looked to the end, asking why we should suffer all this, darkness met us. We turned away groaning and said, How long will these things go on? We said this often, and yet, saying it, we did not give them up, because nothing certain had yet dawned on us that we could take hold of once we had let these things go.

As I looked back and went over things, I was most amazed at how long it had been since my nineteenth year, when I had begun to burn with the desire for wisdom, resolving that once I found her I would abandon all the empty hopes and lying frenzies of vain desires. And here I was, already in my thirtieth year, stuck in the same mud, greedy to enjoy present things that slipped away and scattered me, while I kept saying to myself: "Tomorrow I will find it. It will become plain, and I will grasp it. Look, Faustus the Manichee will come and explain everything! O you great men, you Academics, is it true, then, that nothing certain can be grasped for the conduct of life? No, let us search more diligently and not despair. Look, things in the Church's books that once seemed absurd no longer seem absurd to us, and they can be understood differently and in a good sense. I will plant my feet on the step where my parents set me as a child until the clear truth is found. But where is it to be sought? When is it to be sought? Ambrose has no time; we have no time to read. Where can we even find the books? From where, or when, can we get hold of them? From whom can we borrow them? Let times be set aside and hours assigned for the health of the soul. A great hope has dawned: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought and what we vainly accused it of. Its learned members hold it sacrilege to believe that God is bounded by the shape of a human body. And do we hesitate to 'knock,' so that the rest 'may be opened'? Our students take up the mornings; what do we do with the rest of the day? Why not do this? But then when do we pay calls on our influential friends, whose support we need? When do we prepare what our students will pay for? When do we restore ourselves, relaxing our minds from the strain of our cares?

"Let everything go to ruin! Let us dismiss these empty vanities and give ourselves to the one search for truth! Life is wretched, death uncertain. If it creeps up on us suddenly, in what state will we leave this world? And where will we learn what we neglected here? Will we not rather have to pay the penalty for this neglect? And what if death itself cuts off and ends all care along with all feeling? Then that too must be looked into. But God forbid that it should be so! It is not for nothing, it is no empty thing, that the towering dignity of the authority of the Christian faith has spread over the whole world. Such great things would never have been done for us by God if the life of the soul came to an end with the death of the body. Why, then, do we delay to give up worldly hopes and devote ourselves wholly to seeking God and the happy life? But wait! These things are pleasant too; they have some sweetness of their own, and not a little. We must not lightly break off our pursuit of them, for it would be shameful to go back to them again. Look, how little it would take now to obtain some official post! And what more should we want than that? We have plenty of influential friends. If nothing else comes along, and we press hard, we could at least be given a governorship. And a wife with some money, so that she does not add to our expenses; and that will be the limit of our desire. Many great men, most worthy of imitation, have devoted themselves to the study of wisdom while married."

While I talked like this, and these winds shifted back and forth and drove my heart this way and that, time went by, and I was slow to turn to the Lord. From day to day I put off living in You, and yet I did not put off dying in myself every day. I loved the happy life, yet I feared it in its own dwelling place, and I sought it while running away from it. For I thought I would be too miserable if I were deprived of a woman's embraces. I did not think of the medicine of Your mercy for curing that weakness, because I had never tried it. As for continence, I supposed it lay in our own power (though I did not find that power in myself). I was so foolish that I did not know what is written, that no one can be continent unless You give it; and that You would surely give it if I knocked at Your ears with inward groaning and, with firm faith, cast my care on You.

Alypius, for his part, kept me from marrying. He insisted that if I did, we could in no way live together in the love of wisdom with the undisturbed leisure we had long desired. He himself was even then remarkably pure in this respect, which was all the more wonderful because at the start of his youth he had entered on that experience but had not got stuck in it. Rather, he had felt regret and disgust at it, and from then until now had lived in the most perfect continence. But I countered him with the examples of those who, as married men, had cherished wisdom, served God acceptably, kept their friends and loved them faithfully. I fell far short of their greatness of spirit. Bound by the disease of the flesh and its deadly sweetness, I dragged my chain along, afraid to be set loose, and, as though my wound had been rubbed raw, I pushed away his good advice like the hand of someone trying to unchain me. What is more, through me the serpent spoke to Alypius himself. Through my tongue it wove sweet snares and laid them in his path, to entangle his honest and unencumbered feet.

He was amazed that I, whom he held in no small esteem, should be stuck so fast in the birdlime of that pleasure that I insisted, whenever we discussed it, that I could never live a single life. When I saw his amazement, I defended myself by saying that there was a great difference between his brief and hurried experience, which he barely remembered and so could easily despise, and my own settled habit; and that if the honorable name of marriage were added to it, he ought not to wonder why I could not spurn that way of life. Then he too began to want to marry, not because he was overcome by desire for that pleasure, but out of curiosity. For he said he wanted to know what this thing could be, without which my life, which he found so agreeable, seemed to me not a life but a punishment. His mind, free of that chain, was astonished at my slavery, and through that astonishment it was moving toward a desire to try it, and from there to the trial itself, and from there perhaps to sinking into the very bondage that astonished him, since he was willing to make a covenant with death; and whoever loves danger will fall into it. For whatever honor there is in the duty of rightly ordering a married life and raising children, it attracted neither of us except slightly. For my part, the habit of satisfying an insatiable appetite held me captive and tormented me for the most part and with great force; he, meanwhile, was being drawn toward captivity by wonder. This is how we were, until You, Most High, who do not forsake our dust, took pity on us in our misery and came to our help in wonderful and hidden ways.

I was pressed constantly to marry. I was already making my proposal, and a bride was already being promised to me, chiefly through my mother's efforts. She hoped that once I was married, saving baptism would wash me clean. She rejoiced that I was being made more fit for it day by day, and she saw her prayers and Your promises being fulfilled in my faith. At that time, both at my request and from her own longing, she begged You every day with a strong cry of the heart to show her in a vision something about my future marriage, but You never would. She did see certain empty and fanciful things, such as the force of the human spirit, busy about the matter, conjures up, and she told me about them. But she did not speak with the confidence she usually had when You had shown her something; she made light of them. For she said that by a certain taste, which she could not put into words, she could tell the difference between Your revelations and the dreams of her own soul. Still, the matter was pressed forward, and a girl was asked for in marriage who was about two years short of the marriageable age. Since she was pleasing, we were waiting for her.

Many of us friends, talking together and detesting the turbulent troubles of human life, had considered and had almost decided to live at leisure, away from the crowds. We planned to bring about this leisure as follows: we would put into a common fund whatever each of us could obtain and make a single household out of it all. In this way, through the sincerity of our friendship, nothing would belong to one person or another, but the single whole made up from everyone's goods would belong as a whole to each, and everything to everyone. We thought there might be about ten people in this community. Some of us were very rich, especially Romanianus, a man from our town and a close friend of mine since childhood, whom serious troubles in his affairs had brought to the court at that time. He was the most eager for this project, and his voice carried great weight in urging it, because his large fortune far exceeded the rest. We had also agreed that two of us each year, like magistrates, would see to everything necessary, while the rest remained undisturbed. But when we began to consider whether the wives, whom some of us already had and others hoped to have, would allow this, the whole plan we had been shaping so well fell apart in our hands, and was broken up and thrown aside. After that we turned to sighs and groans, and turned our steps to follow the broad and well-worn roads of the world. For many thoughts were in our heart, but Your counsel stands forever. Out of that counsel You laughed at our plans and prepared Your own for us, intending to give us food in due season, to open Your hand and to fill our souls with blessing.

Meanwhile my sins were multiplying. My concubine was torn from my side as an obstacle to my marriage, and my heart, which clung to her, was cut and wounded and left bleeding. She went back to Africa, vowing to You that she would never know another man, and she left with me the son I had had by her. But I, unhappy man, could not even follow a woman's example. Impatient of delay, since I was not to receive the girl I had asked for until two years had passed, and being not so much a lover of marriage as a slave to lust, I got myself another woman, though certainly not as a wife. In this way the disease of my soul would be kept alive and carried along, either at full strength or even worse, under the guard of an enduring habit, into the realm of marriage. And that wound of mine, made by the cutting away of the first woman, did not heal. After the inflammation and sharpest pain, it festered, and the pain became duller, as it were, but more hopeless.

Praise to You, glory to You, Fountain of mercies! I was becoming more miserable, and You were coming nearer. Your right hand was ready at every moment to snatch me out of the mud and wash me clean, and I did not know it. Nothing called me back from a still deeper whirlpool of fleshly pleasures except the fear of death and of Your judgment to come, which, through all my changes of opinion, never left my heart. In my discussions with my friends Alypius and Nebridius about the ends of good and evil, I held that Epicurus would have won the prize in my mind, if I had not believed that after death the soul lives on and that there are places of reckoning according to people's deserts, which Epicurus refused to believe. And I would ask, "If we were immortal and lived in perpetual bodily pleasure, with no fear of losing it, why would we not be happy, or what else would we be looking for?" I did not know that great misery lay in this very fact: that, sunk and blinded as I was, I could not conceive of that light of virtue and of beauty to be embraced for its own sake, which the eye of the flesh does not see and which is seen from within. Nor did I, wretched as I was, consider where it came from that I could enjoy discussing even these things, foul as they were, with my friends. Nor could I be happy without friends, even by the idea of happiness I had then, however great the abundance of fleshly pleasures. And these friends I certainly loved for their own sake alone, and I felt that they in turn loved me for my own sake alone.

What twisted paths! Woe to the reckless soul that hoped, by leaving You, to have something better! It has turned and turned again, onto its back, its sides, its belly, and everything is hard, and You alone are rest. And look, You are here, and You free us from our miserable wanderings, and set us on Your way, and comfort us, and say, "Run; I will carry you; yes, I will bring you through; and there too I will carry you."

chapters.title: Book 7
paragraphs: By now my wicked and shameful youth was dead, and I was moving on into early manhood. The older I grew, the more I was soiled by empty things, for I could not picture any substance except the kind these eyes normally see. I did not think of You, O God, as shaped like a human body. From the time I first began to hear something of wisdom I had always steered clear of that idea, and I was glad to find the same view in the faith of our spiritual mother, Your Catholic Church. But what else I was to think You were, I had no idea. And I, a man, and a man like me, was trying to think of You, the supreme, the only, the true God. In the very marrow of my soul I believed that You were incorruptible, beyond injury, and unchangeable. I did not know where the certainty came from or how, yet I saw clearly and was sure that what can be corrupted is worse than what cannot; without hesitating I ranked what cannot be injured above what can, and the unchangeable above whatever is open to change. My heart shouted fiercely against all my phantoms, and with this single blow I tried to drive off the whole filthy swarm that circled before the eye of my mind. But no sooner were they brushed aside than, in the twinkling of an eye, they massed together again, rushed at my face and clouded my sight. So although I no longer pictured You in the form of a human body, I was still forced to picture You as something bodily, spread through space — that incorruptible, uninjurable and unchangeable being I ranked above the corruptible, injurable and changeable — whether poured into the world or stretched out endlessly beyond it. For anything I tried to think of without such space seemed to me to be nothing, absolutely nothing, not even an empty void. It was as if a body were removed from its place and the place stayed there emptied of every body, whether of earth or water, air or heaven, and still remained an empty place, a kind of roomy nothing.

So, gross of heart as I was, and not even clearly visible to myself, I judged that whatever was not stretched through some amount of space — spread out, packed together or swelling — or did not take on, or could not take on, some such dimension, was nothing whatsoever. My heart moved among images of exactly the kind of shapes my eyes are used to moving among. I did not yet see that the very act of mind by which I formed those images was not itself anything of that kind, and yet it could never have formed them unless it were itself something great. In the same way I pictured You, Life of my life, as immense, pervading the whole bulk of the universe on every side through infinite spaces, and reaching beyond it in every direction through measureless, endless spaces, so that the earth held You, the heaven held You, all things held You, and they found their limits in You while You were limited nowhere. The body of the air above the earth does not stop the light of the sun from passing through it; the light goes right through, not by tearing it or cutting it but by filling it entirely. In the same way I supposed that the body not only of heaven, air and sea but of the earth as well lay open to You, penetrable in all its parts, largest and smallest, so as to take in Your presence, which governs from inside and outside, by a hidden breathing-in, all the things You have created. That was my guess, only because I could think of nothing else; and it was false. For on that view a larger part of the earth would hold a larger part of You, and a smaller part a smaller; and all things would be full of You in such a way that an elephant's body would contain more of You than a sparrow's, by as much as it is bigger and fills more room. You would then be making the parts of Yourself present to the parts of the world piece by piece, big pieces to big parts and small ones to small. But You are not like that. But You had not yet lit up my darkness.

Against those deceived deceivers and talkative mutes — mute because Your word did not sound from them — I had enough, Lord. I had the argument Nebridius used to put forward long ago, back in Carthage, which shook every one of us who heard it: "What could that so-called race of darkness, which the Manichees like to set up as a hostile mass over against You, have done to You if You had refused to fight it? If the answer were that it would have done You some harm, then You would be open to injury and corruption. But if they said it could have done You no harm, then there was no reason given for You to fight it at all — let alone to fight in such a way that some portion or limb of You, some offspring of Your very Substance, would be mixed up with hostile powers and with natures You never created, and would be so far corrupted by them and changed for the worse that it fell from happiness into misery and needed help to be rescued and cleansed. And this offspring of Your Substance, they say, is the soul: enslaved, stained and corrupted, it is relieved by Your Word, which is free, pure and whole — yet that Word too must be corruptible, since it is of one and the same Substance. So if they called You, whatever You are — that is, the Substance by which You are — incorruptible, then all these claims of theirs were false and detestable; and if they called You corruptible, that statement was itself false and repulsive the moment it was spoken." This argument of Nebridius, then, was enough against people who deserved in every way to be vomited up out of an overloaded stomach. They had no way out, short of horrible blasphemy of heart and tongue, in thinking and saying such things about You.

Yet even I, at that point — though I said, and firmly held, that You, our Lord, the true God, who made not only our souls but our bodies, and not only our souls and bodies but all beings and all things, could not be defiled or altered and were in no respect changeable — still had no clear and untangled grasp of the cause of evil. But whatever that cause might be, I could see that it had to be searched for in a way that would not drive me to believe that the unchangeable God was changeable, or I would myself become the very evil I was looking for. So I looked for it with this much peace of mind: I was certain that what those people taught, from whom I now fled with my whole heart, was not true. For I saw that in asking where evil came from they had become full of evil themselves, since they would rather believe that Your substance suffers evil than that their own does evil.

So I strained to see clearly what I was now being told: that the free choice of the will is the reason we do wrong, and Your just judgment the reason we suffer it. But I could not see it clearly. I tried to draw the eye of my mind up out of that deep pit, and I sank back into it; I tried again and again, and again and again I sank. What lifted me a little toward Your light was this: I knew that I had a will just as surely as I knew that I was alive. So whenever I wanted something or refused it, I was completely sure that it was I and no one else who was wanting and refusing, and I was on the very point of seeing that here lay the cause of my sin. As for what I did unwillingly, I saw that I underwent it rather than did it, and I judged it to be not my fault but my punishment; and because I thought of You as just, I was quick to admit that I was not being punished unjustly. But then I would ask again: Who made me? Wasn't it my God, who is not only good but goodness itself? Then where did I get this power to will evil and refuse good, which gives me a reason to be justly punished? Who put this in me and planted in me this seedling of bitterness, when the whole of me was made by my most sweet God? If the devil is the one responsible, where did the devil come from? And if he too was a good angel who became a devil through his own perverse will, where did that evil will in him come from, by which he became a devil, when the whole angel had been made by a Creator who is supremely good? These thoughts pushed me down again and choked me. Yet I was not dragged down as far as that hell of error where no one confesses to You, the error that thinks You suffer evil rather than that man does it.

For I was trying to discover the rest in the same way that I had already discovered that the incorruptible is better than the corruptible; and that is why I confessed that You, whatever You might be, were incorruptible. No soul ever has been or ever will be able to think of anything better than You, the highest and the best good. And since it is perfectly true and certain that the incorruptible is to be ranked above the corruptible, as I was already ranking it, then if You were not incorruptible I could have reached, in thought, something better than my God. So where I saw that the incorruptible must be preferred to the corruptible, that was where I ought to have been looking for You, and from there I ought to have worked out "where evil is" — that is, where corruption itself comes from, the corruption that cannot damage Your substance in any way at all. Corruption cannot damage our God in any respect: not by any will, not by any necessity, not by any unforeseen accident. For He is God; what He wills for Himself is good, and He Himself is that very good; and being corrupted is not good. Nor are You ever forced into anything against Your will, since Your will is not greater than Your power. It would be greater only if You were greater than Yourself, for the will and the power of God are God Himself. And what can take You by surprise, when You know all things? Nothing has any nature at all except because You know it. Why say so much, then, about "why the substance that God is cannot be corruptible," when, if it were, it would not be God?

And I kept asking "where evil comes from," and I asked in an evil way, and did not see the evil in my very asking. I set out before the gaze of my spirit the whole of creation: everything we can see in it, such as sea, earth, air, stars, trees and mortal creatures; and everything in it we cannot see, such as the firmament of heaven above, and all the angels, and all its spiritual beings. But my imagination arranged even these in their places as if they were bodies. I made Your creation into one enormous mass, divided up by kinds of bodies — some that really were bodies, and some that I had invented to stand for spirits. And I made this mass huge, not as huge as it actually is, which I had no way of knowing, but as huge as I liked, though bounded on every side. You, Lord, I imagined surrounding it and soaking through it from every direction, but infinite in every direction. It was as if there were a sea everywhere, stretching on every side through immeasurable space, a single sea without end, and inside it there were a sponge, as large as you please but still bounded: that sponge would of course be filled in every part from the measureless sea. That is how I thought of Your creation, finite as it is, as full of You, the Infinite. And I said: Look, here is God, and here is what God has created. God is good, and mightily, immeasurably more excellent than all these things. Yet being good He created them good, and see how He surrounds them and fills them. Then where is evil, and where does it come from, and how did it creep in here? What is its root, and what is its seed? Or does it not exist at all? Then why do we fear and guard against something that does not exist? Or if our fear is groundless, then surely the fear itself is evil, since it goads and tortures the heart for nothing; and it is an evil all the worse because there is nothing to fear and still we fear. So either what we fear is evil, or else the evil is that we fear. Where, then, does it come from, since God, who is good, made all these things good? He, the greater and supreme Good, made these lesser goods; but still, Creator and created alike, all are good. Where does evil come from? Or was there some evil matter out of which He made things, and He shaped it and set it in order, but left something in it that He did not turn into good? Why would He do that? Was He unable to turn and change the whole of it, so that no evil remained, when He is almighty? And finally, why would He choose to make anything out of it at all, instead of using that same almighty power to make it not exist at all? Or could it exist against His will? Or if it was eternal, why did He let it stay that way through infinite stretches of time past, and then decide so much later to make something out of it? Or, if He suddenly wanted to act, surely the Almighty would have acted instead to make that matter cease to be, so that He alone would exist, the whole, true, supreme and infinite Good. Or, if it was not right that He who was good should not also build and establish something good, then He could have taken away that evil matter and reduced it to nothing, and set up good matter of His own from which to create all things. For He would not be almighty if He could not establish anything good without the help of matter He had not made Himself. Such were the thoughts I turned over in my wretched heart, weighed down with the most gnawing worries — the fear of death, and the truth not yet found. Yet the faith of Your Christ, our Lord and Savior, as held in the Catholic Church, stayed firmly fixed in my heart. On many points it was still unformed and drifting away from the rule of doctrine; but my mind did not abandon it, and instead drank it in more and more every day.

By this time I had also thrown out the lying predictions and godless ravings of the astrologers. Let Your own mercies confess to You for this too, O my God, from the innermost depths of my soul. For it was You, You entirely — for who else calls us back from the death of every error but the Life that does not know how to die, and the Wisdom that needs no light yet enlightens the minds that need it, the Wisdom by which the universe is governed, down to the fluttering leaves of the trees? — it was You who took care of my stubbornness. I had been arguing against Vindicianus, a shrewd old man, and against Nebridius, a young man with a remarkable mind. The first insisted forcefully, and the second said often, though with a certain hesitation, "that there was no such art of foreseeing the future; that people's guesses often worked like a lottery, and that out of the many things they said would happen, some did happen — without the speakers knowing it, since they simply stumbled on it by saying so much." So You provided me with a friend who was no idle consulter of astrologers, though not deeply versed in their writings either, but, as I said, a curious consulter of them; and yet he knew something that he said he had heard from his father, without realizing how much it could do to overturn belief in that art. This man, Firminus by name, who had a liberal education and was well trained in rhetoric, came to consult me as a very dear friend about certain affairs of his in which his worldly hopes ran high, asking what I thought of them according to his so-called constellations. I had already begun to lean toward Nebridius' opinion on the subject. I did not flatly refuse to make a guess and tell him what occurred to my wavering mind, but I added that I was by now almost convinced these things were ridiculous and empty. At that he told me that his father had been extremely curious about books of this kind and had had a friend just as devoted to them as he was. With shared enthusiasm and comparing of notes they fanned the fire of their hearts' passion for these trifles, so much so that whenever the dumb animals around their houses gave birth, they would note the moment of birth and record the position of the heavens at that time, in order to gather evidence for this so-called art. He said, then, that he had heard from his father that when his mother was pregnant with him, Firminus, a slave woman belonging to that friend of his father's was also expecting. This could not escape her master, who took the most painstaking care to know when even his dogs had their puppies. And so it came about that while the one was counting the days, hours and even the smaller fractions of hours for his wife, and the other for his slave woman, with the most careful observation, the two women gave birth at the same moment. The two men were therefore obliged to cast the very same constellations, down to the smallest detail, the one for his son and the other for his newborn slave. For as soon as the women went into labor, each had informed the other of what was happening in his own house, and each had messengers ready to send to the other the instant the child was born; and they had easily arranged for the news to be carried at once, since each was master in his own domain. And the messengers sent from each side, he said, met each other at a point exactly halfway between the two houses, so that neither man could record any different position of the stars or any difference in the smallest fractions of time. And yet Firminus, born to a high position in his family, ran along the brighter roads of the world, grew richer and rose to honors, while that slave went on serving his masters with the yoke of his condition not loosened in the least — as Firminus himself, who knew him, told me.

When I heard this and believed it — for the man who told it was someone I could trust — all my resistance gave way and collapsed. First I tried to draw Firminus himself away from that curiosity. I told him that if I had examined his constellations in order to foretell the truth, I ought to have seen in them parents who were leading figures among their neighbors, a family of rank in its own city, free birth, a respectable upbringing and a liberal education. But if that slave had consulted me about the same constellations, since they were his as well, then in order to tell him the truth too I ought to have seen in them a family of the lowest sort, the condition of a slave, and everything else utterly different from and far removed from the first case. So if I looked at the same data and told the truth, I would have to say different things; and if I said the same things, I would be saying something false. From this I concluded with complete certainty that whatever true things are said after consulting the constellations are said not by skill but by luck, and whatever false things are said come not from ignorance of the art but from luck turning out false.

Now that a way in had been opened, I went on turning over such things by myself. I did not want any of those crackpots who made their living by this trade — whom I was itching to attack, refute and hold up to ridicule — to be able to counter me by claiming that Firminus had told me a false story, or his father had told him one. So I turned my attention to twins. Most twins come out of the womb one after the other so closely that the tiny interval between them, however much force people may claim it has in the natural order, cannot be caught by human observation or recorded in any way in the figures the astrologer has to examine in order to make a true prediction. And his predictions will not be true, since looking at the same figures he would have had to say the same things about Esau and Jacob, yet the same things did not happen to both of them. So he would be speaking falsely; or, if he spoke truly, he would not be saying the same things, although he would be looking at the same figures. It is not by skill, then, but by luck that he would speak the truth. For You, Lord, the most just ruler of the universe, act by a hidden prompting, without either the consulters or the consulted knowing it, so that each person who consults hears what he ought to hear, according to the hidden merits of souls, out of the depths of Your just judgment. Let no man say to You, What is this? Why that? Let him not say it, let him not say it; for he is man.

So by now, my Helper, You had set me free from those chains, and I was asking "where evil comes from," and there was no way out. But You did not let any waves of thought sweep me away from the faith by which I believed that You exist, that Your substance is unchangeable, that You care for men and will judge them, and that in Christ, Your Son, our Lord, and in the holy Scriptures, which the authority of Your Catholic Church commended to me, You had laid down the way of man's salvation to the life that is to come after this death. With these points secure and unshakably established in my mind, I searched feverishly for "where evil comes from." What torments my heart suffered in its labor pains, what groans, my God! And even there Your ears were listening, though I did not know it. And when I searched hard in silence, the silent agonies of my soul were loud cries to Your mercy. You knew what I was going through, and no human being did. For how much of it did I actually put into words for the ears of my closest friends? Did the whole uproar of my soul reach them, when neither time nor speech was enough for it? Yet all of it reached Your hearing, all that I roared out from the groaning of my heart; my desire was before You, and the light of my eyes was not with me. For that light was within, while I was outside; and it is not in any place, but I was fixed on things contained in places, and there I found no place to rest. Those things did not take me in so that I could say, "That is enough," "that is good," and yet they did not let me go back to where it would be good enough for me. For I was higher than they were, but lower than You; and You were my true joy as long as I was subject to You, and You had made subject to me the things You created beneath me. This was the right balance, the middle ground where my well-being lay: to stay in Your image, and by serving You to be master of the body. But when I rose up proudly against You and ran against the Lord with my neck, with the thick boss of my shield, even these lowest things were placed above me and weighed me down, and there was nowhere to find relief or room to breathe. When I looked, they crowded in on me from every side in heaps and masses; and when I tried to think, the images of bodies themselves stood in my way as I tried to turn back, as if they were saying, "Where do you think you are going, unworthy and filthy as you are?" And all this had grown out of my wound, for You "humbled the proud like one that is wounded"; by my own swelling I was cut off from You, and my face, puffed up with pride, shut my eyes.

But You, Lord, remain forever, yet You are not angry with us forever, because You have taken pity on our dust and ashes. It was pleasing in Your sight to reshape what was misshapen in me. With goads inside me You kept stirring me up, so that I could find no peace until You became certain to me by my inward sight. And so, by the hidden hand of Your healing, my swelling went down, and the troubled and darkened eyesight of my mind was healed from day to day by the stinging salve of wholesome pains.

And first You wanted to show me how You resist the proud, but give grace to the humble, and how great was the mercy with which You had shown men the way of humility, in that Your Word was made flesh, and dwelt among men. So, by means of a certain man swollen with the most monstrous conceit, You brought into my hands some books of the Platonists, translated from Greek into Latin. And there I read — not in these very words, but saying exactly the same thing, argued with many different kinds of reasons — that In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: the same was in the beginning with God: all things were made by Him, and without Him was nothing made: that which was made in Him is life, and the life was the light of men, and the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.
