And I read that the soul of man, though it bears witness to the light, is not itself that light; but the Word of God, being God, is that true light which enlightens every man who comes into the world. And that He was in the world, and the world was made by Him, and the world did not know Him. But that He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him; but as many as received Him, to them He gave power to become the sons of God, as many as believed in His name — this I did not read there.

I also read there that God the Word was born not of flesh, nor of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, I did not read there. For I found in those books, stated in many different ways, that the Son, being in the form of the Father, thought it not robbery to be equal with God, because by nature He was the same Substance. But that He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men, and found in fashion as a man, humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross; so that God exalted Him from the dead and gave Him a name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth, and that every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father — this those books do not have. That Your Only-Begotten Son remains unchangeably before all times and above all times, co-eternal with You; that souls receive of His fullness in order to be blessed; and that they are renewed by sharing in the Wisdom that abides in itself, so that they become wise — that is there. But that in due time He died for the ungodly, and that You did not spare Your Only Son but delivered Him up for us all — that is not there. For You hid these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones, so that those who labor and are heavy laden might come to Him and He might refresh them, because He is meek and lowly in heart. The meek He guides in judgment, and the gentle He teaches His ways, seeing our lowliness and our trouble and forgiving all our sins. But those who strut on the high boots of what they take to be a loftier learning do not hear Him saying, Learn of Me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls. Even though they know God, they do not glorify Him as God or give thanks, but become futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart is darkened; claiming to be wise, they became fools.

And so I also read there that they had changed the glory of Your incorruptible nature into idols and all kinds of images, into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and beasts, and creeping things. This was that Egyptian food for which Esau lost his birthright: Your first-born people honored the head of a four-footed beast in place of You, turning back in their hearts toward Egypt and bowing Your image, their own soul, before the image of a calf that eats hay. I found these things there, but I did not feed on them. For it pleased You, Lord, to take away from Jacob the reproach of being the lesser, so that the elder should serve the younger; and You called the Gentiles into Your inheritance. I had come to You from among the Gentiles, and I set my mind on the gold that You wanted Your people to carry away from Egypt, since it was Yours wherever it was. And You told the Athenians through Your Apostle that in You we live and move and have our being, as some of their own poets had said; and those books certainly came from there. But I did not set my mind on the idols of the Egyptians, which they served with Your gold — those who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.

Warned by all this to return to myself, I went into my own innermost self with You as my guide; and I was able to, because You had become my helper. I went in, and with the eye of my soul, such as it was, I saw above that same eye of my soul, above my mind, the unchangeable Light. It was not this ordinary light that all flesh can see, nor something of the same kind only larger, as if this light were to shine many, many times brighter and fill everything with its size. That Light was not like this; It was something else, utterly different from all these. Nor was It above my mind the way oil floats above water, or the way heaven is above the earth. It was above me because It made me, and I was beneath It because I was made by It. Whoever knows the Truth knows that Light, and whoever knows It knows eternity. Love knows It. O Truth, You who are Eternity! Love, You who are Truth! Eternity, You who are Love! You are my God; to You I sigh night and day. When I first came to know You, You lifted me up so that I could see that there was something to see, and that I was not yet the kind of person who could see it. And You beat back the weakness of my sight, shining on me with overwhelming force, and I trembled with love and dread. I found that I was far away from You, in the region of unlikeness, and it was as if I heard Your voice from on high: "I am the food of the full-grown; grow, and you will feed on Me. And you will not change Me into yourself, as you do the food of your flesh; you will be changed into Me." And I understood that You correct man for iniquity, and You made my soul waste away like a spider. And I said, "Is Truth then nothing, since it is not spread out through space, whether finite or infinite?" And You called to me from far away, "Yes, truly, I AM that I AM." I heard it the way one hears in the heart, and there was no longer any ground at all for doubt. I could more easily doubt that I am alive than doubt that Truth exists, Truth which is clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.

Then I looked at the other things below You, and I saw that they neither fully are nor fully are not. They are, since they come from You; but they are not, because they are not what You are. For what truly is, is what remains unchangeably. So it is good for me to cling to God; for if I do not remain in Him, I cannot remain in myself either. But He, remaining in Himself, makes all things new. And You are my Lord, since You have no need of my goodness.

And it became clear to me that things which are corrupted are good. They could not be corrupted if they were the supreme good, nor could they be corrupted unless they were good. If they were the supreme good, they would be incorruptible; and if they were not good at all, there would be nothing in them to corrupt. For corruption does harm, and it could do no harm unless it lessened some good. So either corruption does no harm, which is impossible, or — and this is absolutely certain — everything that is corrupted is deprived of some good. But if things are deprived of all good, they will not exist at all. For if they went on existing and could no longer be corrupted, they would be better than before, since they would continue incorruptibly. And what could be more absurd than to claim that things become better by losing all their good? So if they are deprived of all good, they will be nothing at all. Therefore, as long as they exist, they are good. Therefore whatever exists is good; and that evil whose origin I was looking for is not a substance, because if it were a substance it would be good. For it would be either an incorruptible substance, and so a great good, or a corruptible substance, which could not be corrupted unless it were good. So I saw, and it was made plain to me, that You made all things good, and that there are no substances whatever that You did not make. And because You did not make all things equal, therefore all things are: each one is good, and all together they are very good, because our God made all things very good.

And for You there is no evil at all — and not only for You, but for Your creation as a whole as well, because there is nothing outside it that could break in and corrupt the order You have laid on it. But within its parts, some things are thought to be evil because they do not fit with certain other things; yet those same things fit with other things and are good, and in themselves they are good. And all these things that do not fit with one another do fit with the lower part of the world, which we call the earth, and which has its own cloudy and windy sky suited to it. Far be it from me, then, to say, "These things should not exist." Even if I saw nothing but these, I would indeed long for better things, but even for these alone I would still owe You praise. For that You are to be praised is shown from the earth by dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice and stormy wind, which fulfill Your word; mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds; kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens, old men and children, praise Your name. And since from the heavens too they praise You, praise You, our God, in the heights, all Your angels, all Your hosts, sun and moon, all the stars and light, the heaven of heavens and the waters that are above the heavens, praise Your name — I no longer longed for better things, because I was thinking of them all. And with a sounder judgment I weighed it up: the higher things are indeed better than the lower, but all things together are better than the higher things alone.

There is no health in people who are displeased by anything in Your creation, just as there was none in me when many things You made displeased me. And because my soul did not dare to be displeased with my God, it preferred not to count as Yours whatever displeased it. That is how it had drifted into the opinion of two substances; and it found no rest, and talked wildly. And coming back from there, it had made itself a god that stretched through the infinite reaches of all space, and took this to be You, and set it up in its heart; and so once again it had become the temple of its own idol, a temple abominable to You. But after You had cradled my head, without my knowing it, and closed my eyes so that they would not look on vanity, I let go of myself a little, and my madness was lulled to sleep. And I woke up in You, and saw You as infinite, but in another way; and this seeing did not come from the flesh.

Then I looked back at other things, and I saw that they owe their existence to You, and that all things are bounded in You — but differently, not as if in a place, but because You hold all things in Your hand by Your Truth. All things are true insofar as they exist, and falsehood is nothing at all except when something is thought to exist that does not. And I saw that each thing fits in not only with its own place but also with its own time; and that You, who alone are eternal, did not begin to work after countless stretches of time had gone by. For no stretches of time, neither those that have passed nor those that will pass, could go or come unless You were working and abiding.

I learned by experience that it is no wonder bread which tastes pleasant to a healthy palate is torture to a sick one, and that light which is lovely to clear eyes is hateful to sore ones. Your justice displeases the wicked; much more, then, do the viper and the worm, which You created good, suited to the lower parts of Your creation. The wicked themselves are suited to those lower parts, all the more as they are unlike You; but they are suited to the higher parts as they become more like You. And I asked what iniquity was, and I found that it is not a substance, but the perversity of a will twisted away from the supreme substance, from You, O God, toward the lowest things — a will that throws away its own inmost life and swells outward.

And I was amazed that I now loved You, and not some phantom in place of You. Yet I did not stand firm in the enjoyment of my God. I was swept up to You by Your beauty, and soon torn away from You by my own weight, and I crashed back down, groaning, into these lower things. That weight was the habit of the flesh. But the memory of You stayed with me, and I had no doubt at all that there was One I should cling to, only that I was not yet able to cling to Him; for the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks about many things. And I was completely certain that Your invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even Your eternal power and Godhead. For I was asking where my approval of the beauty of bodies, whether in the heavens or on earth, came from, and what I had at hand that allowed me to judge soundly about changeable things and to say, "This ought to be so, and that not" — asking, I say, where my judgment came from when I judged in this way — and I had found the unchangeable and true eternity of Truth above my changeable mind. So step by step I went up from bodies to the soul that perceives through the body; and from there to its inner power, to which the bodily senses report what is outside, which is as far as animals can go; and from there again to the reasoning power, to which whatever is taken in from the bodily senses is referred for judgment. This power, too, finding itself changeable in me, raised itself up to its own understanding. It drew my thinking away from habit and pulled itself out of the crowds of contradictory phantoms, in order to discover what light was shed on it when it cried out without any doubt, "The unchangeable is to be preferred to the changeable" — and how it knew the Unchangeable itself; for unless it had somehow known it, it could never have ranked it with certainty above the changeable. And so, in the flash of one trembling glance, it arrived at THAT WHICH IS. Then I saw Your invisible things, understood by the things that are made. But I could not hold my gaze there; my weakness was beaten back and I fell again into my usual ways, carrying nothing with me but a loving memory, and a longing for something I had, as it were, caught the fragrance of but could not yet eat.

So I looked for a way to gain the strength I needed to enjoy You, and I did not find it until I embraced that Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus, who is over all, God blessed forever, who calls to me and says, I am the way, the truth, and the life, and who mixed with our flesh the food I was too weak to take. For the Word was made flesh so that Your wisdom, through which You created all things, might become milk for our infancy. For I did not yet hold on to my Lord Jesus Christ — I was not humble enough to hold the Humble One — and I did not yet know what His weakness was meant to teach. For Your Word, the eternal Truth, towering above the higher parts of Your creation, raises up to Itself those who submit to It. But here in the lower world It built Itself a humble house out of our clay, in order to bring down from themselves those who were to be made subject, and carry them across to Himself — healing their swelling and nourishing their love — so that they would not go any further in trusting themselves, but would rather become weak, seeing at their feet the Godhead made weak by sharing our garment of skin; and so that, worn out, they would throw themselves down upon It, and It would rise and lift them up.

But I thought otherwise. I thought of my Lord Christ only as a man of outstanding wisdom whom no one could equal; especially since, having been born of a virgin in a wonderful way, to give us an example of despising temporal things in order to gain immortality, He seemed through God's care for us to have earned such great authority as a teacher. But what mystery was contained in "The Word was made flesh," I could not even guess. I had only gathered from what has been handed down in writing about Him that He ate and drank, slept, walked, rejoiced, was sad and held conversations, and that the flesh was not joined to Your Word on its own but together with a human soul and mind. Everyone knows this who knows that Your Word is unchangeable, which I now knew as far as I was able, and I had no doubt about it at all. For now to move the limbs of the body by an act of will and now not to move them, now to be stirred by some feeling and now not, now to speak wise sayings through signs and now to stay silent — these are the marks of a soul and mind that are subject to change. If these things had been written about Him falsely, everything else would be under suspicion of being false too, and there would be no saving faith left in those writings for the human race. So, since they were written truthfully, I recognized in Christ a whole man: not just the body of a man, nor a body together with an animal soul lacking a rational mind, but a real man. Yet I judged that He was to be ranked above other men not because He was the very Person of Truth, but because of some great excellence of His human nature and a more perfect sharing in wisdom. Alypius, for his part, supposed that Catholics believed God was clothed in flesh in such a way that in Christ there was nothing besides God and flesh; he did not think they held that He had a human soul and mind. And because he was fully convinced that the actions recorded of Him could not have been done without a living and rational creature, he moved all the more slowly toward the Christian faith itself. But afterward, when he learned that this was the error of the Apollinarian heretics, he rejoiced in the Catholic faith and came into agreement with it. For my part, I admit that it was somewhat later that I learned how, in the words The Word was made flesh, the Catholic truth is distinguished from the falsehood of Photinus. For refuting heretics makes what Your Church holds and what sound doctrine contains stand out clearly. For there must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among the weak.

But at that time, having read those books of the Platonists and been prompted by them to look for truth that is not bodily, I saw Your invisible things, understood by the things that are made. And though I was thrown back, I sensed what it was that the darkness of my mind would not let me contemplate. I was certain "that You exist, and are infinite, yet are not spread out through space, whether finite or infinite; that You truly are, since You are always the same, not different or otherwise in any part or by any movement; and that all other things come from You, on this one most certain proof alone, that they exist." Of these things I was certain, but I was far too weak to enjoy You. I chattered away like an expert; but if I had not sought Your way in Christ our Savior, I would have proved to be not skilled, but killed. For I had now begun to want to be thought wise. I was full of my own punishment, and yet I did not weep over it; I was puffed up with knowledge instead. For where was that love which builds on the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus? When would those books ever have taught me that? I believe You wanted me to come across them before I studied Your Scriptures precisely so that it would be stamped on my memory how they had affected me. Then later, when I had been tamed by Your books and my wounds had been touched by Your healing fingers, I would be able to see and tell apart the difference between presumption and confession: between those who see where they must go but do not see the way, and the way that leads to the blessed homeland, not only to see it but to live in it. For if I had first been shaped by Your holy Scriptures, and You had grown sweet to me through my familiarity with them, and I had only afterward come upon those volumes, they might have torn me away from the solid ground of devotion. Or, if I had held on to the wholesome disposition I had drunk in from Scripture, I might have thought that someone could acquire it from those books alone, if he studied nothing else.

So I seized with the greatest eagerness on the venerable writings of Your Spirit, and above all on the Apostle Paul. And those problems disappeared in which he had once seemed to me to contradict himself, and in which the text of his words had seemed not to agree with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets. The face of those pure words now appeared to me as one and the same, and I learned to rejoice with trembling. I began to read, and I found that whatever truth I had read in those other books is said here with praise for Your grace. It is said so that whoever sees should not boast as if he had not received — not only what he sees, but even the power to see (for what does he have that he has not received?); so that he may be not only urged to see You, who are always the same, but also healed so that he may hold You; and so that whoever cannot see from far away may still walk on the road by which he can come and see and hold You. For though a man delights in the law of God according to the inner man, what will he do about that other law in his members, which wars against the law of his mind and leads him captive to the law of sin that is in his members? For You are righteous, Lord, but we have sinned and committed iniquity and done wickedly, and Your hand has grown heavy upon us. We have been justly handed over to that ancient sinner, the ruler of death, because he persuaded our will to become like his own will, by which he did not stand firm in Your truth. What will wretched man do? Who will deliver him from the body of this death, except Your grace, through Jesus Christ our Lord, whom You begot co-eternal with You and formed in the beginning of Your ways, in whom the prince of this world found nothing worthy of death, and yet he killed Him; and the handwriting that was against us was blotted out? This those writings do not contain. Those pages do not show the face of this devotion: the tears of confession, Your sacrifice, a troubled spirit, a broken and a contrite heart, the salvation of the people, the Bridal City, the pledge of the Holy Spirit, the Cup of our Redemption. No one there sings, Shall not my soul be subject to God? For from Him comes my salvation. For He is my God and my salvation, my protector; I shall be moved no more. No one there hears Him calling, Come to Me, all you who labor. They disdain to learn from Him, because He is meek and lowly in heart; for You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. For it is one thing to see the homeland of peace from a wooded mountaintop, and to find no road to it, and to struggle in vain through trackless country, surrounded and ambushed by runaways and deserters under their leader, the lion and the dragon. It is another thing to keep to the road that leads there, guarded by the care of the heavenly Commander, where no one who has deserted the heavenly army lies in wait to rob, for they shun that road like torture. All this sank into my inmost being in wonderful ways as I read the least of Your apostles; and I had considered Your works, and trembled greatly.

chapters.title: Book 8
paragraphs: O my God, let me remember with thanksgiving and confess to You Your mercies toward me. Let my bones be drenched with Your love, and let them say to You, Who is like You, O Lord? You have broken my bonds apart; I will offer You the sacrifice of thanksgiving. How You broke them I will tell, and all who worship You, when they hear it, will say, "Blessed be the Lord in heaven and on earth; great and wonderful is His name." Your words had fastened deep in my heart, and I was hemmed in on every side by You. Of Your eternal life I was now sure, though I had seen it only in a riddle and as through a glass. Still, every doubt had been taken from me that there is an incorruptible substance from which all other substance comes; and what I wanted now was not to be more certain of You but more steadfast in You. As for my life in time, though, everything was unsteady, and my heart still had to be cleansed of the old leaven. The Way, the Savior Himself, pleased me well, but I still shrank from going through its narrowness. And You put it into my mind, and it seemed good in my sight, to go to Simplicianus, who struck me as a good servant of Yours; Your grace shone in him. I had also heard that he had lived devoted to You with great devotion ever since his youth. By now he had grown old, and after so long a life spent in such earnest pursuit of Your way, he seemed to me to have gained much experience and learned a great deal; and that was true. From that store I wanted him to tell me, once I had laid my turmoil before him, what the right way was for someone in my condition to walk in Your path.

For I saw the church full, and one person went one way and another went another. But the worldly life I was leading displeased me, and it had become a very heavy burden, now that my desires no longer fired me, as they once had, with hopes of honor and money to make such heavy bondage bearable. Those things no longer delighted me, compared with Your sweetness and the beauty of Your house, which I loved. But I was still bound fast by my love of a woman. Nor did the Apostle forbid me to marry, though he urged me toward something better, wishing above all that all men were as he himself was. But I was weaker, and chose the softer place; and because of this one thing I was tossed about in everything else, listless and wasting away with withering cares, because in other matters too, which I did not want to put up with, I was forced to fit myself to married life, to which I had given myself and by which I was bound. I had heard from the mouth of the Truth that there are some eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven's sake; but, He says, let whoever can receive it, receive it. Surely all men are vain who do not have the knowledge of God, and who could not, from the good things that are seen, find Him who is good. But I was no longer in that vanity. I had risen above it, and by the joint testimony of all Your creation I had found You, our Creator, and Your Word, God with You and one God together with You, through whom You created all things. There is also another kind of ungodly people, who knew God but did not glorify Him as God or give thanks. I had fallen into this too, but Your right hand held me up, took me out of it, and set me where I could recover. For You have said to man, Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and, Do not desire to seem wise, because those who claimed to be wise became fools. And I had now found the fine pearl, and I ought to have sold all I had to buy it; and I hesitated.

So I went to Simplicianus, who had been father to Ambrose, now a bishop, when Ambrose received Your grace, and whom Ambrose truly loved as a father. I told him the winding course of my wanderings. When I mentioned that I had read certain books of the Platonists, which Victorinus, once Professor of Rhetoric at Rome (who, I had heard, died a Christian), had translated into Latin, he said how glad he was that I had not stumbled on the writings of other philosophers, which are full of fallacies and deceits, after the elements of this world, whereas the Platonists in every way lead one toward belief in God and His Word. Then, to urge me toward the humility of Christ, which is hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones, he recalled Victorinus himself, whom he had known very closely while he was at Rome; and he told me a story about him that I will not keep silent. For it holds great praise of Your grace, which must be confessed to You: how that aged man, deeply learned and highly skilled in all the liberal arts, who had read and judged so many works of the philosophers; the teacher of so many noble senators; who also, as a mark of his outstanding teaching, had both earned and received a statue in the Roman Forum (something the citizens of this world count a signal honor); he who up to that age had worshipped idols and taken part in the sacrilegious rites to which almost the whole Roman nobility was then given over, and who had filled the people with love of
Anubis, the barking god, and every kind of monster-god, who once took arms against Neptune and Venus and Minerva:

gods whom Rome had once conquered and now worshipped, all of which the aged Victorinus had defended for so many years with thunderous eloquence; he now did not blush to become the child of Your Christ and a newborn infant at Your font, bending his neck to the yoke of humility and bowing his forehead to the shame of the Cross.

O Lord, Lord, who bowed the heavens and came down, who touched the mountains and they smoked, by what means did You make Your way into that heart? He used to read the holy Scripture, as Simplicianus said, and he studied and searched through all the Christian writings with the greatest care. And he would say to Simplicianus, not openly but privately, as a friend, "You should know that I am already a Christian." Simplicianus would answer, "I will not believe it, nor count you among the Christians, until I see you in the Church of Christ." The other would laugh and reply, "So do walls make Christians?" He said this often, that he was already a Christian; Simplicianus gave the same answer just as often; and the joke about the "walls" was just as often repeated. For he was afraid of offending his friends, proud worshippers of demons, and he thought that from the height of their Babylonian grandeur, as from the cedars of Lebanon which the Lord had not yet broken, their hostility would come crashing down heavily on him. But after he had drawn strength from reading and eager longing, he began to fear that Christ would deny him before the holy angels if he were now afraid to confess Christ before men. He saw himself guilty of a great offense in being ashamed of the sacraments of the humility of Your Word, while not being ashamed of the sacrilegious rites of those proud demons, whose pride he had imitated and whose rites he had taken up. So he grew shameless toward vanity and ashamed before the truth, and suddenly, without warning, he said to Simplicianus (as Simplicianus himself told me), "Let us go to the Church; I want to be made a Christian." Simplicianus, beside himself with joy, went with him. He was admitted to the first sacrament and became a catechumen, and not long afterward he also gave in his name to be reborn through baptism, while Rome marvelled and the Church rejoiced. The proud saw it and were furious; they gnashed their teeth and wasted away. But the Lord God was the hope of Your servant, and he paid no attention to vanities and lying madness.

Finally, when the hour came for him to make his profession of faith (which at Rome those who are about to come to Your grace deliver from a raised place, in the sight of all the faithful, in a fixed form of words learned by heart), the presbyters, he said, offered Victorinus the chance to make his profession more privately, as was usually offered to those who seemed likely to be frightened by shyness. But he chose instead to profess his salvation in the presence of the holy congregation. "For what he had taught in rhetoric was not salvation, and yet he had professed it publicly; how much less, then, should he fear Your gentle flock when speaking Your word, when he had not feared crowds of madmen when speaking his own words!" So when he went up to make his profession, everyone who knew him whispered his name to one another in tones of delight. And who there did not know him? A low murmur ran through the mouths of all the rejoicing crowd: Victorinus! Victorinus! Suddenly they broke out in joy at seeing him; suddenly they fell silent so that they could hear him. He declared the true faith with splendid confidence, and all of them wanted to take him into their very hearts; and by their love and joy they did take him there. Those were the hands they took him with.

Good God! What happens in a human being that makes him rejoice more over the salvation of a soul that was given up for lost and rescued from greater danger than if there had always been hope for it, or the danger had been smaller? For You too, merciful Father, rejoice more over one who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance. And we listen with great gladness whenever we hear how joyfully the sheep that had strayed is carried back on the shepherd's shoulders, and how the coin is restored to Your treasury while the neighbors rejoice with the woman who found it. And the joy of the solemn worship in Your house moves us to tears when, in Your house, we hear read about Your younger son, that he was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found. For You rejoice in us and in Your holy angels, who are holy through holy love. For You are always the same; all things that do not stay the same or last forever, You know forever in the same way.

What, then, happens in the soul, that it takes more delight in finding or getting back the things it loves than if it had always had them? Other things bear witness to this too; everything is full of witnesses crying out, "That is how it is." The victorious general celebrates his triumph; yet he would not have won if he had not fought, and the greater the danger in the battle, the greater the joy in the triumph. A storm tosses the sailors and threatens shipwreck; all of them turn pale at the thought of approaching death; then sky and sea grow calm, and their joy is extreme because their fear was extreme. A friend is ill, and his pulse signals danger; all who long for him to recover are sick at heart along with him. He gets better, though he does not yet walk with his old strength; yet there is a joy now that there never was before, when he walked about sound and strong. Indeed, people come by the very pleasures of human life through hardships, not only the ones that fall on us unexpectedly and against our will, but also through troubles they choose for themselves and go looking for. Eating and drinking give no pleasure unless the pinch of hunger and thirst comes first. Drinkers eat certain salty foods to produce an uncomfortable heat, and when the drink relieves it, that gives pleasure. It is also the custom that a promised bride is not handed over at once, so that the husband will not hold cheap the woman he did not long for while she was betrothed to him.

This law holds in shameful and cursed joy; it holds in joy that is permitted and lawful; it holds in the very purest and most honorable friendship; it holds in him who was dead and came back to life, who was lost and was found. Everywhere the greater joy is preceded by the greater pain. What does this mean, O Lord my God, when You Yourself are eternal joy to Yourself, and some beings around You rejoice in You forever? What does it mean that this part of creation swings back and forth between loss and gain, between offense and reconciliation? Is this their appointed measure? Is this all You have given them, when from the highest heavens to the lowest depths of the earth, from the beginning of the world to the end of the ages, from the angel to the worm, from the first motion to the last, You set every kind of good thing and all Your just works each in its own place, and carry out each in its own time? Ah me! How high You are in the heights, and how deep in the depths! You never go away, and we barely find our way back to You.

Come, Lord, act; rouse us and call us back; set us on fire and carry us away; blaze and grow sweet to us; let us love, let us run. Do not many return to You out of a deeper hell of blindness than Victorinus, and come near, and are enlightened, receiving that Light? And those who receive it receive power from You to become Your sons. But if they are less known to the public, even those who know them rejoice less over them. For when many rejoice together, the joy of each one is richer too, because they warm and kindle one another. Then again, people known to many carry weight with many toward salvation, and they lead the way for many to follow. That is why those who went before them also rejoice greatly over them, because they are not rejoicing over them alone. Far be it that in Your tabernacle the persons of the rich should be favored above the poor, or the well-born above the lowly, since You have instead chosen the weak things of the world to put the strong to shame, and You have chosen the lowly things of this world, and the despised things, and the things that are not, to bring to nothing the things that are. And yet that same least of Your apostles, through whose tongue You sounded out these very words, when by his campaigning the proconsul Paulus had his pride overthrown and was sent under the gentle yoke of Your Christ, and became a subject of the great King, he too chose to be called Paul instead of his former name, Saul, as a mark of so great a victory. For the enemy is more thoroughly defeated in someone he holds more tightly and through whom he holds more people. And he holds the proud more tightly through their noble rank, and through them he holds more people by their influence. So the more welcome it was to think of the heart of Victorinus, which the devil had held as a stronghold that could not be taken, and the tongue of Victorinus, the great sharp weapon with which he had killed many, the more abundantly Your sons ought to rejoice, because our King had bound the strong man, and they saw his vessels taken from him, cleansed, and made fit for Your honor, and useful to the Lord for every good work.

But when Your servant Simplicianus told me this about Victorinus, I burned to imitate him; that was exactly why he had told it. And when he added how, in the time of the Emperor Julian, a law was passed forbidding Christians to teach literature and oratory, and how Victorinus embraced that law and chose to abandon the school of chatter rather than Your Word, by which You make eloquent the tongues of those who cannot speak, he seemed to me not so much brave as fortunate, because he had found the chance to give his time to You alone. That was what I was sighing for, bound as I was, not by someone else's irons but by my own iron will. The enemy held my will, and out of it he had made a chain for me and bound me tight. For from a perverse will came lust; lust given in to became habit; and habit not resisted became necessity. By these links, joined one to another (which is why I called it a chain), a harsh bondage held me captive. But the new will that had begun to form in me, the will to serve You freely and to want to enjoy You, O God, the only sure delight, was not yet strong enough to overcome the old will, hardened by long years. So my two wills, one new and the other old, one of the flesh and the other of the spirit, fought with each other inside me, and by their conflict they tore my soul apart.

So I understood from my own experience what I had read, how the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. I myself was on both sides; but I was more myself in what I approved in myself than in what I disapproved of in myself. For in the latter it was now for the most part no longer I, since much of it I suffered unwillingly rather than did willingly. And yet it was through me that habit had gained this power to fight against me, because I had willingly arrived where I did not want to be. And who can rightly object when just punishment follows the sinner? Nor did I any longer have my old excuse, that the reason I still hesitated to rise above the world and serve You was that I had no certain grasp of the truth; for now that too was certain. But I, still tied to the earth, refused to fight in Your service, and I was as afraid of being freed from all my entanglements as one ought to be afraid of being entangled by them. So I was held down pleasantly by the baggage of this world, as if in sleep; and the thoughts in which I turned my mind to You were like the efforts of people who want to wake up but are overpowered by heavy drowsiness and sink back into it again. No one wants to sleep forever, and everyone of sound judgment agrees that being awake is better; and yet a man, feeling a heavy sluggishness in all his limbs, usually puts off shaking off sleep, and even when it is time to get up, he half-reluctantly gives in to it with pleasure. In the same way I was sure it would be much better for me to give myself up to Your love than to surrender to my own desire; but while the first convinced me and was winning, the second pleased me and kept me bound. And I had no answer to give You when You called to me, Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall give you light. And when You showed me on every side that what You said was true, I, convicted by the truth, had nothing at all to answer except those slow and sleepy words: "Soon, yes, soon"; "In a moment"; "Just let me be a little longer." But "soon, soon" never arrived, and my "little longer" went on for a long time. In vain did I delight in Your law according to the inner man, when another law in my members fought against the law of my mind and led me captive to the law of sin that was in my members. For the law of sin is the force of habit, by which the mind is dragged along and held even against its will; and deservedly so, since it slipped into that habit willingly. Who, then, would deliver me, wretched as I was, from the body of this death, except Your grace alone, through Jesus Christ our Lord?

And now I will tell how You set me free from the chain of desire that bound me so tightly to carnal concupiscence, and from the drudgery of worldly affairs, and I will confess it to Your name, O Lord, my helper and my redeemer. With my anxiety growing, I went about my usual business and sighed to You every day. I went to Your Church whenever I was free from the business under whose weight I groaned. Alypius was with me, released from his legal work after his third term as assessor and waiting for someone to sell his advice to, just as I sold skill in speaking, if teaching can really give it. Nebridius, out of regard for our friendship, had now agreed to teach under Verecundus, a citizen and grammarian of Milan and a very close friend of us all, who urgently wanted, and by the right of friendship claimed from our circle, the reliable help he badly needed. So Nebridius was not drawn to this by any wish for gain (he could have made far more of his learning if he had wanted to), but, being a most kind and gentle friend, he would not fail to do a good turn or brush aside our request. He handled this very wisely, though, taking care not to become known to people who are great by this world's standards, and so avoiding the distraction of mind that would follow, since he wanted to keep his mind free and at leisure for as many hours as possible to seek, read or hear something about wisdom.

One day, then, when Nebridius was away (I do not remember why), a man named Pontitianus came to visit Alypius and me. He was our countryman, at least in being an African, and held a high office at the Emperor's court. What he wanted with us I do not know, but we sat down to talk, and it happened that he noticed a book lying on a games table in front of us. He picked it up, opened it, and found, to his surprise, that it was the Apostle Paul; he had assumed it was one of the books I was wearing myself out teaching. At that he smiled, looked at me, and expressed his joy and surprise at suddenly finding this book, and only this one, in front of me. For he was a Christian, baptized, and he often knelt before You, our God, in the Church in frequent and lengthy prayers. When I told him that I was giving those Scriptures a great deal of attention, a conversation began, prompted by his own account, about Antony, the Egyptian monk, whose name was held in great honor among Your servants, though until that hour it was unknown to us. When he found this out, he dwelt all the longer on the subject, telling us about this great man and marvelling at our ignorance of him. We, for our part, were astonished to hear of Your wonderful works, so fully attested, done so recently, almost in our own day, in the true faith and the Catholic Church. All of us were amazed: we, that these things were so great, and he, that they had not reached us.

From there his talk turned to the communities in the monasteries, to their holy way of life, a sweet-smelling fragrance to You, and to the rich fruitfulness of the desert, of which we knew nothing. There was even a monastery at Milan, outside the city walls, full of good brothers and under Ambrose's care, and we had not known it. He went on talking, and we listened in rapt silence. Then he told us how, one afternoon at Triers, while the Emperor was occupied with the games in the circus, he and three companions went out for a walk in the gardens next to the city walls. As it happened, they were walking in pairs: one went off with him, and the other two wandered off on their own. In their wandering these two came upon a small house where some of Your servants lived, poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs, and there they found a little book containing the life of Antony. One of them began to read it, to marvel at it and to catch fire from it; and as he read, he began to think about taking up such a life and giving up his worldly career to serve You. These two belonged to the officials known as agents for public affairs. Then, suddenly filled with holy love and sober shame, and angry with himself, he turned his eyes on his friend and said, "Tell me, please, what are we trying to achieve with all these labors of ours? What are we aiming at? What are we serving for? Can our hopes at court rise any higher than becoming the Emperor's friends? And in that position, what is not fragile and full of dangers? And through how many dangers do we reach a still greater danger? And when will we even get there? But a friend of God, if I want it, I can become right now." That is what he said. And in the pain of giving birth to a new life, he turned his eyes back to the book and read on, and he was changed within, where You saw, and his mind was stripped of the world, as soon became clear. For as he read, and the waves of his heart rolled and churned, he raged at himself for a while, then saw clearly and decided on the better course. And now, being Yours, he said to his friend, "I have now broken away from those hopes of ours, and I have resolved to serve God; and I am beginning it from this hour, in this place. If you do not want to follow me, do not stand in my way." The other replied that he would stay with him, to share so great a reward and so great a service. So both of them, now Yours, were building the tower at the proper cost, which is leaving all that they had and following You. Then Pontitianus and the man with him, who had been walking in other parts of the garden, came looking for them and arrived at the same place. Finding them, they reminded them that it was time to go back, since the day was far gone. But the two told them their decision and their purpose, and how that will had arisen and become fixed in them, and they asked the others, if they would not join them, at least not to trouble them. The other two, though not changed at all from what they had been, nevertheless wept over themselves, as he told us, congratulated their friends devoutly, and commended themselves to their prayers; and so, with their hearts still dragging along the ground, they went off to the palace. But the other two, fixing their hearts on heaven, stayed in the little house. Both of them were engaged to be married, and when their brides-to-be heard of this, they too dedicated their virginity to God.

This was the story Pontitianus told. But while he was speaking, You, O Lord, were turning me around to face myself. You took me from behind my own back, where I had put myself because I did not want to look at myself, and You set me in front of my own face, so that I might see how foul I was, how crooked and filthy, stained and covered with sores. I looked and was horrified, and I found nowhere to run from myself. And if I tried to turn my gaze away from myself, he went on with his story, and You set me face to face with myself again and pushed me before my own eyes, so that I would discover my wickedness and hate it. I had known it, but I pretended not to see it; I shut my eyes to it and forgot it.

But now, the more fiercely I loved those whose healthy feelings I was hearing about, how they had given themselves wholly to You to be healed, the more I loathed myself in comparison with them. For many years of mine, about twelve, had now slipped away since my nineteenth year, when reading Cicero's Hortensius stirred me to an eager love of wisdom; and I was still putting off turning my back on mere earthly happiness and giving myself to the search for that wisdom, of which not merely the finding but even the seeking ought to be valued above the treasures and kingdoms of the world, even if already found, and above the pleasures of the body, even if they flowed around me at my command. But I, wretched, utterly wretched young man that I was, at the very start of my youth had begged You for chastity and said, "Give me chastity and continence, but not yet." For I was afraid that You would hear me quickly and quickly cure me of the disease of concupiscence, which I wanted satisfied rather than put out. And I had gone down crooked paths in a sacrilegious superstition, not because I was really sure of it, but because I preferred it to the others, which I did not seek out in a spirit of devotion but attacked out of malice.

And I had thought that the reason I was putting off, day after day, turning my back on the hopes of this world and following You alone was that I could see nothing certain to steer my course by. And now the day had come when I was to be stripped bare before myself, and my conscience was to rebuke me: "Where are you now, my tongue? You said that you would not throw off the baggage of vanity for the sake of a truth that was uncertain. Well, now it is certain, and still that burden weighs you down, while people who have not worn themselves out searching for it, and have not spent ten years and more thinking about it, have had their shoulders set free and have been given wings to fly away." So I was gnawed at inside, and utterly overwhelmed by a terrible shame, while Pontitianus was speaking. When he had finished his story and the business he had come about, he went his way, and I went into myself. What did I not say against myself? With what whips of condemnation did I not lash my soul, to make it follow me as I struggled to go after You! Yet it held back. It refused, but it offered no excuse. Every argument had been used up and refuted; all that was left was a speechless dread, and it feared, as it would fear death, being held back from the flow of that habit by which it was wasting away to death.

Then, in the middle of that great struggle in my inner house, which I had stirred up so violently against my soul in the private chamber of my heart, troubled in mind and face alike, I turned on Alypius. "What is wrong with us?" I cried. "What is this? What did you hear? The unlearned rise up and take heaven by force, and here we are with all our learning, and no heart, wallowing in flesh and blood! Are we ashamed to follow because others have gone ahead, and not ashamed not even to follow?" I said something like this, and my inner fever tore me away from him, while he stared at me in astonishment and said nothing. For I did not sound like myself; my forehead, cheeks, eyes, color and tone of voice expressed my mind more than the words I spoke. There was a small garden at our lodging, which we were free to use, as we were the whole house, since the master of the house, our host, did not live there. The turmoil in my breast had driven me there, where no one could interrupt the fierce struggle I had begun with myself, until it came to the end that You knew and I did not. I was only going out of my mind in a way that would heal me, dying so as to live, knowing what an evil thing I was, and not knowing what good thing I was soon to become. So I withdrew into the garden, and Alypius followed close behind me. For his being there did not make me any less alone; and how could he leave me in such a state? We sat down as far from the house as we could. I was troubled in spirit, angry with the most violent indignation that I did not enter into Your will and covenant, O my God, which all my bones cried out to me to enter, praising it to the skies. And we do not enter there by ships or chariots or on foot; we do not even need to move as far as I had come from the house to the place where we were sitting. For not only to go there, but to arrive there, was nothing other than to will to go, but to will it strongly and completely; not to twist and toss this way and that a maimed, half-divided will, struggling, with one part rising and the other sinking.

In the very fever of my indecision, I made many movements with my body, the kind that people sometimes want to make but cannot, if they either lack the limbs, or have them tied with bonds, or weakened by illness, or hampered in some other way. So if I tore my hair, if I beat my forehead, if I clasped my knee with my fingers locked together, I did it because I willed it. But I could have willed it and not done it, if my limbs' power of movement had not obeyed. So I did many things where "to will" was not the same as "to be able"; and I did not do the thing I longed to do incomparably more, the thing I would soon be able to do as soon as I willed it, because as soon as I willed it I would will it completely. For in this matter the ability was the same as the will, and to will was already to do; and yet it was not done. My body obeyed the faintest wish of my soul more easily, moving its limbs at a nod, than my soul obeyed itself in carrying out this great will of its own, which needed only to be willed.

Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? Let Your mercy shine, so that I may ask, in case the hidden punishments of mankind and the darkest sufferings of the sons of Adam can perhaps give me an answer. Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? The mind commands the body, and it obeys at once; the mind commands itself, and meets resistance. The mind commands the hand to move, and it does so with such readiness that you can hardly tell the command from its being carried out. And yet the mind is mind, and the hand is body. The mind commands the mind, its own self, to will, and yet it does not. Where does this monstrous thing come from? And why? It commands itself, I say, to will; it would not give the command unless it willed; and yet what it commands is not done. But it does not will fully, and so it does not command fully. For it commands only so far as it wills, and what it commands goes undone just so far as it does not will. For the will commands that there be a will, not some other will, but itself. But it does not command fully, and so what it commands does not happen. For if the will were whole, it would not even command itself to be, because it would already be. So it is not a monstrous thing partly to will and partly not to will; it is a sickness of the mind, which does not rise up wholly, lifted by the truth, because it is weighed down by habit. And so there are two wills, because neither of them is whole, and what one lacks the other has.

Let them perish from Your presence, O God, as empty talkers and deceivers of the mind perish, those who notice that in making a decision there are two wills and then claim that we have two minds of two different natures, one good and the other evil. They themselves are truly evil when they hold these evil views; and they themselves will become good if they hold the truth and agree with the truth, so that Your Apostle may say to them, You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. But they want to be light, not in the Lord but in themselves, imagining that the nature of the soul is the same as what God is; and so they have become a thicker darkness through their terrible arrogance, because they have drawn further away from You, the true Light that enlightens every man who comes into the world. Take care what you say, and blush with shame: come to Him and be enlightened, and your faces will not be put to shame. When I was deliberating about serving the Lord my God at last, as I had long intended, it was I who willed and I who did not will; it was I, I myself. I neither willed completely nor refused completely. So I was at war with myself and torn apart by myself. And this tearing happened to me against my will, and yet it showed not the presence of another mind but the punishment of my own. So it was no longer I who did it, but the sin that dwelt in me, the punishment of a sin committed more freely, because I was a son of Adam.

For if there are as many opposing natures as there are wills in conflict, there will now be not just two but many. If someone is deciding whether to go to their meeting or to the theater, these Manichees cry out, Look, here are two natures: a good one leading him this way, a bad one pulling him back that way. For where else would this wavering between conflicting wills come from? But I say that both are bad, the one that leads him to them and the one that pulls him back to the theater. They, however, do not believe that the will that leads to them can be anything but good. What, then, if one of us is deciding, and wavering as his two wills quarrel within him, whether to go to the theater or to our church? Would these Manichees not be wavering too about what to answer? For either they will have to admit, which they do not want to do, that it is a good will that leads a person to our church, just as it is with those who go there because they have received its sacraments and are held by them; or they will have to suppose that two evil natures and two evil souls are fighting in one man, and then what they say will not be true, that one is good and the other bad; or they will be converted to the truth and stop denying that, when someone deliberates, a single soul is tossed about between different wills.

So let them stop saying, when they notice two wills in conflict within one person, that the conflict is between two opposed souls, made of two opposed substances and coming from two opposed principles, one good and the other bad. For You, O true God, refute them, rebuke them and convict them. Take the case where both wills are bad, as when someone is deciding whether to kill a man with poison or with a sword; whether to seize this estate belonging to someone else or that one, when he cannot take both; whether to buy pleasure through extravagance or to keep his money through greed; whether to go to the circus or to the theater, if both are showing on the same day; or, a third option, to rob someone else's house, if the chance presents itself; or, a fourth, to commit adultery, if the opportunity for that opens up at the same time. Suppose all these come together at the same moment, and all are desired equally, though they cannot all be done at once: then they tear the mind apart among four conflicting wills, or even more, given the huge number of things people desire; and yet these people do not usually claim that there are that many different substances. The same is true of good wills. For I ask them whether it is good to take delight in reading the Apostle, and whether it is good to take delight in a sober Psalm, and whether it is good to discuss the Gospel. To each they will answer, "It is good." What, then, if all of them please us equally and all at the same time? Do not different wills pull the heart in different directions while we decide which one to take up first? And all of them are good, and they compete with one another until one is chosen, so that the whole will, which was divided among many, may be carried toward that one. In the same way, when eternity delights us from above and the pleasure of a temporal good holds us back below, it is the same soul, willing neither this nor that with its whole will, and so it is torn apart by grievous distress, because truth makes it put the first ahead, while habit keeps it from putting the second aside.

So I was sick and in torment, accusing myself far more harshly than usual, rolling and twisting in my chain until it would snap completely, since by now it held me only slightly, but it still held me. And You, O Lord, pressed on me in my inmost depths with a stern mercy, redoubling the lashes of fear and shame, so that I would not give up again, and so that the thin, slight bond that was left would not stay unbroken, regain its strength and tie me down more tightly. For I kept saying to myself inside, "Let it be done now, let it be done now." And as I said it, I was already on the point of deciding. I almost did it, and yet I did not do it. Still, I did not slide back into my old state, but stood close by and caught my breath. Then I tried again, and I was a little nearer, and a little nearer still; I was all but touching it and grasping it. And yet I was not there; I did not touch it or grasp it, hesitating to die to death and to live to life. The worse, which had grown ingrained in me, had more power over me than the better, to which I was unaccustomed; and the very moment at which I was to become something different, the closer it came, the greater the horror it struck into me. Yet it did not drive me back or turn me away, but held me in suspense.

The trifles of trifles and vanities of vanities, my old loves, still held me back. They tugged at my garment of flesh and whispered softly, "Are you sending us away? From this moment will we never be with you again, forever? From this moment will this and that never be allowed to you again, forever?" And what were they suggesting by what I have called "this and that"? What were they suggesting, O my God? Let Your mercy turn it away from the soul of Your servant. What filth they suggested! What shameful things! And by now I heard them far less than half as much. They no longer came out openly to confront me, but muttered, as it were, behind my back, and plucked at me stealthily as I was leaving, to make me look back at them. Yet they did hold me back, so that I hesitated to tear myself away and shake myself free of them and leap across to where I was being called, while a violent habit said to me, "Do you think you can live without them?"

But by now it spoke very faintly. For on the side toward which I had turned my face, and where I trembled to go, the chaste dignity of Continence appeared to me, calm and cheerful but not loose, honorably coaxing me to come and not to hesitate, and stretching out her holy hands, full of crowds of good examples, to receive and embrace me. There were so many boys and girls there, a great throng of young people and of every age, dignified widows and elderly virgins; and in all of them was Continence herself, not barren, but a fruitful mother of children, of joys, born of You, O Lord, her Husband. And she smiled at me with a teasing that urged me on, as if to say, "Can you not do what these young men and these young women can? Or can they do it by themselves, and not rather in the Lord their God? The Lord their God gave me to them. Why do you stand on yourself, and so fail to stand at all? Throw yourself on Him. Do not be afraid; He will not pull away and let you fall. Throw yourself on Him without fear; He will catch you and He will heal you." And I blushed deeply, because I could still hear the muttering of those trifles, and I hung there in suspense. And again she seemed to say, "Shut your ears against those unclean members of yours on the earth, so that they may be put to death. They tell you of delights, but not such as the law of the Lord your God tells." This dispute in my heart was nothing but myself against myself. And Alypius, sitting close beside me, waited in silence to see how my unusual agitation would end.

But when deep reflection had dragged up from the hidden depths of my soul all my misery and piled it up in full view of my heart, a huge storm broke out, bringing a huge downpour of tears. So that I could pour it all out, with all its natural cries, I got up and left Alypius; being alone seemed to me better suited to the business of weeping. So I went off far enough that even his presence could not be a burden to me. That was the state I was in, and he sensed something of it; for I suppose I had said something in which the sound of my voice seemed choked with tears, and that was how I had got up. So he stayed where we had been sitting, utterly astonished. I flung myself down, I do not know how, under a fig tree, and let my tears flow freely; and the floods from my eyes burst out, a sacrifice acceptable to You. And I said many things to You, not in these exact words but to this effect: And You, O Lord, how long? How long, Lord? Will You be angry forever? Do not remember our former iniquities; for I felt that I was still held by them. I cried out these wretched words: How long, how long, "tomorrow, and tomorrow"? Why not now? Why not an end to my uncleanness this very hour?

I was saying these things and weeping in the most bitter contrition of my heart, when suddenly I heard from a house nearby a voice, whether a boy's or a girl's I do not know, chanting and repeating over and over, "Take up and read; take up and read." At once my expression changed, and I began to think very hard whether children used to sing words like these in some kind of game, but I could not remember ever having heard anything like it. So, holding back the rush of my tears, I got up, taking it to be nothing other than a command from God to open the book and read the first passage I came upon. For I had heard about Antony, that he had happened to come in while the Gospel was being read, and took it as a warning addressed to him, as if what was being read were spoken to him: Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me. And by such a sign he was at once converted to You. So I hurried back to the place where Alypius was sitting, because I had put down the volume of the Apostle there when I got up. I snatched it up, opened it, and read in silence the passage my eyes first fell on: Not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, in concupiscence. I did not want to read any further, and there was no need. For instantly, as I reached the end of that sentence, it was as though a light of serenity had been poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt fled away.

Then, putting my finger or some other marker in the page, I closed the book, and with a face now calm I told Alypius. And he in turn told me, in this way, what had been happening in him, which I had not known. He asked to see what I had read. I showed him, and he looked further on than I had read; I did not know what came next. What came next was this: Receive him who is weak in the faith. He applied this to himself and told me so. And he was strengthened by this admonition, and by a good decision and purpose, one very much in keeping with his character, in which he had always been far and away better than I, he joined me without any troubled delay. From there we go in to my mother and tell her; she is glad. We relate how it all happened; she leaps for joy and triumphs, and blesses You, who are able to do more than we ask or think; for she saw that You had granted her far more concerning me than she used to beg for with her pitiful, tearful groans. For You converted me to Yourself, so that I no longer sought a wife or any hope of this world, but stood on that rule of faith where, so many years before, You had shown me to her in a vision. And You turned her mourning into joy, a joy far richer than she had wanted, and far dearer and purer than the one she once looked for in having grandchildren from my body.

chapters.title: Book 9
paragraphs: O Lord, I am Your servant; I am Your servant, and the son of Your handmaid: You have broken my bonds apart. I will offer You the sacrifice of praise. Let my heart and my tongue praise You; yes, let all my bones say, O Lord, who is like You? Let them say it, and then answer me, and say to my soul, I am your salvation. Who am I, and what sort of man am I? What evil has there not been, if not in my deeds, then in my words, and if not in my words, then in my will? But You, O Lord, are good and merciful. Your right hand looked upon the depth of my death, and drained that abyss of corruption from the bottom of my heart. And this was the whole of Your gift: that I should refuse what I had willed, and will what You willed. But where was my free will through all those years, and out of what low and deep hiding place was it called out in a moment, so that I could bow my neck to Your easy yoke and put my shoulders under Your light burden, O Christ Jesus, my Helper and my Redeemer? How sweet it suddenly became to me to be without the sweetness of those trifles! What I had been afraid to lose, I was now glad to let go. For You were driving them out of me, You who are the true and highest sweetness. You drove them out, and in their place You came in Yourself, sweeter than every pleasure, though not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light, yet more inward than any hidden depth; higher than every honor, though not to those who are high in their own eyes. Now my soul was free from the gnawing cares of seeking favor and getting gain, of wallowing in filth and scratching the itch of lust. And like a child I chattered freely to You, my brightness, my riches, my health, the Lord my God.

And I decided, in Your sight, not to tear my tongue's service out of the market of talk in a noisy way, but to withdraw it quietly. I did not want boys who were studying neither Your law nor Your peace, but lying follies and the battles of the courts, to go on buying weapons for their madness from my mouth. And very conveniently, only a very few days now remained before the Vintage Vacation. I resolved to endure them, and then to take my leave in the proper way, so that, having been bought back by You, I would never again return to be put up for sale. Our plan, then, was known to You; but it was not known to other people, apart from our own friends. For we had agreed among ourselves not to spread it around to anyone. And yet, as we climbed up out of the valley of tears and sang that song of ascents, You had given us sharp arrows and destroying coals against the deceitful tongue, the kind of tongue that opposes us as if it were giving us advice, and that devours us out of love, the way it devours its food.

You had pierced our hearts with Your love, and we carried Your words as though they were fixed deep inside us. And the examples of Your servants, whom You had turned from black to bright and from dead to living, were gathered together in the storehouse of our thoughts. They burned away our heavy sluggishness, so that we would not sink toward the depths, and they set us on fire so fiercely that every gust from the deceitful tongues of those who opposed us could only fan the flame higher, not put it out. Nevertheless, for the sake of Your Name, which You have made holy throughout the earth, our vow and purpose would no doubt also find some people to praise it. So it seemed like showing off not to wait for the vacation, now so close, but to walk away early from a public profession that was in front of everyone's eyes. Then everyone, turning to look at what I had done and noticing how near the vintage holiday was that I had chosen to anticipate, would say a great deal about me, as though I had wanted to seem an important person. And what good would it have done me to have people guessing and arguing about my intentions, and to have our good spoken of as evil?

There was more. That very summer, from too much literary work, my lungs had begun to give way. I found it hard to breathe deeply, the pains in my chest showed that they were damaged, and they would not let me speak loudly or for long. At first this had troubled me, because it was almost forcing me to lay down the burden of teaching altogether, or at least to break it off, if I could be treated and recover. But once the full desire to be at leisure, and to see that You are the Lord, had risen up in me and taken firm hold, then, my God, You know that I even began to be glad that I had this further excuse, and not a false one. It could somewhat soften the offense of those who, for their sons' sake, never wanted me to have the freedom of Your sons. So, full of this joy, I put up with that stretch of time until it ran out; I think it was perhaps twenty days. Even so, I endured them bravely; endured them, because the greed that used to carry part of this heavy business with me had gone, and I was left alone with it; I would have been crushed if patience had not taken its place. Perhaps some of Your servants, my brothers, will say that I sinned in this: that with a heart already fully set on Your service I let myself sit even one hour in the chair of lies. I will not argue. But You, most merciful Lord, have You not pardoned and forgiven this sin too, along with my other horrible and deadly sins, in the holy water?

Verecundus was worn down with worry over this happiness of ours, because he saw that the bonds that held him so tightly were going to cut him off from our company. He was not yet a Christian himself, though his wife was one of the faithful; and yet it was precisely by her, more firmly than by any other chain, that he was held back from the journey we had now set out on. For he said he did not want to be a Christian in any other way than the one that was impossible for him. All the same, he very kindly offered to let us stay at his country house for as long as we were there. You will repay him, O Lord, at the resurrection of the just, since You have already given him the lot of the righteous. For while we were away, already in Rome, he was struck by a bodily illness, and during it he became a Christian, one of the faithful, and departed this life. So You had mercy not only on him but on us too, so that we would not be tortured by unbearable grief, remembering our friend's great kindness to us and yet unable to count him among Your flock. Thanks be to You, our God! We are Yours. Your encouragements and consolations tell us so. Faithful to Your promises, You now repay Verecundus for that country house of his at Cassiacum, where we rested in You from the fever of the world, with the loveliness of Your Paradise, green forever. For You have forgiven him his sins on earth, on that rich mountain, the mountain that flows with milk, Your own mountain.

So at that time he was sad, but Nebridius shared our joy. For he too, before he was a Christian, had fallen into the pit of that most destructive error of believing that the flesh of Your Son was a phantom. Yet he had climbed out of it and held the same belief as we did. He had not yet received any of the Sacraments of Your Church, but he was a most passionate seeker of truth. Not long after our conversion and our rebirth through Your Baptism, when he too had become one of the Catholic faithful and was serving You in perfect chastity and continence among his own people in Africa, and his whole household had become Christian through him, You released him from the flesh. And now he lives in Abraham's bosom. Whatever it is that is meant by that bosom, that is where my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, and Your son, O Lord, adopted after being a freedman: that is where he lives. For what other place is there for such a soul? He lives in that place about which he used to ask me, a poor untried man, so many questions. Now he no longer puts his ear to my mouth, but puts his spiritual mouth to Your fountain, and drinks as much wisdom as he can hold, as much as his thirst desires, happy without end. And I do not think he is so drunk with it that he forgets me, since You, Lord, whom he drinks, remember us. That was how things stood with us then. We comforted Verecundus, who was sad about our conversion, though without any harm to our friendship, and we urged him toward the faith suited to his condition, that is, to married life. And we were waiting for Nebridius to follow us, which, being so close, he could do, and he was on the very point of doing it. And then, look, those days finally rolled by. They had seemed long and many, because of my love for the freedom of leisure, so that I could sing to You from my inmost marrow: My heart has said to You, I have sought Your face: Your face, Lord, I will seek.

Then the day came when I was actually released from my Professorship of Rhetoric, from which I had already been released in thought. And it was done. You rescued my tongue, as You had already rescued my heart. And I blessed You, rejoicing, as I set out for the country house with all my people. What I did there in writing, which was now enlisted in Your service, though it was still panting from the school of pride, as if in a pause for breath, my books bear witness: both the discussions I held with those present and the ones I held with myself alone before You. What I discussed with Nebridius, who was absent, my letters bear witness. And when will I have time enough to recount all Your great kindnesses to us in that period, especially when I am hurrying on to still greater mercies? For my memory calls me back, and it is sweet to me, O Lord, to confess to You by what inner goads You tamed me, and how You leveled me by bringing low the mountains and hills of my proud thoughts, straightening what was crooked in me and smoothing my rough places. And I recall how You also brought the brother of my heart, Alypius, to submit to the name of Your Only Begotten, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, a name he at first would not allow to be put into our writings. For he would rather have had them smell of the lofty cedars of the Schools, which the Lord has now broken down, than of the healthy herbs of the Church, which are a remedy against serpents.

Oh, what words I spoke to You, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, those songs of faith, those sounds of devotion that leave no room for a swollen spirit! I was still a Catechumen, a beginner in the true love of You, resting at that country house with Alypius, also a Catechumen, and with my mother staying close to us: a woman in dress, a man in faith, with the calm of old age, a mother's love and a Christian's piety. Oh, what words I poured out to You in those Psalms, and how they set me burning toward You, and how eager they made me to recite them, if I could, to the whole world, against the pride of the human race! And yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and no one can hide himself from Your heat. With what fierce and bitter grief I was angry with the Manichees! And then again I pitied them, because they did not know those Sacraments, those medicines, and raged against the very antidote that could have cured them of their madness.
