How I wish they had been somewhere near me at that time, and, without my knowing they were there, could have watched my face and heard my words when I read the fourth Psalm in that time of rest, and seen what that Psalm did to me: When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in trouble You set me at large. Have mercy on me, O Lord, and hear my prayer. If only they could have heard what I said over these words, without my knowing whether they heard, so that they would not think I was saying it for their benefit! For in truth I would not have said the same things, or said them in the same way, if I had sensed that they were hearing and watching me. Nor, if I had said them, would they have taken them in the way I meant them when I spoke by myself and for myself before You, out of the natural feelings of my soul.

I trembled with fear, and then again I glowed with hope and with joy in Your mercy, O Father. And all of it came out through my eyes and my voice, when Your good Spirit turned to us and said, O sons of men, how long will you be slow of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after lies? For I had loved vanity and sought after lies. And You, O Lord, had already magnified Your Holy One, raising Him from the dead and setting Him at Your right hand, from where, on high, He was to send His promise, the Comforter, the Spirit of truth. And He had already sent Him, but I did not know it. He had sent Him because He was now magnified, having risen again from the dead and ascended into heaven. For until then the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. And the prophet cries out, How long, slow of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek after lies? Know this: the Lord has magnified His Holy One. He cries out, How long? He cries out, Know this. And I, for so long not knowing, had loved vanity and sought after lies. That is why I heard it and trembled, because it was spoken to people like the man I remembered I had been. For in those phantoms that I had taken for truths there was vanity and lying. And I said many things aloud, earnestly and forcefully, in the bitterness of remembering. If only they had heard them, those who still love vanity and seek after lies! Perhaps they would have been shaken and vomited it up, and You would have heard them when they cried to You. For it was by a true death in the flesh that He died for us, He who now intercedes with You for us.

I read on: Be angry, and do not sin. And how it moved me, O my God! I had now learned to be angry with myself for what was past, so that I would not sin in the future. Yes, to be angry with good reason, because it was not some other nature, belonging to a race of darkness, that sinned in me, as those people claim who are not angry with themselves and who store up wrath for themselves against the day of wrath and of the revelation of Your just judgment. My good things were no longer outside me, and I no longer looked for them with eyes of flesh under this earthly sun. For those who want to find their joy outside themselves easily become empty, and pour themselves out on the things that are seen and temporal, and in their starving thoughts they lick at the mere images of them. Oh, if only they would grow tired of their hunger and say, Who will show us good things? Then we would say, and they would hear, The light of Your face is sealed upon us. For we are not the light that enlightens every man; we are enlightened by You, so that we who were once darkness may be light in You. Oh, if only they could see that eternal inward thing! I had tasted it, and I was grieved that I could not show it to them, as long as they brought me their heart in their eyes, wandering outside, away from You, and asked, Who will show us good things? For it was there, where I had been angry with myself, inside, in my own chamber, where I had been pierced to the heart, where I had offered sacrifice, slaying my old self and beginning to plan a new life, putting my hope in You, it was there that You had begun to grow sweet to me and had put gladness in my heart. And I cried out as I read these words outwardly and recognized them inwardly. I did not want to be multiplied with worldly goods, wasting time and being wasted by time, when I had, in Your eternal Simple Essence, a different corn, and wine, and oil.

And with a loud cry of my heart I cried out at the next verse: O in peace! O in the Self-same! O what did he say? I will lie down and sleep. For who will stand against us when the saying that is written comes to pass, Death is swallowed up in victory? And You are the Self-same in the highest degree, You who do not change; and in You is the rest that forgets all toil, for there is no one else beside You, and we are not to go after those many other things that are not what You are. But You, Lord, alone have made me dwell in hope. I read and I burned, and I could not find what to do for those deaf and dead people, of whom I myself had been one: a plague, a bitter and blind barker against those writings that are sweet with the honey of heaven and bright with Your own light. And I wasted away with zeal against the enemies of this Scripture.

When will I call to mind everything that happened in those holidays? Still, I have not forgotten, and I will not pass over, the severity of Your scourge and the wonderful swiftness of Your mercy. At that time You tormented me with toothache. When it became so bad that I could not speak, it came into my heart to ask all my friends who were there to pray for me to You, the God of every kind of health. I wrote this on a wax tablet and gave it to them to read. As soon as we had bent our knees in humble devotion, the pain went away. But what pain was it? And how did it go away? I was terrified, O my Lord, my God, for I had never experienced anything like it since infancy. And the power of Your will was deeply impressed upon me, and rejoicing in faith I praised Your Name. And that faith did not let me be at ease about my past sins, which had not yet been forgiven me through Your baptism.

When the vintage vacation was over, I gave notice to the people of Milan that they should find their students another teacher to sell them words, because I had chosen to serve You, and also because my difficulty in breathing and the pain in my chest made me unfit for the Professorship. And by letter I made known to Your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and my present desire, and asked his advice about which of Your Scriptures I should read first, to become more ready and more fit to receive so great a grace. He told me to read the Prophet Isaiah, because, I believe, he foretells the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles more clearly than the others. But I did not understand the first part of it, and, supposing that the whole book would be like that, I put it aside, meaning to take it up again when I was better practiced in the Lord's own words.

Then, when the time came for me to hand in my name, we left the country and went back to Milan. Alypius also decided to be born again in You along with me. He was already clothed in the humility that suits Your Sacraments, and he was so tough a master of his body that, with unusual daring, he walked the frozen ground of Italy in bare feet. We also took with us the boy Adeodatus, born of my sin according to the flesh. You had made him well. He was not quite fifteen, and in intelligence he outdid many serious and learned men. I confess Your gifts to You, O Lord my God, Creator of all, who are abundantly able to reshape what is misshapen in us; for I had no part in that boy except the sin. As for our bringing him up in Your discipline, it was You, and no one else, who inspired us to do it. I confess Your gifts to You. There is a book of ours called The Master; it is a dialogue between him and me. You know that all the ideas given there to the person talking with me were his, when he was in his sixteenth year. I found many other things in him, still more remarkable. His gifts filled me with awe. And who but You could be the craftsman of such wonders? Soon You took his life from the earth, and I now remember him without anxiety, fearing nothing for his childhood or his youth or for him at all. We took him with us, the same age as ourselves in grace, to be brought up in Your discipline. And we were baptized, and the anxiety about our past life fled from us. In those days I could not have enough of the wonderful sweetness of reflecting on the depth of Your counsels for the salvation of the human race. How I wept at Your Hymns and Canticles, moved to the core by the voices of Your sweetly singing Church! The voices flowed into my ears, and the Truth was distilled into my heart. From it the feelings of my devotion overflowed, and tears ran down, and I was happy in them.

The Church of Milan had not long before begun to use this kind of consolation and encouragement, with the brothers singing together eagerly, in harmony of voice and heart. It was a year, or not much more, since Justina, mother of the boy Emperor Valentinian, had persecuted Your servant Ambrose for the sake of her heresy, into which she had been led by the Arians. The devout people kept watch in the church, ready to die with their Bishop, Your servant. There my mother, Your handmaid, who carried a leading share of those anxieties and vigils, lived on prayer. We ourselves, not yet warmed by the heat of Your Spirit, were still stirred by the sight of the city in alarm and turmoil. It was then that hymns and psalms first began to be sung after the manner of the Eastern Churches, so that the people would not lose heart through the weariness of grief. From that day to this the custom has been kept, and many, indeed almost all, of Your congregations in other parts of the world have followed it.

Then in a vision You revealed to the Bishop I have named the place where the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius lay hidden. You had kept them uncorrupted for so many years in Your secret treasury, so that at the right time You could bring them out to check the fury of a woman, though an Empress. For when they had been found and dug up, and were being moved with due honor to the Ambrosian Basilica, not only were people tormented by unclean spirits healed, with the demons themselves confessing it, but a certain man who had been blind for many years, a citizen well known in the city, asked what the people's excited joy was about. When he heard, he leapt up and asked his guide to lead him there. When he had been led there, he begged to be allowed to touch the bier of Your saints, whose death is precious in Your sight, with his handkerchief. He did so, and put it to his eyes, and at once they were opened. From that point the news spread; from that point Your praises glowed and shone; from that point the mind of that enemy, though not brought to the health of believing, was at least turned back from her fury of persecution. Thanks be to You, my God! From where, and to where, have You led my memory, so that I should confess these things to You as well? Great as they are, I had forgotten them and passed them by. And yet even then, when the scent of Your ointments was so fragrant, we did not run after You. That is why I wept all the more while Your Hymns were being sung: I had long sighed for You, and now at last I was breathing You in, as far as breath can come into this house of grass of ours.

You who make people of one mind to live in one house also brought Euodius to join us, a young man from our own town. He had been an officer at court, had been converted to You and baptized before us, and had left the service of the world to enlist in Yours. We were together, and meant to live together in our holy purpose. We looked for the place where we could serve You most usefully, and we were returning to Africa together. On the way, when we had come as far as Ostia, my mother departed this life. I leave out much, because I am hurrying on. Accept my confessions and my thanks, O my God, for countless things I pass over in silence. But I will not leave out whatever my soul brings forth about that handmaid of Yours, who brought me forth both in the flesh, so that I might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, so that I might be born into eternal Light. It is not her gifts I want to speak of, but Yours in her; for she neither made nor brought herself up. You created her, and her father and mother did not know what kind of person would come from them. It was the scepter of Your Christ, the discipline of Your only Son, in a Christian household, a good member of Your Church, that brought her up in Your fear. Yet for her good training she used to praise not so much her mother's care as that of a certain very old maidservant, who had carried her father about when he was a baby, the way little ones used to be carried on the backs of older girls. Because of this, and because of her great age and excellent character, she was highly respected by the heads of that Christian household. So she was also given charge of her master's daughters, and she looked after them carefully. When it was necessary she restrained them firmly with a holy strictness, and she taught them with serious good sense. Except at the times when they ate their very moderate meals at their parents' table, she would not let them drink even water, however thirsty they were. She was guarding against a bad habit, and she added this sound advice: "You drink water now because you have no wine at your disposal. But when you are married and become mistresses of storerooms and cellars, you will turn up your noses at water, but the habit of drinking will stay with you." By this way of teaching, and by the authority she had, she held back the greediness of childhood and shaped the girls' very thirst to such a fine moderation that what they ought not to want, they did not want.

And yet, as Your handmaid told me, her son, a love of wine had crept up on her. For when her parents, as was the custom, would tell her, as a sober girl, to draw wine from the cask, she would hold the cup under the opening and, before pouring the wine into the jug, take a small sip with the tip of her lips; her natural feelings would not let her take more. She did this not from any craving for drink, but from the high spirits of youth, which boil over into playful mischief, and which in young people are usually kept in check by the seriousness of their elders. And so, by adding a little each day to that little (for whoever despises small things will fall little by little), she had slipped into such a habit that she would greedily drain her small cup when it was almost full of wine. Where was that wise old woman then, and her strict forbidding? Would anything be any use against a hidden disease, if Your healing hand, O Lord, did not watch over us? Her father, her mother and her nurses were absent, but You were present, You who create, who call, and who even through those set over us work something toward the salvation of our souls. What did You do then, O my God? How did You cure her? How did You heal her? Did You not draw out of another soul a hard, sharp taunt, like a surgeon's knife from Your secret store, and with one stroke cut away all that rotten matter? For a maidservant who used to go down to the cellar with her got into a quarrel, as happens, with her young mistress when they were alone, and threw this fault in her face with the most bitter insult, calling her a drunkard. Stung to the quick by that taunt, she saw how ugly her fault was, and at once condemned it and gave it up. Just as flattering friends corrupt us, so insulting enemies often correct us. Yet You repay them not for what You do through them, but for what they themselves intended. For the servant in her anger wanted to hurt her young mistress, not to cure her, and she did it in private, either because the time and place of the quarrel happened to find them alone, or because she was afraid she herself would be blamed for having revealed it so late. But You, Lord, Ruler of all things in heaven and on earth, who turn to Your own purposes the deepest currents of the torrent, the ordered turbulence of the flow of the ages, healed one soul through the very sickness of another. You did it so that no one who notices this should credit his own power when someone else he wanted to see reformed is reformed through his words.

So she was brought up modestly and soberly, made subject to her parents by You rather than to You by her parents. As soon as she was old enough to marry, she was given to a husband, and she served him as her lord. She did all she could to win him for You, preaching You to him by the way she lived. By this You adorned her, and made her someone her husband respected, loved and admired. She bore his unfaithfulness to her bed in such a way that she never had a quarrel with her husband about it. For she was waiting for Your mercy upon him, hoping that he would believe in You and become chaste. Besides this, he was hot-tempered, as warm in his anger as in his affection. But she had learned not to oppose an angry husband, not only in what she did but not even in what she said. Only when he had calmed down and was quiet, and in a mood to listen, would she explain what she had done, if it happened that he had taken offense too hastily. In short, many married women whose husbands were gentler than hers still bore shameful marks of blows on their faces, and when they talked among friends they would blame their husbands' behavior. She would blame their tongues, and give them serious advice as if in jest: "From the time you heard the marriage contract read out to you, you should have regarded it as a deed of service, by which you became servants. So, remembering your position, you ought not to set yourselves up against your lords." And they knew what a violent-tempered husband she put up with. So they were amazed that no one had ever heard, or seen any sign, that Patricius had beaten his wife, or that there had been any quarrel at home between them for even a single day. When they asked her privately how this could be, she taught them the practice I have just described. The wives who followed it found it good and thanked her; those who did not follow it found no relief and went on suffering.

Her mother-in-law, too, had at first been turned against her by the whispering of malicious servants. But she won her over so completely by respectful attention, by patient endurance and by gentleness, that the older woman went of her own accord to her son and exposed the meddling tongues that had been disturbing the peace of the household between herself and her daughter-in-law, and asked him to punish them. So, in obedience to his mother, and for the good order of the family, he had those she had exposed whipped, as she wished. Then she promised the same reward to anyone who spoke badly of her daughter-in-law to her in the hope of pleasing her. After that no one dared to, and the two of them lived together in a remarkable sweetness of mutual kindness.

You also gave this great gift, O my God, my mercy, to that good handmaid of Yours, in whose womb You created me. Wherever she could, she showed herself such a peacemaker between people who disagreed and were at odds that, though she heard the most bitter things from each side, the sort of thing that swollen, undigested resentment tends to belch out when the raw matter of hatred is breathed out in sour conversation to a friend who is present against an enemy who is absent, she never revealed anything of what one said to the other, except what might help to reconcile them. This might seem a small good to me, if I did not know, to my sorrow, countless people who, through some horrible and far-spreading infection of sin, not only report to angry enemies what their angry enemies have said, but even add things that were never said at all. Yet to a humane person it ought to seem too little merely to avoid stirring up or increasing people's hostility by speaking ill, unless he also tries to put it out by speaking well. Such was she, and it was You, her innermost Teacher, who taught her in the school of the heart.

In the end she also won her own husband for You, toward the very close of his earthly life. And once he was a believer, she did not have to mourn in him what she had put up with from him before he believed. She was also the servant of Your servants. Any of them who knew her praised, honored and loved You greatly in her, because they sensed Your presence in her heart, witnessed by the fruits of her holy way of life. For she had been the wife of one husband, had repaid her parents, had managed her household devoutly, and was well known for good works. She had brought up children, going through the labor of giving birth to them again each time she saw them straying from You. Lastly, O Lord, as for all of us Your servants (since by Your gift You allow us to speak), who before she fell asleep in You were already living together as companions, having received the grace of Your baptism, she took care of us as though she had been the mother of us all, and served us as though she had been the child of us all.

As the day drew near on which she was to leave this life, a day You knew and we did not, it happened, through You arranging it, I believe, in Your hidden ways, that she and I were standing alone, leaning on a window that looked out onto the garden of the house where we were staying, there at Ostia. There, far from the crowds, after the hardships of a long journey, we were regaining our strength for the sea voyage. So we were talking together alone, very sweetly. Forgetting the things that are behind and reaching out to the things that are ahead, we were asking each other, in the presence of the Truth, which You are, what the eternal life of the saints would be like, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man. And yet we opened wide the mouth of our heart to the streams on high from Your fountain, the fountain of life that is with You, so that, sprinkled from it as far as we could take it in, we might in some way think about so great a thing.

And our conversation reached this point: that the greatest delight of the bodily senses, in the purest bodily light, seemed, beside the joy of that life, not only unworthy of comparison but not even worth mentioning. Then, lifting ourselves up with a more burning love toward the "Self-same," we passed step by step through all bodily things, even through the heaven itself from which sun and moon and stars shine down on the earth. And we climbed higher still, by inward thought and talk and wonder at Your works. And we came to our own minds, and went beyond them, to reach that region of unfailing abundance where You feed Israel forever on the food of truth. There life is Wisdom, through whom all these things are made, both those that have been and those that will be; and she herself is not made, but is as she has been, and will be so forever. Or rather, "having been" and "going to be" are not in her at all, but only "being," since she is eternal. For "having been" and "going to be" are not eternal. And while we were speaking of her and longing for her, we touched her slightly, with the whole force of our heart. And we sighed, and left the first fruits of the Spirit bound there, and came back to the sound of our own mouths, where a word has both a beginning and an end. And what is like Your Word, our Lord, who remains in Himself without growing old, and makes all things new?

So we said: Suppose that for someone the tumult of the flesh fell silent; that the images of earth and water and air fell silent; that the poles of heaven fell silent too; that the soul itself fell silent to itself and passed beyond itself by not thinking of itself; that dreams and imagined revelations fell silent, and every tongue and every sign, and everything that exists only by passing away. For if anyone could hear them, all these things say, We did not make ourselves; He made us who remains forever. Suppose that, having said this, they too fell silent, having turned our ears toward Him who made them, and He alone spoke, not through them but through Himself, so that we heard His Word, not through any tongue of flesh, nor the voice of an Angel, nor the sound of thunder, nor the dark riddle of a likeness, but heard Him whom we love in these things, heard His very Self without them, just as we two had now stretched ourselves out and in swift thought touched that eternal Wisdom which remains above all things. Suppose this went on, and all other visions of a far lower kind were taken away, and this one alone seized, absorbed and wrapped up its beholder in these inward joys, so that life might be forever like that one moment of understanding we had sighed for: would this not be, Enter into the joy of your Lord? And when will that be? When we all rise again, though we shall not all be changed?

These were the things I was saying, and if not in exactly this way or in these same words, still, Lord, You know that on that day, as we talked of these things and this world with all its delights grew worthless to us while we spoke, my mother said, "Son, for my own part, I no longer take delight in anything in this life. What I am still doing here, and why I am here, I do not know, now that my hopes in this world have been fulfilled. There was one thing for which I wanted to stay a little longer in this life: to see you a Catholic Christian before I died. My God has done this for me more abundantly, so that I now see you even despising earthly happiness and become His servant. What am I doing here?"

What answer I gave her to this, I do not remember. For hardly five days later, or not much more, she fell sick with a fever. During that illness she fainted one day and was for a while cut off from the things around her. We hurried to her side, but she soon came back to her senses. Looking at me and my brother standing beside her, she asked us, as if searching, "Where was I?" Then, looking steadily at us as we stood stunned with grief, she said, "Here you will bury your mother." I kept silent and held back my tears. But my brother said something to the effect that he wished, as the happier fate, that she might die not in a foreign place but in her own country. When she heard this, she gave him an anxious look, rebuking him with her eyes for still thinking of such things. Then she looked at me and said, "See what he is saying." And soon afterward she said to us both, "Lay this body anywhere. Do not let any concern about it trouble you at all. I ask only this of you: that you remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you may be." When she had expressed this wish in what words she could manage, she fell silent, as her illness grew worse and wore her down.

But I, reflecting on Your gifts, You unseen God, which You plant in the hearts of Your faithful and from which wonderful fruits grow, rejoiced and gave thanks to You. I remembered what I had known before: how careful and anxious she had always been about her burial place, which she had provided and prepared for herself beside the body of her husband. Because they had lived together in great harmony, she had also wished (so little can the human mind grasp divine things) to have this added to that happiness, and to have it remembered among people, that after her journey across the sea it had been granted that the earthly part of this united couple should be joined together under the same earth. When this emptiness had begun, through the fullness of Your goodness, to fade from her heart, I did not know; and I rejoiced, marveling at what she had revealed to me in this way. And yet even in our conversation at the window, when she said, "What am I still doing here?" there had been no sign of a desire to die in her own country. I heard afterward, too, that while we were at Ostia, one day when I was away she talked, with a mother's openness, with some of my friends about how little this life is worth and about the blessing of death. They were amazed at such courage, which You had given to a woman, and asked her whether she was not afraid to leave her body so far from her own city. She replied, "Nothing is far from God. There is no fear that at the end of the world He will not know where to raise me up from." So on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third of mine, that devout and holy soul was set free from the body.

I closed her eyes, and an immense sorrow came flooding into my heart and was about to overflow in tears. At the same moment my eyes, under the forceful command of my mind, drank their spring back until it was quite dry, and I was in misery in such a struggle. But when she breathed her last, the boy Adeodatus burst out into loud wailing; then, restrained by all of us, he fell silent. In the same way something childish in me, which was slipping into tears, was restrained by the grown-up voice of my heart and fell silent. For we did not think it right to mark that funeral with tearful complaints and groaning, since these are usually how people mourn the dead as if they were wretched, or as if they had been wholly destroyed. But she did not die wretched, nor did she wholly die. We were sure of this on good grounds: the evidence of her way of life and her unfeigned faith.

What was it, then, that hurt me so badly inside, if not a fresh wound, made by the sudden tearing apart of that very sweet and dear habit of living together? I did rejoice in her testimony when, in that last illness of hers, responding to my attentions with her own endearments, she called me a "good son," and told me with deep affection that she had never heard any harsh or reproachful word from my mouth against her. But still, O my God, who made us, what comparison is there between the honor I showed her and the way she slaved for me? So, having lost the great comfort I had in her, my soul was wounded, and my life was torn apart, as it were, because hers and mine together had been made into one.

So when the boy had been calmed from his weeping, Euodius took up the Psalter and began to sing a Psalm, with our whole household answering him: I will sing of mercy and judgment to You, O Lord. And when they heard what was happening, many brothers and devout women gathered. While those whose task it was made the arrangements for the burial, as is the custom, I withdrew to a part of the house where I could properly do so, together with those who thought I should not be left alone, and talked about something suited to the occasion. With this soothing balm of truth I eased my torment, which was known to You but not to them. They listened attentively and supposed I felt no sorrow at all. But in Your ears, where none of them could hear, I scolded the softness of my feelings and held back the flood of my grief. It gave way to me a little, but then it swept back again with force, though not so far as to burst into tears or to change my expression; still, I knew what I was pressing down in my heart. And because I was deeply displeased that these human things, which must happen in the proper order and by the lot of our condition, had such power over me, I grieved over my grief with a second grief, and so was worn down by a double sadness.

And then the body was carried out for burial. We went, and we came back, without tears. For not even during the prayers we poured out to You when the Sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her, with the body already beside the grave before being laid in it, as is the custom there, not even during those prayers did I weep. Yet all day long I was deeply sad in secret, and with a troubled mind I begged You, as well as I could, to heal my pain; but You did not. I believe You were impressing on my memory, by this single example, how strong the bond of every habit is, even on a mind that no longer feeds on a deceiving word. I also decided to go and take a bath, because I had heard that baths (balneum) got their name from the Greek Balaneion, since they drive anxiety out of the mind. And this too I confess to Your mercy, Father of the fatherless: I bathed, and I was the same after bathing as before. For the bitterness of grief could not sweat out of my heart. Then I slept, and woke up, and found my grief softened to no small degree. And as I lay alone in my bed, I remembered those true verses of Your Ambrose. For You are the

"Maker of all things, Lord and Ruler of the heights, who clothe the day in splendid light and pour gentle sleep over the night, so that rest may give our limbs back their strength for work, lift up weary minds that sink and cower, and set anxious sorrows free."

And then, little by little, my old thoughts of Your handmaid came back to me: her devout life toward You, and her holy tenderness and attentiveness toward us, of which I had suddenly been deprived. And I felt like weeping in Your sight, about her and for her, about myself and for myself. And I let the tears I had held back before flow as much as they wanted, and I made them a bed for my heart. It rested on them, because it was Your ears that heard, not those of some man who would have given my weeping a scornful interpretation. And now, Lord, I confess it to You in writing. Let anyone who wants to read it, and interpret it however he likes. And if he finds sin in it, that I wept for my mother for a small part of an hour, the mother who was dead for the time being to my eyes, who had wept for me for so many years so that I might live in Your eyes, let him not laugh at me. Rather, if he is a person of great love, let him himself weep for my sins before You, the Father of all the brothers of Your Christ.

But now, with my heart healed of that wound, in which it might be blamed for a feeling of the flesh, I pour out to You, our God, on behalf of that handmaid of Yours, a very different kind of tears. They flow from a spirit shaken by the thought of the dangers facing every soul that dies in Adam. Although she had been made alive in Christ, and even before her release from the flesh had lived in such a way that Your name was praised for her faith and her way of life, still I do not dare to say that from the time You gave her new birth in baptism, no word came out of her mouth against Your Commandment. Your Son, the Truth, has said, Whoever says to his brother, You fool, will be in danger of the fire of hell. And woe even to the praiseworthy life of human beings, if You were to set mercy aside and examine it! But because You do not search out our sins to the uttermost, we hope with confidence to find some place with You. And whoever lists his true merits before You, what is he listing but Your own gifts? Oh, if only human beings would recognize that they are human, and that whoever boasts would boast in the Lord!

So I, O my Praise and my Life, God of my heart, setting aside for a while her good deeds, for which I thank You with joy, now plead with You for my mother's sins. Hear me, I beg You, through the Medicine for our wounds, who hung on the tree and who now, sitting at Your right hand, intercedes with You for us. I know that she acted mercifully, and forgave her debtors their debts from her heart. Now You also forgive her debts, whatever she may have run up in all those years since the water of salvation. Forgive her, Lord, forgive her, I beg You; do not enter into judgment with her. Let Your mercy triumph over Your justice, since Your words are true and You have promised mercy to the merciful. It was You who gave them to be merciful, You who will have mercy on whom You will have mercy, and will have compassion on whom You have had compassion.

And I believe You have already done what I am asking. But accept, O Lord, the freely given offerings of my mouth. For when the day of her dissolution was near, she gave no thought to having her body wrapped in costly cloths or embalmed with spices. She did not wish for a special monument, or to be buried in her own country. She gave us no instructions about such things. She wished only that her name be remembered at Your Altar, which she had served without missing a single day. For she knew that from it the holy Sacrifice is given out, by which the written charge against us is wiped away, and through which the enemy was defeated: he who adds up our offenses and looks for something to accuse us of found nothing in Him, in whom we conquer. Who will give back to Him His innocent blood? Who will pay Him back the price with which He bought us, and so take us away from Him? To the Sacrament of this ransom of ours Your handmaid bound her soul with the bond of faith. Let no one tear her away from Your protection. Let neither the lion nor the dragon thrust himself in, whether by force or by trickery. For she will not answer that she owes nothing, in case she is convicted and seized by the cunning accuser. She will answer that her sins have been forgiven her by Him to whom no one can repay the price that He, who owed nothing, paid for us.

So may she rest in peace with her husband, before and after whom she had no other; whom she obeyed, bringing forth fruit for You with patience, so that she might win him for You as well. And inspire, O Lord my God, inspire Your servants, my brothers, Your sons, my masters, whom I serve with voice and heart and pen, so that all who read these Confessions may remember at Your Altar Monnica, Your handmaid, together with Patricius, once her husband, through whose bodies You brought me into this life, how I do not know. May they remember with devout affection those who were my parents in this passing light, my brothers under You our Father in our Catholic Mother, and my fellow citizens in that eternal Jerusalem which Your pilgrim people long for from their setting out until their return there. So may my mother's last request of me be fulfilled for her more richly through the prayers of many, by means of my confessions, than by my own prayers.

chapters.title: Book 10
paragraphs: Let me know You, O Lord, who know me: let me know You, even as I am known. Power of my soul, come into it and fit it for Yourself, so that You may have and hold it without spot or wrinkle. This is my hope, and that is why I speak; and in this hope I rejoice, whenever my rejoicing is sound. As for the other things of this life, the more people weep over them, the less they deserve weeping; and the more they deserve weeping, the less people weep over them. For see, You love the truth, and whoever does it comes to the light. This is what I want to do: in my heart, before You, in confession, and in my writing, before many witnesses.

And indeed, O Lord, to Your eyes the abyss of human conscience lies bare; so what in me could be hidden from You, even if I were unwilling to confess it to You? I would only be hiding You from me, not me from You. But now that my groaning bears witness that I am displeased with myself, You shine out, and You are pleasing, and loved, and longed for, so that I may be ashamed of myself, and cast myself away, and choose You, and please neither You nor myself except through You. So to You, O Lord, I lie open, whatever I am; and I have already said what fruit I gain by confessing to You. Nor do I do it with words and sounds of the flesh, but with the words of my soul and the cry of my thought, which Your ear knows. For when I am evil, confessing to You is nothing other than being displeased with myself; but when I am holy, it is nothing other than not claiming the credit for myself, because You, O Lord, bless the righteous, but first You justify him when he is ungodly. So my confession, O my God, is made in Your sight silently and yet not silently. It is silent in sound, but in feeling it cries aloud. For I say nothing right to people that You have not first heard from me; nor do You hear anything of that kind from me that You have not first said to me.

What, then, do I have to do with people, that they should hear my confessions, as though they were the ones to heal all my infirmities? They are a race eager to know other people's lives, and lazy about correcting their own. Why do they want to hear from me what I am, when they do not want to hear from You what they are? And when they hear about me from me myself, how do they know whether I am telling the truth, since no one knows what goes on in a man except the spirit of man that is in him? But if they hear about themselves from You, they cannot say, "The Lord is lying." For what is hearing about themselves from You, if not knowing themselves? And who knows something and then says, "It is false," unless he himself is lying? But because love believes all things (at least among those whom it binds to itself and makes one), I too, O Lord, confess to You in such a way that people may hear, even though I cannot prove to them whether my confession is true; yet those whose ears love opens to me believe me.

But You, my inmost Physician, make clear to me what fruit I gain by doing this. For the confessions of my past sins, which You have forgiven and covered so that You might make me blessed in You, changing my soul by faith and Your Sacrament, stir up the heart when they are read and heard. They keep it from sleeping in despair and saying, "I cannot," and wake it instead in the love of Your mercy and the sweetness of Your grace, by which everyone who is weak becomes strong, once through it he has become aware of his own weakness. And good people are glad to hear of the past evils of those who are now free of them, not because they are evils, but because they once were and now are not. With what fruit, then, O Lord my God, to whom my conscience confesses every day, trusting more in the hope of Your mercy than in its own innocence, with what fruit, I ask, do I through this book confess to people as well, in Your presence, what I am now, not what I have been? For that other fruit I have seen and spoken of already. But what I am now, at this very time of making my confessions, many people want to know, some who know me and some who do not, some who have heard something from me or about me; yet their ear is not at my heart, where I am whatever I am. So they want to hear me confess what I am within, where neither their eye nor their ear nor their mind can reach. They want this as people ready to believe; but will they know? For love, which makes them good, tells them that I am not lying when I confess about myself, and it is love in them that believes me.

But for what fruit do they want to hear this? Do they wish to rejoice with me when they hear how near I come to You by Your gift, and to pray for me when they hear how much I am held back by my own weight? To people like that I will show myself. For it is no small fruit, O Lord my God, that many should give thanks to You on our account, and that many should ask You on our behalf. Let a brother's mind love in me what You teach is to be loved, and grieve in me over what You teach is to be grieved over. Let it be a brother's mind that does this, not a stranger's, not the mind of the strange children, whose mouth speaks vanity, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity, but that brotherly mind which rejoices for me when it approves of me, and is sad for me when it disapproves of me, because whether it approves or disapproves, it loves me. To people like that I will show myself. Let them breathe freely at my good deeds and sigh over my bad ones. My good deeds are Your work and Your gifts; my bad ones are my offenses and Your judgments. Let them breathe freely at the one and sigh over the other, and let hymns and weeping rise into Your sight from the hearts of my brothers, which are Your censers. And You, O Lord, delighted by the fragrance of Your holy temple, have mercy on me according to Your great mercy, for Your name's sake; and never abandoning what You have begun, make my imperfections perfect.

This is the fruit of confessing what I am, not what I have been: to confess it not only before You, in a secret exultation with trembling and a secret sorrow with hope, but also in the ears of the believing sons of men, who share my joy and share my mortality, my fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, those who have gone before, those who will follow, and those who walk with me on my way. These are Your servants, my brothers, whom You have willed to be Your sons; they are my masters, whom You have commanded me to serve, if I want to live with You and from You. But this Word of Yours would mean little to me if it only commanded by speaking and did not go before me by doing. So I do this in deed and in word; I do it under Your wings, and the danger would be far too great, were it not that under Your wings my soul is subject to You and my weakness is known to You. I am a little child, but my Father lives forever, and my Guardian is enough for me. For He who begot me is the same One who protects me; and You Yourself are all my good, You, the Almighty, who are with me even before I am with You. So to those You command me to serve I will reveal, not what I have been, but what I am now and what I still am. But I do not judge myself either. This, then, is how I want to be heard.

For it is You, Lord, who judge me. For although no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of man that is in him, there is still something of a man that even the spirit of man within him does not know. But You, Lord, who made him, know everything about him. And I, though in Your sight I despise myself and count myself dust and ashes, still know something about You that I do not know about myself. And certainly, for now we see through a glass darkly, not yet face to face. So as long as I am a pilgrim away from You, I am more present to myself than to You; and yet I know that You cannot in any way be harmed, while I do not know which temptations I can resist and which I cannot. And there is hope, because You are faithful, who will not let us be tempted beyond what we are able, but with the temptation will also make a way of escape, so that we may be able to bear it. So I will confess what I know about myself, and I will also confess what I do not know about myself. For what I do know about myself, I know because You shine on me; and what I do not know about myself, I will go on not knowing until my darkness becomes as the noonday in Your presence.

Not with doubt, but with sure awareness, I love You, Lord. You struck my heart with Your word, and I loved You. Heaven and earth too, and everything in them, look, on every side they tell me to love You, and they never stop saying it to everyone, so that they are without excuse. But more deeply will You have mercy on whom You will have mercy, and show compassion to whom You have been compassionate; otherwise heaven and earth speak Your praises to deaf ears. But what do I love when I love You? Not the beauty of bodies, nor the fair harmony of time, nor the brightness of light, so pleasant to our eyes, nor the sweet melodies of songs of every kind, nor the fragrant smell of flowers and ointments and spices, not manna and honey, not limbs that welcome the embraces of the flesh. None of these do I love when I love my God; and yet I do love a kind of light, and melody, and fragrance, and food, and embrace when I love my God: the light, melody, fragrance, food and embrace of my inner self, where something shines into my soul that no space can contain, and something sounds that time does not carry away, and something gives off a fragrance that no wind scatters, and something has a taste that no eating lessens, and something holds fast that no fullness pulls apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

And what is this? I asked the earth, and it answered me, "I am not He"; and everything in it made the same confession. I asked the sea and the deeps and the creeping things that live, and they answered, "We are not your God; look above us." I asked the moving air, and the whole air with its inhabitants answered, "Anaximenes was mistaken; I am not God." I asked the heavens, the sun, the moon, the stars; "Nor are we the God you are looking for," they said. And I said to all the things that stand around the doors of my flesh, "You have told me about my God, that you are not He; tell me something about Him." And they cried out with a loud voice, "He made us." My questioning of them was my attention to them, and their beauty was their answer. And I turned to myself and said to myself, "Who are you?" And I answered, "A man." And look, here in me are a body and a soul, presenting themselves to me, one outside and the other within. Through which of these should I have looked for my God? I had already looked for Him through the body, from earth to heaven, as far as I could send the beams of my eyes as messengers. But the inner part is the better, for it was to this, as it presided and judged, that all the bodily messengers reported the answers of heaven and earth and everything in them, as they said, "We are not God, but He made us." My inner self knew these things through the service of the outer; I, the inner self, knew them, I, the mind, through the senses of my body. I asked the whole mass of the world about my God, and it answered me, "I am not He, but He made me."

Is this bodily form not plain to everyone whose senses are sound? Why, then, does it not say the same thing to everyone? Animals, small and great, see it, but they cannot question it, because no reason has been set over their senses to judge what the senses report. But human beings can question it, so that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; but by loving these things they become subject to them, and those who are subject cannot judge. Nor do created things answer those who question them unless the questioners can judge. Nor do they change their voice (that is, their appearance) if one person merely sees while another both sees and questions, so as to appear one way to the first and another way to the second; rather, appearing the same way to both, it is mute to the one and speaks to the other. Or rather, it speaks to everyone, but only those understand who compare the voice they receive from outside with the truth within. For truth says to me, "Neither heaven nor earth nor any other body is your God." Their very nature says this to anyone who sees them: "They are a mass; a mass is less in any part of it than in the whole." Now I speak to you, my soul: you are my better part, for you quicken the mass of my body, giving it life, which no body can give to a body; but your God is, even to you, the Life of your life.

What, then, do I love when I love my God? Who is He, above the very summit of my soul? By means of my soul itself I will climb up to Him. I will pass beyond the power by which I am joined to my body and fill its whole frame with life. It is not by that power that I find my God; for then the horse and the mule, which have no understanding, might find Him too, since it is the same power by which their bodies also live. But there is another power: not only the one by which I give life to my flesh, but the one by which I give it sense, the flesh that the Lord fashioned for me. He commanded the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but gave me the eye to see through and the ear to hear through, and to each of the other senses its own proper seat and function; and though these are different, I, the one mind, carry them out through them. I will pass beyond this power of mine as well, for the horse and the mule have this too, since they also perceive through the body.

So I will pass beyond this power of my nature too, climbing by steps toward Him who made me. And I come to the fields and spacious palaces of memory, where the treasures of countless images are kept, brought in from things of every kind that the senses have perceived. Stored there too is whatever we think up besides, by enlarging or shrinking or in any other way altering what the senses have touched; and whatever else has been entrusted to it and laid up there, which forgetfulness has not yet swallowed and buried. When I go in there, I ask for whatever I want to be brought out, and some things come at once; others have to be searched for longer and are dug out, as it were, from some more hidden storeroom; others come rushing out in crowds, and while I am asking and searching for something else, they leap out into the middle as if to say, "Is it us, perhaps?" These I brush away with the hand of my heart from the face of my remembrance, until the thing I want comes out of the mist and steps into view from its hiding place. Other things come up easily and in unbroken order, just as they are called for; those in front make way for those behind, and as they make way they are put back out of sight, ready to come out again when I want them. All of this happens when I recount something from memory.

There all things are kept distinct and sorted by kind, each having come in by its own entrance: light, and all the colors and shapes of bodies, by the eyes; all kinds of sounds by the ears; all smells by the entrance of the nostrils; all tastes by the mouth; and by the sense of the whole body, what is hard or soft, hot or cold, rough, heavy or light, whether outside the body or inside it. All these the great harbor of memory takes in, in its countless hidden and indescribable recesses, to be available and brought out again when needed; each enters by its own door and is laid up there. Yet the things themselves do not go in; only the images of the things perceived are there, ready for thought to call them to mind. And who can say how these images are formed, even though it is plain by which sense each was caught and stored away inside? For even when I sit in darkness and silence, I can bring out colors in my memory if I want, and tell black from white and any others I choose; and sounds do not break in and disturb the image drawn in through my eyes that I am looking over, though they too are there, lying hidden and stored away, as it were, by themselves. For I can call for them as well, and they are there at once. And with my tongue at rest and my throat silent, I can sing as much as I like; and those images of colors, which are nonetheless there, do not push in and interrupt when I am handling another store, the one that flowed in through the ears. In the same way I recall at will the other things brought in and heaped up by the other senses. I can tell the scent of lilies from that of violets while smelling nothing at all; and I prefer honey to sweet wine, and smooth to rough, while at that moment I am neither tasting nor touching anything, but only remembering.

I do these things inside, in the vast hall of my memory. For there heaven, earth and sea are present to me, along with everything in them that I have been able to perceive, except what I have forgotten. There I also meet myself and recall myself, what I have done, when and where, and how I felt when I did it. There is everything I remember, whether from my own experience or on the word of others. From the same store I myself keep weaving new and further likenesses of things, either things I have experienced or things I have believed on the basis of what I have experienced, into what is past; and from them I also infer future actions, events and hopes, and I think over all of these again as if they were present. "I will do this or that," I say to myself in that great recess of my mind, full of the images of so many and such great things, "and this or that will follow." "Oh, if only this or that could be!" "God forbid this or that!" I say these things to myself, and as I say them, the images of everything I speak of are there, from the same treasury of memory; and I could not speak of any of them at all if the images were missing.

Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, O my God, a vast and boundless inner chamber! Who has ever reached the bottom of it? Yet this is a power of my mind and belongs to my nature, and I myself cannot grasp all that I am. So the mind is too narrow to contain itself. Then where is the part of it that it does not contain? Is it outside the mind and not in it? Then how does the mind not contain it? Great wonder rises up in me at this, and amazement takes hold of me. And people go out to marvel at the heights of mountains, the huge waves of the sea, the broad currents of rivers, the sweep of the ocean and the circling of the stars, and they pass themselves by. They do not wonder that when I spoke of all these things I was not seeing them with my eyes, and yet I could not have spoken of them unless I was actually seeing, inwardly in my memory, the mountains, waves, rivers and stars that I have seen, and the ocean that I believe in, and with the same vast distances between them as if I were seeing them outside. Yet when I saw them with my eyes, I did not swallow them into myself by seeing them; nor are the things themselves with me, only their images. And I know by which sense of the body each one was impressed on me.

Yet these are not the only things that the immeasurable capacity of my memory holds. Here too is everything I have learned of the liberal sciences and not yet forgotten, set apart, as it were, in some inner place that is yet no place; and what I carry here are not images of them, but the things themselves. For what literature is, what the art of debate is, how many kinds of questions there are, whatever I know of these, is in my memory in such a way that I have not kept the image and left the thing outside. Nor is it as if it had sounded and passed away, like a voice that leaves its impress on the mind through the ear, by which it can be recalled as though it were sounding when it no longer sounds; or like a smell which, while it passes and fades into the air, affects the sense of smell and so conveys an image of itself into the memory, which we renew by remembering; or like food, which certainly has no taste any longer in the stomach and yet in the memory still tastes, in a way; or like anything the body perceives by touching, which the memory still pictures even when it has been taken away from us. For those things are not brought into the memory themselves; only their images are caught up with marvelous speed and stored away, as it were, in marvelous compartments, and then marvelously brought out again by the act of remembering.

But now, when I hear that there are three kinds of questions, "Whether a thing is? What it is? Of what kind it is?", I do hold the images of the sounds that make up those words, and I know that those sounds passed noisily through the air and now no longer exist. But the things themselves that those sounds signify I never reached with any sense of my body, and I never saw them anywhere except in my mind; yet what I have stored in my memory is not their images but the things themselves. How they got into me, let them say if they can. For I run through all the doorways of my flesh and cannot find by which one they came in. The eyes say, "If they had color, we reported them." The ears say, "If they made a sound, we made them known." The nostrils say, "If they had a smell, they passed through us." The sense of taste says, "If they have no flavor, do not ask me." Touch says, "If it has no bodily bulk, I did not handle it; and if I did not handle it, I reported nothing about it." Where did these things come from, and how did they get into my memory? I do not know how. For when I learned them, I did not take them on trust from someone else's mind; I recognized them in my own, and, approving them as true, I entrusted them to it, laying them up, as it were, where I could bring them out whenever I wished. So they were in my heart even before I learned them, but they were not in my memory. Where were they, then? Or why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, "That is so, it is true," unless they were already in the memory, but pushed so far back and buried, as it were, in such deep hollows that, if someone else's prompting had not drawn them out, I might perhaps have been unable to think of them?

So we find that learning these things, whose images we do not take in through the senses but which we perceive inwardly by themselves, without images, as they actually are, is nothing other than this: by thinking, we gather together, so to speak, the things the memory already held scattered and in disorder, and by paying attention we see to it that they are placed ready to hand, as it were, in that same memory where before they lay hidden, scattered and neglected, so that now they readily come to a mind that has grown familiar with them. And how many things of this kind my memory carries which have already been found and, as I said, placed ready to hand, things we are said to have learned and to know! Yet if I stop calling them to mind for even a short space of time, they sink down again and slip away, as it were, into the more remote recesses, so that they have to be thought out again from there as if they were new, for they have no other dwelling place; and they have to be driven together again so that they can be known, that is, they have to be collected, as it were, out of a kind of scattering. That is where the word "cogitation" comes from. For cogo (collect) and cogito (re-collect) are related to each other as ago and agito, facio and factito. But the mind has claimed this word for itself, so that it is not what is "collected" just anywhere, but what is "recollected," that is, gathered together, in the mind, that is properly said to be cogitated, or thought.

The memory also contains the principles and countless laws of numbers and dimensions, none of which any bodily sense has impressed on it, since they have no color, sound, taste or smell, and cannot be touched. I have heard the sounds of the words by which they are signified when people discuss them, but the sounds are one thing and the principles another. For the sounds are different in Greek and in Latin, but the principles themselves are neither Greek nor Latin nor any other kind of language. I have seen lines drawn by craftsmen, even the very finest, like a spider's thread; but those lines are different: they are not images of the lines that the eye of the flesh reported to me. Anyone who recognizes them within himself, without thinking of any body whatsoever, knows them. I have also perceived with all the senses of my body the numbers of the things we count; but the numbers by which we count are different, and they are not images of these, and for that very reason they truly are. Let anyone who does not see them laugh at me for saying these things, and I will pity him while he laughs at me.

All these things I remember, and I remember how I learned them. I have also heard, and remember, many arguments raised against them with great falsity; and though these are false, it is not false that I remember them. And I also remember that I have distinguished between those truths and the falsehoods raised against them. And I see that distinguishing these things now is one thing, and remembering that I have often distinguished them, when I often thought about them, is another. So I remember that I have often understood these things; and what I now distinguish and understand I store in my memory, so that later on I may remember that I understand it now. So I also remember that I have remembered; just as, if later on I recall that I have been able to remember these things now, it will be by the power of memory that I recall it.

The same memory also contains the affections of my mind, not in the way the mind itself holds them when it is experiencing them, but in a very different way, according to a power that belongs to memory. For I remember that I once rejoiced without rejoicing now, and I recall my past sadness without being sad; I remember without fear that I once was afraid, and I call to mind a past desire without desire. Sometimes, on the contrary, I remember my past sadness with joy, and my past joy with sadness. This is not surprising in the case of the body, for the mind is one thing and the body another. So if I remember some past pain of the body with gladness, it is not so surprising. But this memory is itself the mind (for when we tell someone to keep something in memory, we say, "See that you keep it in mind," and when we forget, we say, "It did not come to mind," and "It slipped my mind," calling the memory itself the mind). Since this is so, how is it that when I remember my past sadness with joy, the mind has joy and the memory has sadness, and the mind is joyful because of the joy that is in it, yet the memory is not sad because of the sadness that is in it? Does the memory perhaps not belong to the mind? Who would say that? The memory, then, is like the stomach of the mind, and joy and sadness are like sweet and bitter food: when they are entrusted to the memory, they have, as it were, passed into the stomach, where they can be stored but cannot be tasted. It is ridiculous to think these are alike; and yet they are not entirely unlike.

But look: it is out of my memory that I bring it when I say that there are four perturbations of the mind, desire, joy, fear and sorrow. And whatever I can say about them in argument, dividing each into the species that belong to its kind and defining it, I find there in my memory what to say, and I bring it out from there. Yet I am not disturbed by any of these perturbations when I call them to mind and speak of them. Indeed, even before I recalled and went over them, they were there; that is why they could be brought out from there by recollection. Perhaps, then, just as food is brought up from the stomach when an animal chews the cud, so these things are brought up from the memory by recollection. Why, then, does the one who argues about them, that is, the one who recollects them, not taste in the mouth of his thinking the sweetness of joy or the bitterness of sorrow? Is the comparison unlike in this, because it is not like in every respect? For who would willingly speak about such things, if every time we named sorrow or fear we were forced to feel sad or afraid? And yet we could not speak of them at all unless we found in our memory not only the sounds of their names, according to the images impressed by the senses of the body, but also notions of the things themselves. These we never received through any doorway of the flesh; rather the mind itself, perceiving them through the experience of its own passions, entrusted them to the memory, or else the memory retained them by itself, even without their being entrusted to it.

But whether this happens by means of images or not, who can easily say? For I name a stone, I name the sun, when the things themselves are not present to my senses; but their images are certainly present in my memory. I name bodily pain, and yet it is not present to me when nothing hurts; but unless its image were present in my memory, I would not know what I was saying, nor could I tell it apart from pleasure in discussion. I name bodily health when I am healthy in body, and the thing itself is present to me. Yet unless its image were also in my memory, I could in no way recall what the sound of this name meant. Nor would sick people understand what was being said when health was named, unless that same image were held by the power of memory, even though the thing itself was absent from the body. I name the numbers by which we count, and there they are in my memory, not their images but the numbers themselves. I name the image of the sun, and that image is present in my memory; for I do not recall the image of its image, but the image itself is present to me when I call it to mind. I name memory, and I recognize what I name. And where do I recognize it, if not in memory itself? Is memory, too, present to itself by means of its image, and not by itself?

What about when I name forgetfulness and likewise recognize what I name? How could I recognize it if I did not remember it? I do not mean the sound of the name, but the thing it signifies; if I had forgotten that, I would certainly not be able to recognize what the sound means. So when I remember memory, memory itself is present to itself through itself; but when I remember forgetfulness, both memory and forgetfulness are present: memory, by which I remember, and forgetfulness, which I remember. But what is forgetfulness, except the absence of memory? How, then, is it present so that I remember it, when, if it is present, I cannot remember? But if what we remember we hold in memory, and yet unless we remembered forgetfulness we could never recognize the thing signified when we hear the name, then forgetfulness is held in the memory. So it is present so that we do not forget it, and yet when it is present, we forget. Or are we to understand from this that forgetfulness, when we remember it, is present in the memory not by itself but by its image, since if forgetfulness were present by itself, it would make us not remember but forget? And who, in the end, will search this out? Who will grasp how it is?

As for me, Lord, I truly labor over this, and I labor over myself. I have become to myself a hard soil that demands too much sweat of the brow. For we are not now exploring the regions of the sky, or measuring the distances of the stars, or investigating how the earth is balanced. It is I who remember, I, the mind. It is not so surprising if what I am not is far from me. But what is nearer to me than myself? And look, the power of my own memory is beyond my understanding, even though without it I cannot even speak of myself. For what am I to say, when I am certain that I remember forgetfulness? Am I to say that what I remember is not in my memory? Or am I to say that forgetfulness is in my memory for this purpose, so that I do not forget? Both are utterly absurd. What third way is there? How can I say that it is the image of forgetfulness that my memory holds, not forgetfulness itself, when I remember it? How can I say this either, since when the image of anything is impressed on the memory, the thing itself must first be present, so that the image can be impressed from it? For this is how I remember Carthage, and all the places I have been, and the faces of people I have seen, and what the other senses have reported; this is how I remember the health or the pain of the body itself. When these things were present, my memory took images from them, which I could look at as present and go over in my mind when I remembered the things themselves in their absence. If, then, forgetfulness is held in the memory through its image and not through itself, then it must itself have been present once, so that its image could be taken. But when it was present, how did it write its image in the memory, since forgetfulness by its presence wipes out even what it finds already recorded there? And yet, in whatever way it happens, though that way is beyond grasping and beyond explaining, I am certain that I also remember forgetfulness itself, by which what we remember is buried.

Great is the power of memory, a fearful thing, O my God, a deep and boundless multiplicity; and this is the mind, and this is I myself. What, then, am I, O my God? What is my nature? A life varied and manifold, and utterly immense. Look at the plains and caves and caverns of my memory, countless and countlessly full of countless kinds of things, present either through images, as all bodies are, or in person, as the arts are, or through certain notions or impressions, as the affections of the mind are, which the memory retains even when the mind is not feeling them, though whatever is in the memory is also in the mind. Through all these I run and fly this way and that; I dive in as far as I can, and there is no end anywhere. So great is the power of memory, so great the power of life, even in man living this mortal life! What, then, shall I do, O You, my true life, my God? I will pass beyond even this power of mine that is called memory; yes, I will pass beyond it, so as to reach You, O sweet Light. What do You say to me? See, I am climbing up through my mind toward You who dwell above me. I will pass beyond this power of mine that is called memory too, wanting to reach You where You can be reached, and to cling to You where one can cling to You. For even cattle and birds have memory; otherwise they could not find their way back to their lairs and nests, or to the many other things they grow used to; indeed they could not grow used to anything except through memory. So I will pass beyond memory too, to reach Him who set me apart from the four-footed beasts and made me wiser than the birds of the air. I will pass beyond memory too; and where shall I find You, You who are truly good, You sure and certain sweetness? Where shall I find You? If I find You outside my memory, then I do not keep You in mind. And how shall I find You, if I do not remember You?

For the woman who had lost her coin and searched for it with a lamp would never have found it unless she had remembered it. For once it was found, how would she know whether it was the same coin, unless she remembered it? I remember having looked for and found many things; and from this I know that when I was looking for any of them and someone asked me, "Is this it?" "Is that it?" I kept saying, "No," until the thing I was looking for was shown to me. If I had not remembered it, whatever it was, then even if it had been shown to me, I would not have found it, because I could not have recognized it. And it is always like this when we look for and find something lost. Still, when something is lost by chance from sight but not from memory, such as any visible body, its image is still held within, and it is looked for until it is restored to sight; and when it is found, it is recognized by the image that is within. And we do not say we have found what was lost unless we recognize it, and we cannot recognize it unless we remember it. But this thing was lost to the eyes while it was kept in the memory.

But what about when the memory itself loses something, as happens when we forget something and look for it so as to recall it? Where do we search in the end, if not in the memory itself? And there, if one thing happens to be offered to us in place of another, we reject it until the thing we are looking for comes to meet us; and when it does, we say, "This is it." We would not say that unless we recognized it, and we would not recognize it unless we remembered it. So we had certainly forgotten it. Or had the whole of it not slipped away, and was the lost part being sought by means of the part we still had hold of? Was it that the memory felt that it was not turning over together everything it used to hold together, and, limping as it were because its old habit had been cut short, demanded the return of what was missing? For example, if we see or think of someone we know and have forgotten his name and try to recover it, anything else that comes to mind does not connect with him, because it was not used to being thought of together with him; so it is rejected, until that name presents itself on which our knowledge can rest evenly, as on what it is accustomed to. And where does it present itself from, if not out of the memory itself? For even when we recognize it after someone else reminds us, that is where it comes from. We do not believe it as something new; we remember, and agree that what was named is right. But if it were wiped out of the mind entirely, we would not remember it even when reminded. For we have not yet entirely forgotten something if we remember that we have forgotten it. So what we have entirely forgotten, we cannot even look for as something lost.

How, then, do I look for You, O Lord? For when I look for You, my God, I am looking for the happy life. I will look for You, so that my soul may live. For my body lives by my soul, and my soul lives by You. How, then, do I look for the happy life, since I do not have it until I can say, where I ought to say it, "It is enough"? How do I look for it? By remembering, as though I had forgotten it and still remembered that I had forgotten it? Or by wanting to learn it as something unknown, either something I never knew or something I have forgotten so completely that I do not even remember having forgotten it? Is the happy life not the very thing that everyone wants, and is there anyone at all who does not want it? Where did they come to know it, that they want it so much? Where did they see it, that they love it so? Clearly we have it, how I do not know. There is indeed one way of having it, in which a person who has it is then happy; and there are those who are happy in hope. These have it in a lower way than those who are already happy in reality, but they are still better off than those who are happy neither in reality nor in hope. Yet even these, if they did not have it in some way, would not want so much to be happy; and that they do want it is quite certain. So they have come to know it, I do not know how, and they have it through some kind of knowledge, I do not know what; and I am troubled over whether it is in the memory. For if it is there, then we were once happy. Whether each of us was happy individually, or in that man who first sinned, in whom we all died too, and from whom we are all born into misery, I do not ask now; I ask only whether the happy life is in the memory. For we would not love it unless we knew it. We hear the name, and we all admit that we desire the thing itself; for it is not the mere sound that delights us. For when a Greek hears it in Latin, he is not delighted, since he does not know what has been said; but we Latins are delighted, just as he would be if he heard it in Greek, because the thing itself is neither Greek nor Latin, the thing that Greeks and Latins and people of every other language long so eagerly to obtain. So it is known to everyone; for if they could all be asked with one voice whether they want to be happy, they would answer without any hesitation that they do. And this could not happen unless the thing itself, of which this is the name, were held in their memory.

But is it held there in the way that someone who has seen Carthage remembers it? No. For the happy life is not seen with the eyes, because it is not a body. Is it, then, the way we remember numbers? No. For whoever has numbers in his knowledge does not go on seeking to obtain them; but the happy life we have in our knowledge, and that is why we love it, and yet we still want to obtain it, so that we may be happy. Is it, then, the way we remember eloquence? No. For although some people, on hearing this name too, call the thing to mind, even though they are not yet eloquent, and many want to be (which shows that it is in their knowledge), still these people have noticed through their bodily senses that others are eloquent, and have been delighted, and want to be like them (though in fact they would not be delighted except through some inward knowledge of it, and would not want to be like them unless they were delighted); whereas the happy life is something we do not experience in others through any bodily sense. Is it, then, the way we remember joy? Perhaps so.
