For I remember my joy even when I am sad, as I remember the happy life when I am unhappy; and I never saw, heard, smelled, tasted or touched my joy with any bodily sense, but I experienced it in my mind when I rejoiced, and the knowledge of it clung to my memory, so that I can call it back, sometimes with disgust and sometimes with longing, depending on the kind of things I remember having rejoiced in. For I have been steeped in a kind of joy over shameful things too, which now, when I recall it, I detest and curse; and at other times over good and honorable things, which I recall with longing, though perhaps they are no longer present, and so I recall my former joy with sadness.

Where, then, and when did I experience my happy life, so that I remember it and love it and long for it? And it is not I alone, or a few others with me, but all of us who want to be happy; and unless we knew it by some sure knowledge, we would not want it with so sure a will. But what does this mean? If two people are asked whether they want to join the army, it may happen that one answers that he does and the other that he does not; but if they are asked whether they want to be happy, both would say at once, without any hesitation, that they do. And the one wants to join the army and the other does not for no other reason than to be happy. Is it perhaps that, though one finds his joy in this thing and another in that, they all agree in wanting to be happy, just as they would agree, if they were asked, that they want to have joy, and this joy is what they call the happy life? So although one reaches this joy by one route and another by another, there is one goal they are all striving to reach, and that is to have joy. And since this is something no one can say he has never experienced, it is found in the memory and recognized whenever the name of the happy life is heard.

Far be it, Lord, far be it from the heart of Your servant who is confessing to You here, far be it from me to think myself happy because of any and every joy I may rejoice in. For there is a joy that is not given to the ungodly, but to those who worship You for Your own sake, whose joy You Yourself are. And this is the happy life: to rejoice toward You, in You, and for Your sake; this is it, and there is no other. Those who think there is another pursue some other joy, and not the true one. Yet their will is not turned away from some image of joy.

So it is not certain that everyone wants to be happy, since those who do not want to rejoice in You, which is the only happy life, do not really want the happy life. Or does everyone want this, but because the flesh lusts against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh, so that they cannot do what they want, they fall back on what they can do and are content with it, because what they are not able to do they do not want strongly enough to make them able? For I ask everyone whether they would rather rejoice in truth or in falsehood. They will no more hesitate to say "in the truth" than they hesitate to say "that they want to be happy." For the happy life is joy in the truth: that is, joy in You, who are the Truth, O God, my light, the health of my countenance, my God. This is the happy life that everyone wants; this life, which alone is happy, everyone wants; joy in the truth is what everyone wants. I have met many people who wanted to deceive, but no one who wanted to be deceived. Where, then, did they come to know this happy life, if not where they also came to know the truth? For they love the truth too, since they do not want to be deceived. And when they love the happy life, which is nothing other than joy in the truth, they certainly love the truth as well; and they would not love it unless there were some knowledge of it in their memory. Why, then, do they not rejoice in it? Why are they not happy? Because they are more strongly taken up with other things, which have more power to make them miserable than that which they remember so faintly has to make them happy. For there is still a little light in people. Let them walk, let them walk, so that the darkness does not overtake them.

But why does "truth breed hatred," and why does a man of Yours, when he preaches the truth, become an enemy to them, when the happy life, which is nothing other than joy in the truth, is loved? Is it not because truth is loved in such a way that those who love something else want the thing they love to be the truth; and because they do not want to be deceived, they do not want to be shown that they are deceived? So they hate the truth for the sake of the thing they love in place of the truth. They love the truth when it shines on them, and hate it when it rebukes them. For since they do not want to be deceived, and do want to deceive, they love it when it reveals itself to them, and hate it when it reveals them. And so it will repay them: those who did not want to be exposed by it, it will expose against their will, while it does not reveal itself to them. Thus, thus, yes, thus the human mind, blind and sick, foul and unsightly as it is, wants to stay hidden itself, but does not want anything to be hidden from it. But the opposite is what it gets in return: it cannot hide from the Truth, while the Truth is hidden from it. Yet even in this misery it would rather rejoice in truths than in falsehoods. So it will be happy when, with nothing coming in between to distract it, it rejoices in that one Truth by whom all things are true.

See how far I have ranged through my memory in search of You, O Lord, and I have not found You outside it. Nor have I found anything about You that I have not kept in memory from the time I first came to know You. For since I came to know You, I have not forgotten You. Where I found Truth, there I found my God, Truth itself, and since I came to know it, I have not forgotten it. So from the time I came to know You, You have dwelt in my memory, and there I find You whenever I call You to mind and delight in You. These are my holy delights, which You have given me in Your mercy, looking kindly on my poverty.

But where in my memory do You dwell, O Lord, where do You dwell there? What kind of resting place have You shaped for Yourself? What kind of sanctuary have You built for Yourself? You have given my memory this honor, that You should dwell in it; but in which part of it You dwell, that is what I am now considering. For in calling You to mind I went beyond those parts of it that the beasts also have, since I did not find You there among the images of bodily things. And I came to the parts where I have stored the affections of my mind, and I did not find You there either. And I went into the very seat of my mind, which it has in my memory, since the mind also remembers itself, and You were not there. For just as You are not a bodily image, nor the affection of a living being (such as we feel when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, forget, and the like), so neither are You the mind itself, because You are the Lord God of the mind. All these things change, but You remain unchangeable above them all, and yet You have been pleased to dwell in my memory ever since I came to know You. And why do I now ask in which place of it You dwell, as though there really were places in it? This much is certain: You dwell in it, since I have remembered You from the time I came to know You, and I find You there whenever I call You to mind.

Where, then, did I find You, so that I could come to know You? For You were not in my memory before I came to know You. Where, then, did I find You, so that I could come to know You, except in Yourself, above me? There is no place at all; we move back and we move forward, and there is no place. Everywhere, O Truth, You preside over all who seek counsel from You, and You answer all of them at once, even though they ask Your counsel about many different things. You answer clearly, but not all hear clearly. All consult You about what they wish, but they do not always hear what they wish. Your best servant is the one who is intent not so much on hearing from You what he himself wants, as on wanting what he hears from You.

Late have I loved You, O Beauty so ancient and so new, late have I loved You! And see, You were within, and I was outside, and there I searched for You; and I, deformed, rushed headlong into those lovely things that You had made. You were with me, but I was not with You. Things held me far from You which, unless they were in You, would not exist at all. You called and cried out and broke through my deafness. You flashed, You shone, and You put my blindness to flight. You breathed Your fragrance, and I drew in my breath, and now I pant for You. I tasted, and now I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I burned for Your peace.

When I cling to You with my whole self, I shall have no sorrow or toil anywhere, and my life will be truly alive, being wholly full of You. But now, since You lift up the one You fill, and I am not full of You, I am a burden to myself. Joys I should weep over contend with sorrows I should rejoice in, and which side will win I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have pity on me. My evil sorrows contend with my good joys, and which side will win I do not know. Woe is me! Lord, have pity on me. Woe is me! See, I do not hide my wounds. You are the Physician, I am the sick one; You are merciful, I am miserable. Is not the life of man upon earth all trial? Who wants troubles and hardships? You command that they be endured, not loved. No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it. For though he is glad that he endures, he would still prefer that there were nothing for him to endure. In adversity I long for prosperity; in prosperity I fear adversity. What middle ground is there between the two, where the life of man is not all trial? Woe to the prosperities of the world, once and again, because of the fear of adversity and the corruption of joy! Woe to the adversities of the world, once and again and a third time, because of the longing for prosperity, and because adversity itself is hard, and because it may shatter endurance. Is not the life of man upon earth all trial, without any respite?

All my hope lies nowhere but in Your exceedingly great mercy. Give what You command, and command what You will. You command us to be continent; and when I knew, as someone says, that no one can be continent unless God gives it, this too was part of wisdom, to know whose gift it is. For it is by continence that we are gathered up and brought back into the One, from whom we had scattered ourselves into the many. He loves You too little who loves anything along with You that he does not love for Your sake. O Love, ever burning and never quenched! O Charity, my God, set me on fire! You command continence: give what You command, and command what You will.

You certainly command me to be continent from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. You have commanded me to abstain from sexual union, and as for marriage itself, You have counseled something better than what You have allowed. And since You gave me the gift, it was done, even before I became a minister of Your Sacrament. But there still live in my memory, of which I have said so much, the images of such things, fixed there by my bad habit. They come at me when I am awake, but then they have no strength; in sleep, however, they bring me not only to pleasure but even to consent, and to something very like the act itself. The illusion of the image has such power in my soul and in my flesh that false visions persuade me when I am asleep to what true sights cannot persuade me when I am awake. Am I not myself at such a time, O Lord my God? And yet what a difference there is between myself and myself in the moment in which I pass from waking into sleep, or come back from sleep to waking! Where is my reason then, the reason which resists such suggestions when I am awake, and which remains unshaken even if the things themselves are pressed upon it? Is it shut along with the eyes? Is it lulled to sleep along with the bodily senses? And how is it that often, even in sleep, we resist, and, mindful of our resolve and holding to it most chastely, give no consent to such enticements? And yet the difference is so great that when it turns out otherwise, we return on waking to peace of conscience; and by this very difference we discover that we did not do what we still grieve was somehow done in us.

Are You not mighty, God Almighty, able to heal all the diseases of my soul, and by Your more abundant grace to quench even the impure motions of my sleep! You will increase Your gifts in me more and more, Lord, so that my soul may follow me to You, freed from the birdlime of concupiscence; so that it may not rebel against itself, and so that even in dreams it may not only refrain from committing, through sensual images, those degrading corruptions that go as far as the defilement of the flesh, but may not even consent to them. For to bring it about that nothing of this sort should have even the slightest hold over the chaste affections of a sleeper, not even so slight a one as a passing thought could check, and to do this not only in this life but even at my present age, is no great thing for the Almighty, for You are able to do more than we ask or think. But what I still am in this kind of evil of mine, I have told my good Lord, rejoicing with trembling in what You have given me and mourning over what is still unfinished in me, hoping that You will perfect Your mercies in me, even to that perfect peace which my inner and outer man will have with You, when death is swallowed up in victory.

There is another evil of the day, and I wish it were sufficient for it. For by eating and drinking we repair the daily decay of our body, until You destroy both belly and food, when You will slay my emptiness with a wonderful fullness, and clothe this corruptible body with an eternal incorruption. But for now the necessity is sweet to me, and I fight against that sweetness so as not to be taken captive by it. I wage a daily war by fasting, often bringing my body into subjection, and my pains are driven away by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are pains of a kind; they burn and kill like a fever unless the medicine of food comes to our aid. And since that medicine is ready to hand through the comfort of Your gifts, by which land and water and sky serve our weakness, our affliction is called a delight.

This You have taught me: that I should come to taking food as I would to taking medicine. But while I am passing from the discomfort of hunger to the contentment of being filled, in the very passage the snare of concupiscence lies in wait for me. For the passage itself is pleasure, and there is no other way of passing to where necessity compels us to pass. And although health is the reason for eating and drinking, a dangerous pleasure attaches itself to it like a servant following behind, and most of the time tries to go in front, so that I end up doing for pleasure's sake what I say, or intend, that I am doing for health's sake. Nor do the two have the same measure: what is enough for health is too little for pleasure. And it is often unclear whether it is the necessary care of the body still asking for support, or whether a pleasure-loving and deceitful greed is offering its services. The unhappy soul is glad of this uncertainty, and makes ready in it an excuse to defend itself, pleased that it is not clear what is enough for the moderate needs of health, so that under the cover of health it may hide the business of pleasure. I try every day to resist these temptations, and I call on Your right hand and bring my perplexities to You, because I have not yet reached a settled judgment on this matter.

I hear the voice of my God commanding, Let not your hearts be weighed down with overeating and drunkenness. Drunkenness is far from me; You will have mercy, so that it does not come near me. But overeating sometimes creeps up on Your servant; You will have mercy, so that it may be put far from me. For no one can be continent unless You give it. You grant us many things when we pray for them, and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from You; and we received it from You so that we might afterwards know this. I have never been a drunkard, but I have known drunkards made sober by You. So it was Your doing that those who never were drunkards did not become so, just as it was Your doing that those who had been did not remain so forever; and it was Your doing that both should know whose doing it was. I heard another voice of Yours: Do not go after your lusts, and turn away from your pleasure. And by Your favor I have heard this saying too, which I have loved very much: neither if we eat shall we have more, nor if we do not eat shall we have less; that is to say, the one will not make me rich, nor the other wretched. I heard yet another: for I have learned, in whatever state I am, to be content with it; I know how to abound, and I know how to suffer need. I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me. Here is a soldier of the heavenly camp, not the dust that we are. But remember, Lord, that we are dust, and that from dust You made man; and he was lost, and is found. Nor could that man do this of himself, for he too was of the same dust, the man whom I have so loved for saying this by the breath of Your inspiration: I can do all things, he says, through Him who strengthens me. Strengthen me, so that I can. Give what You command, and command what You will. He confesses that he has received, and when he glories, he glories in the Lord. I have heard another begging that he might receive: Take from me, he says, the desires of the belly. From this it is clear, O my holy God, that it is You who give, whenever what You command to be done is done.

You have taught me, good Father, that to the pure all things are pure, but that it is evil for the man who eats with offense; and that every creature of Yours is good, and nothing is to be refused that is received with thanksgiving; and that food does not commend us to God; and that no one should judge us in food or drink; and that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat should not judge the one who eats. These things I have learned, thanks be to You, praise be to You, my God, my Teacher, who knock at my ears and enlighten my heart: deliver me from all temptation. It is not the uncleanness of food I fear, but the uncleanness of craving. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh that was fit for food; that Elijah was fed with flesh; that John, endowed with wonderful abstinence, was not defiled by feeding on living creatures, namely locusts. I know too that Esau was deceived by craving for lentils, that David blamed himself for longing for a drink of water, and that our King was tempted not with flesh but with bread. And so the people in the wilderness also deserved to be rebuked, not for desiring flesh, but because in their desire for food they murmured against the Lord.

Placed, then, among these temptations, I struggle every day against concupiscence in eating and drinking. For it is not the kind of thing I can decide to cut off once and for all and never touch again, as I was able to do with sexual union. So the reins of the throat must be held with a balanced mix of slackness and tightness. And who is there, O Lord, who is not carried somewhat beyond the limits of necessity? Whoever he is, he is a great man; let him magnify Your Name. But I am not such a man, for I am a sinful man. Yet I too magnify Your Name; and He who has overcome the world intercedes with You for my sins, counting me among the weak members of His body; for Your eyes have seen what is imperfect in Him, and in Your book all shall be written.

The allurements of smells do not trouble me much. When they are absent, I do not look for them; when they are present, I do not refuse them; and I am always ready to do without them. So it seems to me; perhaps I am deceived. For this too is a darkness to be lamented, that the capacities within me are hidden from me, so that my mind, questioning itself about its own powers, does not think it can readily trust itself; because even what is in it is for the most part hidden, unless experience brings it to light. And no one ought to feel secure in this life, the whole of which is called a trial, as though one who could be made better from worse could not also be made worse from better. Our only hope, our only confidence, our only sure promise is Your mercy.

The pleasures of the ear had entangled and subdued me more tightly, but You loosened me and set me free. Now, when I hear those melodies into which Your words breathe life, sung with a sweet and skilled voice, I do rest in them a little; yet not so as to be held fast by them, but so that I can rise and leave when I wish. Yet together with the words that are their life, and by which they gain admission to me, they seek a place of some honor in my heart, and I can hardly give them a fitting one. For at times I seem to myself to give them more honor than is right, when I feel that our minds are stirred more devoutly and more fervently into a flame of devotion by the holy words themselves when they are sung in this way than when they are not; and that all the affections of our spirit, in their sweet variety, have their own proper measures in voice and song, by which they are roused through some hidden kinship. But this gratification of my flesh, to which the mind ought not to be handed over to be weakened, often deceives me, when the sense does not accompany reason in such a way as to follow patiently behind it, but, having been admitted only for reason's sake, tries even to run ahead of it and lead it. So in these things I sin without noticing, and afterwards I notice.

At other times, guarding too anxiously against this very deception, I err by excessive strictness, sometimes so far as to wish that the whole melody of the sweet chants to which David's Psalter is sung were banished from my ears, and from the Church's too. And the safer way seems to me the one I remember often being told about Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, who had the reader of the psalm deliver it with so slight an inflection of the voice that it was closer to speaking than to singing. Yet when I remember the tears I shed at the singing of Your Church in the first days of my recovered faith, and how even now I am moved, not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and a most fitting melody, I acknowledge once again the great usefulness of this practice. So I waver between the danger of pleasure and the proven benefit, and I am inclined rather (though I do not pronounce an irrevocable opinion) to approve the custom of singing in church, so that through the delight of the ears weaker minds may rise to a feeling of devotion. Yet when it happens that I am moved more by the singing than by what is sung, I confess that I sin in a way that deserves punishment, and then I would rather not hear the singer. See where I stand! Weep with me and weep for me, you who so govern your feelings within that good actions follow. For you who do not act, these things do not touch you. But You, O Lord my God, hear me; look and see, have mercy and heal me, You in whose sight I have become a problem to myself, and that is my sickness.

There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, about which I shall make my confessions in the hearing of the ears of Your temple, those brotherly and devout ears, and so conclude the temptations of the lust of the flesh, which still assail me as I groan and long to be clothed with my dwelling that is from heaven. The eyes love beautiful and varied forms, bright and pleasing colors. Let these not take hold of my soul; let God take hold of it instead, who made these things very good indeed; yet He is my good, not they. And these things touch me all day long while I am awake, and I am given no rest from them, as I am given rest from musical sounds, and sometimes, in silence, from all sounds. For light itself, the queen of colors, bathing everything we see, wherever I am during the day, glides over me in many forms and soothes me while I am busy with other things and not paying attention to it. And it works its way into me so strongly that if it is suddenly taken away, it is sought with longing, and if it is gone for long, it saddens the mind.

O Light, which Tobias saw when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life and went before him with the feet of love, never straying! Or which Isaac saw, when his fleshly eyes were heavy and closed with old age, and it was granted him to bless his sons, not by knowing them, but to know them by blessing them. Or which Jacob saw, when he too, blind with great age, with an illumined heart shed light on the different races of the future people, foreshadowed in his sons; and laid his hands, mystically crossed, on his grandsons by Joseph, not as their father outwardly tried to correct them, but as he himself inwardly discerned. This is the light; it is one, and all who see and love it are one. But that bodily light I was speaking of seasons the life of this world for its blind lovers with an enticing and dangerous sweetness. Yet those who know how to praise You for it too, "O God, Creator of all," take it up into Your hymn and are not taken over by it in their sleep. That is how I long to be. I resist these seductions of the eyes, so that my feet, with which I walk along Your way, may not be entangled; and I lift up my invisible eyes to You, that You may pluck my feet out of the snare. Again and again You pluck them out, for they are ensnared. You never stop plucking them out, while I often get caught in the snares laid on every side; because You who keep Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep.

What countless things, made by all sorts of arts and crafts, in clothing, shoes, vessels and every kind of manufacture, in paintings too and images of every kind, far exceeding all necessary and moderate use and all devout meaning, have people added to entice their own eyes! Outwardly they follow what they themselves make; inwardly they abandon Him by whom they themselves were made, and destroy what they themselves were made to be. But I, my God and my Glory, even from this sing a hymn to You, and consecrate my praise to Him who consecrates me, because the beautiful designs that pass through people's souls into their skillful hands come from that Beauty which is above our souls, which my soul sighs after day and night. But those who make and pursue outward beauties draw from there the rule for judging them, but not the rule for using them. And He is there, though they do not see Him, so that they might not wander off, but keep their strength for You, and not squander it on pleasures that only weary them. And I, though I say this and see it clearly, still entangle my steps in these outward beauties; but You pluck me out, O Lord, You pluck me out, because Your loving-kindness is before my eyes. For I am caught miserably, and You pluck me out mercifully; sometimes without my noticing, when I had only lightly landed on them, and at other times painfully, because I had already stuck fast in them.

To this is added another form of temptation, dangerous in many more ways. For besides the concupiscence of the flesh, which lies in the delight of all the senses and pleasures, and whose slaves, going far from You, waste away and perish, the soul has, through those same bodily senses, a certain vain and curious desire, cloaked under the name of knowledge and learning: a desire not to take delight in the flesh, but to gain experience through the flesh. Because this desire has its seat in the appetite for knowing, and because sight is the chief of the senses for gaining knowledge, it is called in the language of Scripture the lust of the eyes. For seeing belongs properly to the eyes; yet we use this word for the other senses too, when we employ them in seeking knowledge. We do not say, listen how it flashes, or smell how it glows, or taste how it shines, or feel how it gleams; for all these things are said to be seen. Yet we say not only, see how it shines, which only the eyes can perceive, but also, see how it sounds, see how it smells, see how it tastes, see how hard it is. And so the general experience of the senses, as was said, is called the lust of the eyes, because the function of seeing, in which the eyes hold first place, is borrowed by the other senses by way of likeness whenever they explore any kind of knowledge.

From this it can be seen more clearly what part pleasure plays and what part curiosity plays in the use of the senses. Pleasure goes after what is beautiful, melodious, fragrant, tasty and soft; but curiosity, for the sake of the experiment, goes after the opposite as well, not in order to suffer discomfort, but out of the lust for trying and knowing things. For what pleasure is there in looking at a mangled corpse that makes you shudder? And yet if one is lying somewhere nearby, people flock to it, to be made sad and turn pale. They are even afraid of seeing it in their sleep, as if someone had forced them to look at it while they were awake, or some report of its beauty had drawn them there! It is the same with the other senses, which it would take too long to go through. From this disease of curiosity come all the strange spectacles exhibited in the theater. From this people go on to search out the hidden workings of nature, which lies outside us, which it profits nothing to know, and which people desire to know simply for the sake of knowing. From this, too, comes any inquiry by magical arts undertaken for the same end of perverted knowledge. From this, even in religion itself, God is put to the test, when signs and wonders are demanded of Him, desired not for any saving purpose but merely for the experience.

In this vast forest, so full of snares and dangers, see how many of them I have cut away and driven out of my heart, as You have enabled me to do, O God of my salvation. And yet when would I dare to say — since so many things of this kind buzz around our daily life on every side — when would I dare to say that nothing of this sort catches my attention to make me look, or captures me with idle interest? True, the theaters no longer carry me away, I do not care to know the courses of the stars, and my soul has never sought answers from the spirits of the dead; I detest all sacrilegious rites. Yet, O Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and single-hearted service, with what schemes and suggestions the enemy works on me to make me ask You for some sign! But I beg You, by our King and by our pure and holy homeland, Jerusalem, that as any consent to this is far from me now, so it may always be further and further away. But when I pray to You for someone's salvation, my purpose and intention are very different. You grant me, and will grant me, to follow You willingly as You do what You will.

And yet in how many very small and contemptible things is our curiosity tempted every day, and how often do we slip, who can count? How often, when people tell idle stories, do we begin by seeming merely to put up with them, so as not to offend the weak, and then little by little listen with real interest! I no longer go to the circus to watch a dog chasing a hare; but in the countryside, if I happen to be passing by, that same chase may well distract me even from some serious thought and draw me after it: not so that I turn my mount aside, but so that my heart leans that way. And unless You, having shown me my weakness, quickly warned me either to rise up to You through some reflection on the sight itself, or to despise it altogether and pass on, I stand there dull and absorbed. What about when I am sitting at home, and a lizard catching flies, or a spider entangling them as they rush into her web, often holds my attention? Is it a different thing because they are only small creatures? From them I go on to praise You, the wonderful Creator and Orderer of all things, but that is not what first catches my attention. It is one thing to get up quickly, another not to fall at all. My life is full of such things, and my one hope is Your wonderfully great mercy. For when our heart becomes a storehouse for such things and is loaded with crowds of this abundant vanity, then our prayers too are often interrupted and disturbed by it; and while, in Your presence, we direct the voice of our heart to Your ears, so great a matter is broken off by the rush of who knows what idle thoughts. Shall we then count this, too, among things of little importance? Or will anything bring us back to hope except Your full mercy, since You have begun to change us?

And You know how far You have already changed me, You who first healed me of the lust to vindicate myself, so that You might forgive all the rest of my iniquities, and heal all my infirmities, and redeem my life from corruption, and crown me with mercy and pity, and satisfy my desire with good things; You who curbed my pride with Your fear and tamed my neck to Your yoke. And now I bear it, and it is light to me, because this is what You promised and what You have done; and truly it was so, and I did not know it, when I was afraid to take it on.

But, O Lord, You who alone rule without pride, because You are the only true Lord, who has no lord over You: has this third kind of temptation also ceased for me, or can it cease at all in this whole life? I mean the wish to be feared and loved by people for no other reason than to get from it a joy that is no joy. It is a wretched life and an ugly boastfulness! It is above all from this that people neither love You purely nor fear You purely. And that is why You resist the proud and give grace to the humble; You thunder against the ambitions of the world, and the foundations of the mountains tremble. Now, because certain duties of human society make it necessary for us to be loved and feared by people, the adversary of our true happiness presses hard upon us, spreading everywhere his snares of "well done, well done," so that while we greedily snatch them up we may be caught off our guard, and detach our joy from Your truth and place it in the deceitfulness of men; so that we may enjoy being loved and feared, not for Your sake, but in Your place. In this way he may keep those who have been made like himself as his own, bound not in the harmony of love but in the fellowship of punishment: he who resolved to set his throne in the north, so that, dark and chilled, they might serve him as he imitates You in a perverse and crooked way. But we, O Lord, see, we are Your little flock; take us as Your own. Stretch out Your wings over us, and let us flee beneath them. Be our glory; let us be loved for Your sake, and let Your word be feared in us. Whoever wants to be praised by people while You blame him will not be defended by people when You judge, nor rescued when You condemn. But when it is not the sinner who is praised in the desires of his soul, nor the one who does wickedly who is blessed, but a man is praised for some gift You have given him, and he rejoices more that he himself is praised than that he has the gift for which he is praised, then he too is praised while You blame him; and the one who gave the praise is better than the one who received it. For the one was pleased by the gift of God in a man, while the other was better pleased by the gift of man than by the gift of God.

We are tempted by these temptations every day, O Lord; we are tempted without ceasing. Our daily furnace is the human tongue. In this area too You command us to be continent. Give what You command, and command what You will. You know the groans of my heart on this matter, and the floods from my eyes. For I cannot easily work out how far I have been cleansed of this plague, and I greatly fear my hidden faults, which Your eyes know, though mine do not. In other kinds of temptation I have some sort of means of examining myself; in this one, almost none. For with the pleasures of the flesh and idle curiosity, I can see how far I have succeeded in restraining my mind when I do without them, whether by choice or because they are absent. Then I ask myself how much more or less it troubles me not to have them. As for riches, which are sought so that they may serve one or two or all three of these concupiscences, if the soul cannot tell whether it despises them while it has them, they can be given up, so that it may put itself to the test. But in order to do without praise and test our strength in that, must we live badly, so recklessly and monstrously that no one who knows us does not detest us? What greater madness could be spoken or imagined? But if praise usually does and ought to accompany a good life and good works, we ought no more to give up its company than the good life itself. Yet I do not know whether I can do without something calmly or only with difficulty, until it is gone.

What, then, do I confess to You in this kind of temptation, O Lord? What else but that I take delight in praise, though I delight more in truth itself than in praise? For if I were asked whether I would rather be praised by everyone while raving mad and wrong about everything, or be blamed by everyone while steady and utterly settled in the truth, I can see which I would choose. Yet I would not wish another person's approval to add even a little to my joy in any good that is in me. But I admit that it does add to it, and not only that: blame takes away from it. And when I am troubled by this wretchedness of mine, an excuse slips in, and how much it is worth, You know, O God, for it leaves me uncertain. You have commanded us not only continence, that is, what things to hold our love back from, but also righteousness, that is, on what to bestow it; and You have willed that we love not only You but also our neighbor. So often, when I am pleased by the praise of someone who understands, I seem to myself to be pleased by my neighbor's progress or promise; and again, to be grieved by the fault in him when I hear him criticize what he does not understand, or what is good. For I am sometimes saddened by my own praise, either when things are praised in me that I myself dislike, or when lesser and trivial goods are valued more highly than they deserve. But then again, how do I know whether I feel this way because I do not want the one who praises me to disagree with me about myself, not because I am moved by concern for his good, but because the same good things that please me in myself please me more when they also please someone else? For in a way it is not I who am praised when my own judgment of myself is not praised, since either things are praised that displease me, or things are praised more that please me less. Am I then uncertain about myself in this matter?

See, in You, O Truth, I see that I ought to be moved by my own praises not for my own sake but for the good of my neighbor. And whether I am like that, I do not know. For in this I know myself less than I know You. I beg You, O my God, show me to myself as well, so that I may confess to my brothers, who are going to pray for me, whatever I find wounded in me. Let me question myself again, more carefully. If in my praises I am moved by my neighbor's good, why am I less moved when someone else is unjustly blamed than when I am? Why does an insult hurled at me sting me more than one hurled at another in my presence with the same injustice? Do I not know this either? Or is it finally the case that I deceive myself, and do not do the truth before You in my heart and on my tongue? Put this madness far from me, O Lord, lest my own mouth be to me the sinner's oil to anoint my head. I am poor and needy; yet I am better when, in hidden groaning, I am displeased with myself and seek Your mercy, until what is lacking in my failing state is restored and made perfect, on to that peace which the eye of the proud does not know.

Yet the word that comes out of the mouth, and deeds that become known to people, carry a most dangerous temptation from the love of praise, which begs for and gathers up people's votes to build up some private excellence of its own. It tempts me even when I condemn it in myself, and precisely because I condemn it; and often it glories all the more vainly in its very contempt for vainglory, and so it is no longer contempt for vainglory that it glories in, for it does not despise vainglory while it glories.

Within, too, deep within, there is another evil arising from the same kind of temptation, by which people become empty, pleasing themselves with themselves, even if they do not please others, or even displease them, or do not care to please them. But in pleasing themselves they greatly displease You, not only by taking pleasure in things that are not good as though they were good, but in Your good things as though they were their own; or, if as Yours, then as though earned by their own merits; or, if as coming from Your grace, then not rejoicing in fellowship with others but begrudging that grace to them. In all these and similar dangers and struggles You see the trembling of my heart, and I feel my wounds being healed by You again and again, rather than no longer being inflicted by me.

Where have You not walked with me, O Truth, teaching me what to guard against and what to desire, when I brought to You what I could discover here below and consulted You? With my outward senses, as far as I could, I surveyed the world, and I observed the life that my body has from me, and these senses of mine. From there I entered the recesses of my memory, those manifold and spacious chambers, wonderfully filled with countless stores; and I considered them, and I was struck with awe. I could make out none of these things without You, and I found that none of them was You. Nor was I myself You, I who discovered these things, who went through them all and labored to distinguish them and to value each according to its worth, receiving some things on the report of my senses, questioning others that I felt to be mingled with myself, numbering and distinguishing the messengers themselves, and, in the wide treasure-house of my memory, turning some things over, storing others away, drawing others out. Nor was I myself You when I was doing this, that is, the power by which I did it was not You, for You are the abiding light which I consulted about all these things, whether they existed, what they were, and how much they were worth; and I heard You teaching me and commanding me. And I often do this; it delights me, and whenever I can get free from necessary duties, I take refuge in this pleasure. Yet in all these things that I run through as I consult You, I find no safe place for my soul except in You, where my scattered parts may be gathered together, and nothing of me may depart from You. And sometimes You admit me, in my inmost being, into a state of feeling that is most unusual, rising to a strange sweetness which, if it were brought to completion in me, would be something, I know not what, that this present life is not. But through my wretched burdens I fall back into these lower things, and I am swallowed up again by my usual habits, and I am held; and I weep greatly, but I am greatly held. So heavy is the burden of bad habit! Here I am able to stay, but do not want to; there I want to be, but am not able; miserable both ways.

And so I have considered the sicknesses of my sins in that threefold concupiscence, and I have called on Your right hand to save me. For with a wounded heart I saw Your brightness, and, beaten back, I said, "Who can reach it? I am cast out from the sight of Your eyes." You are the Truth who presides over all things, but I, in my greed, did not want to lose You; I wanted to possess a lie along with You, just as no one wants to speak falsely in such a way that he himself does not know what is true. So I lost You, because You do not consent to be possessed together with a lie.

Whom could I find to reconcile me to You? Was I to turn to the Angels? With what prayers? With what sacraments? Many who were trying to return to You and could not do so by themselves have, as I hear, tried this, and have fallen into a craving for curious visions, and have been judged to deserve delusion. For in their pride they sought You with the arrogance of learning, puffing out their chests rather than beating them; and so, through the likeness of their hearts, they drew to themselves the powers of the air, fellow conspirators in their pride, by whom they were deceived through magical powers. They were looking for a mediator through whom they might be cleansed, and there was none. For it was the devil, transforming himself into an Angel of light. And it greatly enticed their proud flesh that he himself had no body of flesh. For they were mortal and sinners; but You, Lord, to whom they proudly sought to be reconciled, are immortal and without sin. But a mediator between God and man must have something like God and something like men, so that he is not, by being like men in both respects, far from God, or, by being like God in both respects, far from men, and so not a mediator at all. That deceitful mediator, then, by whom, through Your secret judgments, pride deserves to be deluded, has one thing in common with men, namely sin; the other he wishes to appear to have in common with God, so that, since he is not clothed in the mortality of flesh, he may pass himself off as immortal. But since the wages of sin is death, he has this in common with men: that together with them he is condemned to death.

But the true Mediator, whom in Your secret mercy You have shown to the humble, and sent, so that by His example they too might learn that same humility, that Mediator between God and man, the Man Christ Jesus, appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal Just One: mortal with men, just with God. And because the wages of righteousness is life and peace, He did this so that, by a righteousness joined to God, He might make void the death of sinners who have been made righteous, a death which He chose to share with them. So He was shown to the holy men of old, so that they might be saved through faith in His Passion still to come, as we are saved through faith in His Passion now past. For as Man, He is Mediator; but as the Word, He is not in the middle between God and man, because He is equal to God, and God with God, and together one God.

How You have loved us, good Father, who did not spare Your only Son, but gave Him up for us ungodly ones! How You have loved us, for whom He, who did not think it robbery to be equal with You, was made subject even to the death of the cross; He who alone was free among the dead, having power to lay down His life and power to take it up again: for us, to You, both Victor and Victim, and Victor because Victim; for us, to You, both Priest and Sacrifice, and Priest because Sacrifice; making us, who were servants, into Your sons, by being born of You and serving us. Rightly, then, is my hope strong in Him, that You will heal all my infirmities through Him who sits at Your right hand and intercedes for us; otherwise I would despair. For my infirmities are many and great, many they are and great; but Your medicine is mightier. We might have thought that Your Word was far removed from any union with man, and despaired of ourselves, had He not become flesh and dwelt among us.

Terrified by my sins and the weight of my misery, I had turned it over in my heart and had planned to flee into the wilderness; but You forbade me and strengthened me, saying, Therefore Christ died for all, that those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them. See, Lord, I cast my care upon You, that I may live and consider wonderful things out of Your law. You know my ignorance and my weakness; teach me and heal me. He, Your only Son, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, has redeemed me with His blood. Let not the proud speak evil of me, because I meditate on my ransom, and eat and drink it, and share it out; and, being poor, I long to be filled from Him among those who eat and are filled; and they shall praise the Lord who seek Him.

chapters.title: Book 11
paragraphs: Lord, eternity is Yours: are You then unaware of what I am telling You? Or do You see in time what takes place in time? Why, then, am I setting out so many stories in order before You? Certainly not so that You can learn them from me. I do it to stir up my own devotion toward You, and the devotion of those who read this, so that all of us may say, Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. I have said it before and I will say it again: I do this out of love for Your love. After all, we pray, even though Truth has said, Your Father knows what you need before you ask. So what we lay open before You is our own heart, as we confess to You our miseries and Your mercies toward us. We do it so that You may set us entirely free, since You have already begun, and so that we may stop being wretched in ourselves and become blessed in You. For You have called us to be poor in spirit, and meek, and mourners, and hungry and thirsty for righteousness, and merciful, and pure in heart, and peacemakers. Look: I have told You many things, as far as I was able and as far as I wished, because You first willed that I should confess to You, my Lord God. For You are good, and Your mercy endures forever.

But how could I ever be equal to setting down, with the tongue of my pen, all Your urgings and all Your terrors, Your comforts and Your guidance, by which You led me to preach Your Word and to dispense Your Sacrament to Your people? And even if I were equal to telling them in order, the drops of time are costly to me. For a long while now I have been burning to meditate on Your law, and in it to confess to You both what I know and what I do not know, the first dawn of Your light and the remnants of my darkness, until my weakness is swallowed up by strength. I do not want the hours I find free to drain away into anything else: the hours left over from the necessities of refreshing my body and the powers of my mind, and from the service we owe to other people, or the service we do not owe and give all the same.

O Lord my God, attend to my prayer, and let Your mercy listen to my longing. It does not burn for my sake alone; it wants to be of use to brotherly love, and You see in my heart that this is so. Let me offer You in sacrifice the service of my thought and my tongue, and give me what I am to offer You. For I am poor and needy, while You are rich toward all who call on You; You are free of all care, and yet You take care of us. Circumcise my lips, inside and out, from all rashness and all lying. Let Your Scriptures be my pure delight; let me not be deceived in them, nor deceive anyone out of them. Lord, listen and have pity, O Lord my God, Light of the blind and Strength of the weak, and Light too of those who see and Strength of the strong: listen to my soul, and hear it as it cries out of the depths. For if Your ears are not with us in the depths as well, where are we to go? Where are we to cry? The day is Yours and the night is Yours; the moments fly past at Your nod. Grant us out of that time some room for our meditations on the hidden things of Your law, and do not shut it against us when we knock. You did not have the dark secrets of so many pages written for nothing; those forests are not without their deer, which retreat into them and roam and walk about, graze, lie down and chew the cud. Bring me to completion, O Lord, and open those pages to me. See, Your voice is my joy; Your voice is beyond any abundance of pleasures. Give me what I love, for I do love, and this too is Your gift. Do not abandon Your own gifts, and do not scorn Your grass when it is thirsty. Let me confess to You whatever I find in Your books, and hear the voice of praise, and drink You in, and consider the wonderful things of Your law, from the very beginning, in which You made heaven and earth, to the everlasting reign of Your holy city with You.

Lord, have mercy on me and hear my longing. For I do not think it is a longing for anything of this earth: not for gold and silver and precious stones, or fine clothes, or honors and positions of power, or the pleasures of the flesh, or the things the body needs for this life of our pilgrimage. All these are added to those who seek Your kingdom and Your righteousness. Look, O Lord my God, at where my longing comes from. The wicked have told me of delights, but none like Your law, O Lord. Look, that is where my longing comes from. Look, Father; look and see and approve. May it please You, as You look on me with mercy, that I find grace before You, so that the inner depths of Your words may be opened to me as I knock. I beg You by our Lord Jesus Christ, Your Son, the Man of Your right hand, the Son of Man, whom You have established for Yourself as Your Mediator and ours. Through Him You sought us when we were not seeking You, and You sought us so that we would seek You. He is Your Word, through whom You made all things, and me among them; He is Your Only-Begotten, through whom You called the believing people to adoption, and me among them. I beg You by Him, who sits at Your right hand and intercedes with You for us, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden. It is these treasures I look for in Your books. Moses wrote of Him; He Himself says so; the Truth says so.

I want to hear and understand how "In the beginning You made heaven and earth." Moses wrote this. He wrote it and went away; he passed from here, from You to You, and he is not in front of me now. If he were, I would take hold of him and question him, and implore him by You to explain these things to me, and I would open the ears of my body to the sounds breaking from his mouth. If he spoke Hebrew, the sounds would beat on my senses in vain, and none of it would reach my mind; but if he spoke Latin, I would know what he was saying. Yet how would I know whether what he said was true? And even if I knew that too, would I know it from him? No: within me, deep within, in the dwelling place of my thought, Truth, which is neither Hebrew nor Greek nor Latin nor barbarian, and needs no organs of mouth or tongue and no sound of syllables, would say, "He is telling the truth." And at once, with full confidence, I would say to that man of Yours, "You are telling the truth." Since, then, I cannot question him, I ask You, Truth, who filled him when he spoke true things; I ask You, my God: forgive my sins. You granted Your servant to say these things; grant me too to understand them.

Look: heaven and earth exist. They cry out that they were made, for they change and vary. Whatever exists without having been made has nothing in it that was not there before, and that is exactly what it means to change and vary. They cry out, too, that they did not make themselves: "We exist because we were made. So we did not exist before we existed, in order to make ourselves." And the voice in which they say this is the evidence itself. So You, Lord, made them. You are beautiful, for they are beautiful; You are good, for they are good; You are, for they are. Yet they are not beautiful or good, nor do they exist, in the way that You their Creator are; compared with You they are neither beautiful nor good, nor do they exist at all. This we know, thanks be to You; and our knowledge, compared with Your knowledge, is ignorance.

But how did You make heaven and earth? What machinery did You use for so vast a work? It was not the way a human craftsman does it, shaping one body out of another at the discretion of his mind, which has some power to impose on a material the form it sees within itself with its inner eye. And where would the mind get that power, unless You had made it? The craftsman imposes a form on something that already exists and has being, such as clay or stone or wood or gold or the like. And where would these come from, if You had not established them? You made the craftsman's body; You made the mind that commands his limbs; You made the material out of which he makes anything; You made the understanding by which he grasps his art and sees inwardly what he is making outwardly; You made the bodily sense through which, as through an interpreter, he carries what he is making over from mind to material, and reports back to his mind what has been done, so that the mind within may consult the truth that presides over it and ask whether the work is well done. All these things praise You, the Creator of all. But how do You make them? How, O God, did You make heaven and earth? Certainly You did not make heaven and earth in heaven or on earth; nor in the air or the waters, since these too belong to heaven and earth; nor did You make the whole world within the whole world, because there was no place in which to make it before it was made, so that it might exist. Nor were You holding anything in Your hand out of which to make heaven and earth. Where would You have got anything You had not made, in order to make something out of it? For what exists at all, except because You exist? So You spoke, and they were made, and in Your Word You made them.

But how did You speak? Was it in the way the voice came out of the cloud, saying, This is my beloved Son? That voice sounded and was over; it began and it ended. Its syllables rang out and passed, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so on in order, until the last came after all the rest, and silence after the last. From this it is perfectly clear and plain that it was the motion of a creature that expressed it, a motion itself temporal, serving Your eternal will. These words of Yours, made for a passing moment, were carried by the outer ear to the understanding soul, whose inner ear was turned toward Your eternal Word. And the soul compared these words sounding in time with Your eternal Word in its silence, and said, "It is different, utterly different. These words are far below me; in fact they do not truly exist, because they flee and pass away. But the Word of my God abides above me forever." If, then, You said in words that sounded and passed away that heaven and earth should be made, and made heaven and earth in that way, there must already have been a bodily creature before heaven and earth, through whose movements in time that voice could run its course in time. But there was nothing bodily before heaven and earth; or if there was, You had certainly made it without any passing voice, so as to make from it the passing voice by which to say, Let the heaven and the earth be made. For whatever it was from which such a voice could be made, it would not exist at all unless You had made it. So, in order that a body might be made from which these words could then be made, by what Word did You speak?

So You call us to understand the Word, God who is with You, God, the Word spoken eternally, in whom all things are spoken eternally. For what is spoken there is not spoken in sequence, one thing brought to an end so that the next can be said, but all things at once and eternally. Otherwise we would already have time and change, and neither true eternity nor true immortality. This I know, my God, and I give thanks. I know it, I confess it to You, O Lord, and everyone who is not ungrateful to sure Truth knows it with me and blesses You. We know, Lord, we know: to the extent that anything no longer is what it was, and now is what it was not, to that extent it dies and comes to be. So nothing in Your Word gives way or takes another's place, because Your Word is truly immortal and eternal. And therefore, by the Word who is coeternal with You, You say all that You say at once and eternally, and whatever You say should be made is made. You make nothing except by saying; and yet not all the things You make by saying come to be at once, or last forever.

Why is that, I beg You, O Lord my God? I see it after a fashion, but I do not know how to put it into words, unless it is this: whatever begins to exist and ceases to exist begins and ceases at the point when, in Your eternal Reason, it is known that it ought to begin or cease; and in that Reason nothing begins or ceases. That Reason is Your Word, which is also "the Beginning, because it also speaks to us." So in the Gospel He speaks through the flesh, and this sounded outwardly in human ears, so that He might be believed and sought inwardly and found in the eternal Truth, where the good and only Master teaches all His disciples. There, Lord, I hear Your voice speaking to me, because the one who speaks to us is the one who teaches us; whoever does not teach us, even if he speaks, is not speaking to us. And who teaches us now, except the unchanging Truth? Even when we are prompted through some changeable creature, we are only being led to the unchanging Truth, where we learn truly, as we stand and listen to Him and rejoice greatly at the Bridegroom's voice, which gives us back to the One from whom we are. That is why He is the Beginning: if He did not remain when we wandered off, there would be nowhere for us to return to. But when we come back from error, it is by knowing that we come back; and so that we may know, He teaches us, because He is the Beginning and He speaks to us.

In this Beginning, O God, You made heaven and earth: in Your Word, in Your Son, in Your Power, in Your Wisdom, in Your Truth, speaking in a wonderful way and making in a wonderful way. Who will grasp it? Who will tell of it? What is this that shines through to me and strikes my heart without wounding it, so that I shudder and I burn? I shudder insofar as I am unlike it; I burn insofar as I am like it. It is Wisdom, Wisdom itself, that shines through to me, tearing apart my cloud; and yet the cloud wraps around me again as I sink back from that light, under the darkness that piles up on me as my punishment. For my strength has been so weakened by want that I cannot bear even my own blessings, until You, Lord, who have been merciful to all my iniquities, heal all my infirmities as well. For You will also redeem my life from corruption, and crown me with loving-kindness and tender mercies, and satisfy my desire with good things, because my youth will be renewed like the eagle's. For in hope we are saved, and so we wait with patience for Your promises. Let whoever is able hear You speaking inwardly; for my part, I will cry out boldly from Your own oracle: How wonderful are Your works, O Lord; in Wisdom You have made them all! And that Wisdom is the Beginning, and in that Beginning You made heaven and earth.

Look: are they not still full of their old leaven, the people who say to us, "What was God doing before He made heaven and earth? If He was at leisure," they say, "and doing nothing, why does He not stay that way from now on and forever, just as He always did in the past? For if some new motion arose in God, a new will to make a creature He had never made before, how could that be true eternity, when a will arises that was not there before? The will of God is not a creature; it comes before the creature, since nothing could be created unless the Creator's will came first. So God's will belongs to His very Substance. And if anything has arisen in God's Substance that was not there before, that Substance cannot truly be called eternal. But if it was God's will from eternity that the creature should exist, why was the creature not also from eternity?"

People who talk this way do not yet understand You, O Wisdom of God, Light of souls; they do not yet understand how the things are made that are made through You and in You. They try to grasp eternal things, but their heart still flutters among the movements of things past and things to come, and is still unsteady. Who will hold that heart and pin it down, so that it stands still for a little while, and for a little while catches the splendor of that eternity which is always still, and compares it with times that are never still, and sees that there is no comparison? Who will make it see that a long time becomes long only out of many movements passing by, which cannot all be stretched out at once; that in the eternal nothing passes, but the whole is present, whereas no time is ever present all at once; that all past time is driven on by the future, and all the future follows on from the past, and all past and future is created by, and flows out from, that which is always present? Who will hold the human heart still, so that it stands and sees how eternity, itself standing still, neither past nor future, utters the times past and to come? Is my hand strong enough for this? Or can the hand of my mouth, by speaking, accomplish so great a thing?

Here is my answer to anyone who asks, "What was God doing before He made heaven and earth?" I do not give the answer someone is said to have given as a joke, to dodge the force of the question: "He was preparing hell," he said, "for people who pry into mysteries." Answering questions is one thing; making fun of the people who ask them is another. So that is not my answer. I would much rather answer "I do not know" about what I do not know than give an answer that makes a laughingstock of someone who asks about deep things and wins praise for someone who answers with falsehoods. What I say is that You, our God, are the Creator of every creature; and if the name "heaven and earth" is taken to mean every creature, I say boldly, "Before God made heaven and earth, He did not make anything." For if He was making something, what could He have been making but a creature? I only wish I knew everything I long to know for my good as surely as I know that no creature was made before any creature was made.

But suppose someone's restless mind roams among images of bygone times, and marvels that You, God Almighty, Creator of all and Sustainer of all, Maker of heaven and earth, held back from so great a work for countless ages before You chose to undertake it. Let him wake up and realize that what he is marveling at is false. How could countless ages pass by that You had not made, when You are the Author and Creator of all ages? What times could there have been that were not made by You? And how could they pass by if they never existed? Since, then, You are the Maker of all times, if there was any time before You made heaven and earth, why do people say that You were refraining from work? You had made that very time, and no times could pass by before You made times. But if there was no time before heaven and earth, why do they ask what You were doing then? There was no "then" when there was no time.

Nor do You go before times by means of time; otherwise You would not go before all times. You go before all past times by the height of an eternity that is always present, and You stand above all future times, because they are future, and once they have come they will be past; but You are the Same, and Your years do not fail. Your years neither come nor go, whereas ours come and go, so that all of them may come. Your years stand all together, because they stand still; the years that go are not pushed out by the years that come, because Your years do not pass away. But ours will all exist only when none of them exists any longer. Your years are one day, and Your day is not one day after another, but Today, because Your Today does not give way to tomorrow, just as it does not take the place of yesterday. Your Today is Eternity. That is why You begot the Coeternal, to whom You said, Today I have begotten You. You made all times, and before all times You are; nor was there ever a time when there was no time.

So there was no time at which You had not made anything, because You had made time itself. And no times are coeternal with You, because You remain, whereas if times remained they would not be times. For what is time? Who can explain it easily and briefly? Who can even grasp it in thought clearly enough to put it into words? And yet what do we mention in conversation more familiarly and knowingly than time? We certainly understand it when we speak of it, and we understand it when we hear someone else speak of it. What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Yet I say with confidence that I know this much: if nothing passed away, there would be no past time; if nothing were coming, there would be no future time; and if nothing existed, there would be no present time. Those two times, then, the past and the future: how do they exist, when the past no longer exists and the future does not exist yet? As for the present, if it were always present and never passed into the past, it would no longer be time at all, but eternity. So if the present, in order to be time, comes into being only by passing into the past, how can we say that it exists, when the very reason it exists is that it is about to stop existing? In other words, we cannot truly say that time exists, except in the sense that it is tending toward not existing.

And yet we speak of "a long time" and "a short time," though only of the past or the future. For example, we call a hundred years ago a long time past, and a hundred years from now a long time to come. A short time past, let us say, is ten days ago, and a short time to come ten days from now. But how can something be long or short when it does not exist? The past no longer exists, and the future does not exist yet. So let us not say "it is long," but say of the past "it was long," and of the future "it will be long." My Lord, my Light, will Your Truth not laugh at us humans here too? Take that past time which was long: was it long once it was already past, or while it was still present? It could be long only at the time when there was something to be long. Once past, it no longer existed, and so it could not be long, since it did not exist at all. So let us not say "the past time was long," for we will not find anything that was long, since from the moment it became past it no longer exists. Let us say instead "that present time was long," because while it was present it was long. It had not yet passed away and ceased to exist, and so there was something that could be long; but once it had passed, it stopped being long at the same moment that it stopped existing.

Let us see, then, human soul, whether present time can be long; for you have been given the power to perceive and to measure spans of time. What will you answer me? Is a hundred years, when present, a long time? First see whether a hundred years can be present at all. If the first of those years is under way, that year is present, but the other ninety-nine are still to come, and so they do not exist yet. If the second year is under way, one is already past, one is present, and the rest are to come. In the same way, whichever year in the middle of this hundred we take as present, all the years before it will be past and all the years after it future. So a hundred years cannot be present. But see at least whether the one year that is under way is itself present. If its first month is under way, the rest are still to come; if the second, the first has already gone and the rest do not exist yet. So not even the year now under way is present as a whole; and if it is not present as a whole, then the year is not present. For a year is twelve months, and whichever single month is under way is present, while the rest are either past or future. And yet not even the current month is present, but only one day: if it is the first day, the rest are to come; if it is the last, the rest are past; if it is one in the middle, it stands between days past and days to come.

Look how the present time, which we found was the only time that could be called long, has shrunk to the span of barely one day. But let us examine even that, because not even one day is present as a whole. It is made up of the twenty-four hours of night and day. The first of these has all the others still to come; the last has all of them past; and any hour in between has those before it past and those after it to come. And that single hour itself goes by in fleeting fragments: whatever part of it has flown off is past, and whatever part is left is future. If we can conceive of some instant of time that cannot be divided into even the tiniest parts of moments, that alone can be called present. Yet it flies so swiftly from future to past that it is not stretched out by even the briefest pause. For if it is stretched out, it is divided into past and future. The present has no extent. Where, then, is the time we can call long? Is it the future? We do not say of the future, "It is long," because it does not yet exist to be long; we say, "It will be long." When, then, will it be long? If, even at that point, it is still future, it will not be long, since what could be long does not exist yet. But if it will be long only when it has begun to exist, coming out of a future that does not yet exist and becoming present, so that there is something that could be long, then the present time cries out, in the words we used above, that it cannot be long.

And yet, Lord, we are aware of intervals of time; we compare them with one another and say that some are longer and others shorter. We even measure how much longer or shorter one time is than another, and we answer that this one is double or triple, and that one single, or just as long as the other. But it is passing times we measure, when we measure them by perceiving them. Who can measure past times, which no longer exist, or future ones, which do not exist yet? Unless someone will dare to claim that what does not exist can be measured. So while time is passing, it can be perceived and measured; but once it has passed, it cannot, because it no longer exists.

I am asking, Father, not asserting. O my God, govern and guide me. "Who will tell me that there are not three times, past, present and future, as we learned when we were boys and taught to boys ourselves, but only the present, because the other two do not exist? Or do they exist as well? When the future becomes present, does it come out of some hidden place, and when the present becomes past, does it withdraw into one? For where did those who foretold things to come see them, if those things do not exist yet? What does not exist cannot be seen. And those who tell of things past could not tell of them truly unless they discerned them in their mind; and if those things did not exist at all, they could not be discerned in any way. So things past and things to come do exist."

Let me search further, Lord, O my hope; do not let my purpose be thrown into confusion. For if past and future times exist, I want to know where they are. Even if I cannot know that yet, I do know that wherever they are, they are not there as future or past, but as present. For if they are future there too, they are not there yet; and if they are past there too, they are no longer there. So wherever they are, and whatever they are, they exist only as present. And yet when past events are recounted truly, what is brought out of the memory is not the things themselves, which have passed, but words formed from their images, which those things, as they passed through the senses, left imprinted in the mind like footprints. My childhood, for instance, which no longer exists, lies in past time, which no longer exists; but when I call up its image and tell of it, I look at that image in the present, because it is still in my memory. Whether there is a similar explanation for foretelling the future, so that images of things that do not yet exist are perceived in advance as already existing, I confess, my God, I do not know. This much I do know: we often think ahead about our future actions, and that thinking ahead is present, while the action we are thinking ahead about does not exist yet, because it is future. Once we have set about it and begun to do what we were thinking ahead about, then that action will exist, because then it will be not future but present.

So whatever this mysterious foreseeing of future things may be, nothing can be seen except what exists. And what exists already is not future but present. So when future things are said to be seen, what is seen is not the things themselves, which do not exist yet (that is, the things that are going to be), but perhaps their causes or signs, which already exist. These, then, are not future but present to those who see them now, and from them the future is conceived in the mind and foretold. These conceptions in turn already exist, and those who foretell the future look at them as present within themselves. Let the vast variety of things supply me with an example. I watch the dawn, and I announce that the sun is about to rise. What I am watching is present; what I announce is future. It is not the sun that is future, since the sun already exists, but its rising, which does not exist yet. And yet unless I pictured the sunrise itself in my mind, as I am doing now while I speak of it, I could not foretell it. But neither is the dawn I see in the sky the sunrise, even though it goes before it, nor is the picture in my mind. These two are seen as present, so that the sunrise, which is still to come, can be foretold. So future things do not exist yet; and if they do not exist yet, they do not exist; and if they do not exist, they cannot be seen at all. But they can be foretold from present things, which already exist and are seen.

You, then, Ruler of Your creation, how do You teach souls the things that are to come? For You did teach Your Prophets. How do You, for whom nothing is future, teach future things? Or rather, do You teach present things about the future? For what does not exist certainly cannot be taught. This way lies far beyond my sight; it is too strong for me, and I cannot reach it by myself. But I can reach it from You, when You grant it, O sweet light of my hidden eyes.

What is now clear and plain is that neither future nor past things exist. Nor is it correct to say, "There are three times: past, present and future." Perhaps it would be correct to say, "There are three times: a present of past things, a present of present things, and a present of future things." For these three do exist in some way in the soul, and I do not see them anywhere else: the present of past things is memory; the present of present things is sight; the present of future things is expectation. If we are allowed to speak this way, I see three times, and I admit that there are three. Let people go on saying, too, "There are three times: past, present and future," in the loose way we usually talk. See, I do not mind, I do not object, I do not find fault, as long as what is said is understood: that neither what is to be, nor what is past, exists now. For there are few things we say correctly and many we say incorrectly; but what we mean is understood.

I said a moment ago, then, that we measure times as they pass, so that we can say that this stretch of time is double that one, or that this one is just as long as that, and so on for any other parts of time we are able to measure.
