So, as I was saying, we measure times as they pass. And if someone asks me, "How do you know?" I might answer, "I know that we do measure, and we cannot measure things that do not exist; and past and future things do not exist." But how do we measure present time, when it has no extent? It is measured while it is passing; once it has passed it is not measured, because there will be nothing to measure. But while it is being measured, where does it come from, by what way does it pass, and where does it go? Where from, if not from the future? By what way, if not through the present? Where to, if not into the past? From what does not exist yet, then, through what has no extent, into what no longer exists. Yet what do we measure, if not time in some extent? For when we speak of single, double, triple and equal, or anything else of that kind in time, we are speaking of nothing but spans of time. In what extent, then, do we measure time as it passes? In the future, from which it comes? But we do not measure what does not exist yet. Or in the present, through which it passes? But we do not measure what has no extent. Or in the past, into which it passes? But we do not measure what no longer exists either.

My mind is on fire to understand this most tangled riddle. Do not shut it away, O Lord my God, good Father; I beg You through Christ, do not shut these things, so familiar and yet so hidden, away from my longing, so that it cannot get inside them; let them grow clear, Lord, as the light of Your mercy dawns on them. Whom shall I ask about these things? And to whom could I more fruitfully confess my ignorance than to You, who are not wearied by my studies, burning so fiercely toward Your Scriptures? Give me what I love; for I do love, and this You have given me. Give, Father, You who truly know how to give good gifts to Your children. Give, because I have set myself to understand, and the labor is before me until You open it. I beg You by Christ, in His name, the Holy of holies, let no one disturb me. I believed, and therefore I speak. This is my hope; for this I live: that I may contemplate the delights of the Lord. See, You have made my days old, and they pass away, and how, I do not know. And we talk about time and time, times and times: "How long did he take to say this?" "How long did he take to do this?" "How long it is since I saw that!" and "This syllable takes double the time of that short single syllable." We say these things and we hear them; we are understood and we understand. They are perfectly plain and utterly ordinary, and yet these same things are also deeply hidden, and to discover them would be something new.

I once heard a learned man say that the movements of the sun, moon and stars are themselves time, and I did not agree. Why should the movements of all bodies not be times instead? Suppose the lights of heaven stopped and a potter's wheel went on turning: would there be no time by which we could measure its revolutions and say that it turned at equal intervals, or, if it sometimes went slower and sometimes faster, that some turns were longer and others shorter? And while we were saying this, would we not also be speaking in time? Would some syllables in our words be long and others short, except because the long ones sounded for a longer time and the short ones for a shorter? God, grant human beings to see in a small thing the notions common to things both small and great. The stars and lights of heaven are for signs, and for seasons, and for years, and for days. So they are; but I would not say that the turning of that little wooden wheel was a day, and neither could that learned man say that it was therefore not time.

I want to know the power and nature of time, by which we measure the movements of bodies and say, for instance, that this movement lasts twice as long as that one. Here is my question. The word "day" means not only the time the sun is above the earth (in which sense day is one thing and night another), but also its whole circuit from east back to east, in which sense we say, "So many days have passed," counting the nights in when we say "so many days" and not reckoning them separately. Since, then, a day is completed by the sun's movement and its circuit from east back to east, I ask whether the day is the movement itself, or the length of time in which that movement is completed, or both. If it is the first, then there would be a day even if the sun completed its course in a span of time as short as an hour. If it is the second, then it would not be a day if the interval from one sunrise to the next were as short as an hour; the sun would have to go round twenty-four times to complete one day. If it is both, then it could not be called a day if the sun ran its whole round in the space of an hour, nor could it if the sun stood still while as much time went by as the sun usually takes to make its whole round from morning to morning. So I will not ask now what it is that is called a day, but what time is: the time by which, measuring the sun's circuit, we would say that it had been completed in half the time it usually takes, if it had been completed in a span as short as twelve hours; and by which, comparing the two times, we would call the one single and the other double, even if the sun sometimes ran its round from east to east in the single time and sometimes in the double. So let no one tell me that the movements of the heavenly bodies are times, because when the sun stood still at one man's prayer, so that he could fight his battle through to victory, the sun stood still, but time went on. That battle was fought and finished in its own span of time, as much as it needed. I see, then, that time is a kind of distension. But do I see it, or do I only seem to see it? You, Light and Truth, will show me.

Do You tell me to agree if someone defines time as "the movement of a body"? You do not. I hear that no body moves except in time: You say so. But I do not hear that the movement of a body is time: You do not say that. For when a body moves, it is by time that I measure how long it moves, from the moment it starts moving until it stops. And if I did not see where it started, and it keeps moving so that I do not see when it stops, I cannot measure it, except perhaps from the moment I begin watching until I stop. And if I watch for a long while, I can report only that it is a long time, not how long, because when we say "how long," we are making a comparison, as in "this is as long as that," or "this is twice as long as that," or something of the kind. But if we can mark the distance between the places a moving body, or its parts if it turns as on a lathe, comes from and goes to, then we can say precisely how much time the movement of that body, or of its part, took from this place to that. Since, then, the movement of a body is one thing, and the means by which we measure how long it lasts is another, who cannot see which of the two should rather be called time? For if a body sometimes moves and sometimes stands still, we measure by time not only its movement but also its standing still, and we say, "It stood still as long as it moved," or "It stood still twice or three times as long as it moved," or give any other span our measuring has either determined exactly or estimated, more or less, as we usually say. Time, then, is not the movement of a body.

And I confess to You, O Lord, that I still do not know what time is. And again I confess to You, O Lord, that I know I am saying this in time, and that I have now been speaking about time for a long while, and that this very "long while" is long only because of a stretch of time. How, then, do I know this, when I do not know what time is? Or is it perhaps that I do not know how to put into words what I do know? Poor me, who do not even know what it is that I do not know! See, my God, before You I am not lying: as I speak, so is my heart. You will light my lamp; You, O Lord my God, will light up my darkness.

Does my soul not confess to You, and truly, that I do measure times? Is it so, then, my God, that I measure and do not know what I am measuring? I measure the movement of a body by time; and do I not measure time itself? Could I really measure the movement of a body, how long it lasts and how long it takes to get from here to there, without measuring the time in which it moves? How, then, do I measure this time itself? Do we measure a longer time by a shorter one, the way we measure the length of a beam by the length of a cubit? That, after all, is how we seem to measure the length of a long syllable by the length of a short one, and to say that it is double. In the same way we measure the length of stanzas by the length of lines, the length of lines by the length of feet, the length of feet by the length of syllables, and the length of long syllables by the length of short ones. We do not do this on the page, for that way we would be measuring spaces, not times; we do it as the words pass by while we pronounce them, and we say, "It is a long stanza, because it is made up of so many lines; the lines are long, because they consist of so many feet; the feet are long, because they stretch over so many syllables; the syllable is long, because it is double a short one." But not even this way do we arrive at any fixed measure of time, since it can happen that a shorter line, if drawn out in the speaking, takes up more time than a longer one hurried through. The same goes for a stanza, a foot, a syllable. So it seemed to me that time is nothing other than a distension; but a distension of what, I do not know, and I would be surprised if it were not of the mind itself. For what am I measuring, I beg You, my God, when I say either loosely, "This time is longer than that," or precisely, "This is double that"? I know that I am measuring time. But I am not measuring future time, because it does not exist yet; nor present time, because it is not stretched over any extent; nor past time, because it no longer exists. What, then, am I measuring? Times as they pass, not times that have passed? For that is what I said.

Keep at it, my mind, and press on with all your strength. God is our helper; He made us, and not we ourselves. Press on to where the truth begins to dawn. Suppose, now, that a bodily voice begins to sound, and sounds, and goes on sounding, and then, look, it stops. Now there is silence, and that voice is past and is no longer a voice. Before it sounded, it was future and could not be measured, because it did not exist yet; and now it cannot be measured, because it no longer exists. So it could be measured while it was sounding, because then there was something that could be measured. But even then it was not standing still; it was moving on and passing away. Could it be measured all the better for that? For as it passed, it was being stretched over some span of time in which it could be measured, since the present has no extent. If, then, it could be measured at that point, look: suppose another voice has begun to sound and is still sounding, in one continuous tone without any break. Let us measure it while it is sounding, since once it has stopped it will be past, and there will be nothing left to measure. Let us measure it, then, and say how long it is. But it is still sounding, and it cannot be measured except from the moment it began to the point where it stops. For what we measure is precisely the interval from some beginning to some end. So a voice that has not yet ended cannot be measured, so as to say how long or short it is, nor can it be called equal to another, or single or double in relation to another, or anything of that kind. But once it has ended, it no longer exists. How, then, can it be measured? And yet we do measure times: not those that do not exist yet, nor those that no longer exist, nor those that are not stretched out by any duration, nor those that have no limits. So we measure neither future times, nor past, nor present, nor passing ones; and yet we do measure times.

"Deus Creator omnium": this line of eight syllables alternates short and long syllables. So the four short ones, the first, third, fifth and seventh, are single in relation to the four long ones, the second, fourth, sixth and eighth. Each long one takes double the time of each short one. I pronounce them, I report on them, and I find that it is so, as far as plain perception can tell. As far as plain perception goes, I measure a long syllable by a short one and perceive that it has twice as much. But when one sounds after the other, if the first is short and the second long, how am I to hold on to the short one, and how, in measuring, am I to lay it against the long one to find that the long one has twice as much, since the long one does not begin to sound until the short one has stopped? And do I measure the long one itself as present, when I do not measure it until it has ended? Its ending is its passing away. What, then, is it that I measure? Where is the short syllable I measure with? Where is the long one I am measuring? Both have sounded, flown off, passed away; they no longer exist. And yet I measure, and I answer with confidence, as far as a trained ear can be trusted, that in span of time this one is single and that one double. And I could not do this unless they had already passed and ended. So it is not the syllables themselves that I measure, since they no longer exist, but something in my memory that stays fixed there.

It is in you, my mind, that I measure times. Do not interrupt me; that is, do not interrupt yourself with the crowding tumult of your impressions. In you, I say, I measure times. The impression that things make on you as they pass remains after they have gone, and it is this impression I measure, as something present, not the things that passed by to produce it. That is what I measure when I measure times. So either this is what times are, or I do not measure times at all. What about when we measure silences, and say that this silence lasted as long as that voice did? Do we not stretch our thought out to the length of a voice, as if it were sounding, so that we can report something about the intervals of silence in a span of time? For even when voice and tongue are still, we go through poems and lines and any kind of speech in our thought, or the measures of any movements, and we report on spans of time, how long this is compared with that, just as if we were saying them aloud. Suppose someone wants to utter a rather long sound, and has decided beforehand how long it is to be. He has already gone through that span of time in silence, and, committing it to memory, he begins to utter the sound, which goes on until it is brought to the end he set for it. Or rather, it has sounded and it will sound: the part of it already completed has sounded, and the rest will sound. And so it goes on, while the present intent of the mind carries the future over into the past, the past growing as the future shrinks, until the future is used up and the whole is past.

But how can the future, which does not exist yet, shrink or be used up? And how can the past, which no longer exists, grow? Only because in the mind that does this there are three things at work. It expects, it attends, it remembers, so that what it expects passes, through what it attends to, into what it remembers. Who, then, denies that future things do not exist yet? And yet there is already in the mind an expectation of future things. And who denies that past things no longer exist? And yet there is still in the mind a memory of past things. And who denies that present time has no extent, since it passes in an instant? And yet attention lasts, and through it what is about to be present moves on toward being absent. So it is not future time that is long, since it does not exist; a long future is "a long expectation of the future." Nor is it past time that is long, since it no longer exists; a long past is "a long memory of the past."

I am about to recite a Psalm I know. Before I begin, my expectation stretches over the whole of it; but once I have begun, however much of it I have plucked off into the past stretches over my memory as well. So the life of this action of mine is stretched out two ways: into my memory, for what I have recited, and into my expectation, for what I am about to recite. Yet my attention is present, and through it what was future is carried across to become past. The further this goes on, the shorter the expectation grows and the longer the memory, until the whole expectation is used up, when the whole action is finished and has passed into memory. And what happens in the whole Psalm happens in each part of it and in each syllable; it happens in the longer action of which this Psalm may be a part; it happens in the whole life of a human being, of which all that person's actions are parts; it happens in the whole age of the sons of men, of which all human lives are parts.

But because Your loving-kindness is better than all lives, see: my life is nothing but distension, and Your right hand has held me up in my Lord, the Son of Man, the Mediator between You, the One, and us, the many, who are many also in our many distractions among many things, so that through Him I may lay hold, as in Him I have been laid hold of, and be gathered back from my old way of life to follow the One, forgetting what lies behind; not distended but extended, not toward the things that will come and pass away but toward the things that are ahead, not in distension but in intention, I press on toward the prize of my heavenly calling, where I may hear the voice of Your praise and contemplate Your delights, which neither come nor pass away. But now my years are spent in mourning, and You, O Lord, are my comfort, my Father everlasting. I, though, have been scattered among times whose order I do not know, and my thoughts, the innermost depths of my soul, are torn to pieces by tumultuous changes, until I flow together into You, purified and melted by the fire of Your love.

And I will stand, and be made firm in You, in my mold, Your truth. I will not put up with the questions of people who, through a disease that is a punishment, thirst for more than they can hold, and ask, "What was God doing before He made heaven and earth?" or "How did it come into His mind to make anything, when He had never made anything before?" Grant them, O Lord, to think carefully about what they are saying, and to discover that "never" cannot be said when "time" does not exist. So when He is said "never to have made" anything, what else is that but saying that there was "no time" at which He made it? Let them see, then, that there can be no time without created being, and let them stop talking such empty nonsense. Let them also stretch forward to the things that are ahead, and understand that You are before all times, the eternal Creator of all times, and that no times are coeternal with You, nor is any creature, even if there is some creature above all times.

O Lord my God, how deep is that hidden recess of Your mysteries, and how far the consequences of my sins have thrown me from it! Heal my eyes, so that I may share the joy of Your light. Certainly, if there is a mind endowed with such vast knowledge and foreknowledge that it knows all things past and future as well as I know one very familiar Psalm, that mind is exceedingly wonderful and astonishing enough to make one tremble. Nothing past and nothing still to come in the ages ahead is hidden from it, any more than, when I sing that Psalm, it is hidden from me what and how much of it has gone by since the beginning, and what and how much is left before the end. But far be it from You, Creator of the universe, Creator of souls and bodies, far be it from You to know all things past and future in that way. You know them far, far more wonderfully and far more mysteriously. For when someone sings a song he knows, or hears a familiar song, his feelings vary with his expectation of the words to come and his memory of those that are past, and his senses are distended; but nothing of the kind happens to You, who are unchangeably eternal, that is, truly eternal, the Creator of minds. So just as in the Beginning You knew heaven and earth without any variation in Your knowledge, so in the Beginning You made heaven and earth without any distension in Your action. Let whoever understands this confess to You, and let whoever does not understand it confess to You. Oh, how high You are, and yet the humble in heart are Your dwelling place! For You raise up those who are bowed down, and those whose height You are do not fall.

chapters.title: Book 12
paragraphs: My heart, Lord, struck by the words of Your Holy Scripture, is kept very busy in this poverty of my life. And that is why the poverty of human understanding is usually so rich in words: because searching has more to say than finding, asking takes longer than obtaining, and the hand that knocks has more work to do than the hand that receives. We hold the promise; who will make it void? If God is for us, who can be against us? Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and whoever seeks finds; and to the one who knocks it shall be opened. These are Your own promises; and who need fear being deceived when it is the Truth that promises?

The lowliness of my tongue confesses to Your Highness that You made heaven and earth: this heaven that I see, and this earth that I walk on, from which comes this earth that I carry about with me. You made it. But where, Lord, is that heaven of heaven which we hear of in the words of the Psalm: The heaven of heaven is the Lord's, but the earth He has given to the children of men? Where is that heaven which we do not see, compared with which all this that we see is earth? For this whole bodily universe, which is not whole everywhere, has received its share of beauty even in these lower parts, the lowest of which is this earth of ours; yet compared with that heaven of heaven, even the heaven of our earth is only earth. Indeed, both of these great bodies may without absurdity be called earth when set beside that unknown heaven which belongs to the Lord and not to the sons of men.

And certainly this earth was invisible and unformed, and there was some depth of abyss, I do not know what, over which there was no light, because it had no shape. That is why You commanded it to be written that darkness was upon the face of the deep. What is that but the absence of light? For if there had been light, where would it have been except above everything, rising over it and lighting it up? So where there was not yet light, what did the presence of darkness mean except the absence of light? Darkness, then, was upon it, because light was not upon it, just as where there is no sound there is silence. And what does it mean to have silence there, except to have no sound there? Have You not, Lord, taught this soul which confesses to You? Have You not taught me, Lord, that before You formed and differentiated this formless matter, there was nothing: no color, no figure, no body, no spirit? And yet it was not absolutely nothing; there was a certain formlessness, without any beauty.

How, then, was it to be named, so that it might somehow be conveyed even to slower minds, except by some ordinary word? And among all the parts of the world, what can be found closer to complete formlessness than earth and the deep? For since they stand on the lowest level, they are less beautiful than the other, higher parts, which are all transparent and shining. Why, then, should I not take the formlessness of matter, which You had created without beauty in order to make this beautiful world from it, to be fittingly suggested to human beings by the name of earth invisible and unformed?

So when thought looks for what the senses might grasp in this, and says to itself, "It is not an intelligible form, like life or justice, because it is the matter of bodies; nor is it something perceived by the senses, because in what is invisible and unformed there was nothing to be seen or sensed" — while human thought says this to itself, it may try either to know it by not knowing it, or not to know it by knowing it.

But as for me, Lord, if I were to confess to You with my tongue and my pen the whole of what You Yourself have taught me about that matter — I first heard its name without understanding it, when people who did not understand it themselves told me about it, and so I pictured it as having countless and varied forms, and therefore did not picture it at all. My mind turned over foul and horrible "forms" in complete disorder, but "forms" all the same; and I called it formless, not because it lacked all form, but because it had the kind of form that my mind would turn away from, as strange and jarring, if it were presented to it, and that human frailty would be disturbed by. Even so, what I pictured was formless not by being deprived of all form, but only by comparison with more beautiful forms; and true reason urged me to strip it completely of every last remnant of form whatever, if I wanted to conceive of matter that was absolutely formless. And I could not. For I could sooner imagine that something deprived of all form did not exist at all than conceive of something between form and nothing, neither formed nor nothing, a formless almost-nothing. So my mind gave up questioning my spirit about it, since my spirit was full of the images of formed bodies, changing and varying them as it pleased; and I turned my attention to bodies themselves and looked more deeply into their changeableness, by which they cease to be what they had been and begin to be what they were not. And I suspected that this same passing from form to form takes place through some formless state, not through sheer nothing; but I longed to know this, not merely to suspect it. If, then, my voice and my pen were to confess to You the whole of it, all the knots You untied for me in this question, what reader would hold out long enough to take it all in? Yet my heart will not on that account cease to give You honor and a song of praise for the things it cannot put into words. For the changeableness of changeable things is itself capable of all the forms into which changeable things are changed. And this changeableness, what is it? Is it soul? Is it body? Is it some form belonging to soul or body? If one could say "a nothing-something," or "an is-that-is-not," this is what I would call it; and yet in some way it already existed even then, since it was capable of receiving these visible and compound figures.

But where could it have had even this degree of being, except from You, from whom all things are, to whatever extent they are? Yet the more unlike You a thing is, the farther it is from You; for this is not a distance of place. So You, Lord, who are not one thing in one place and something different in another, but the Selfsame, and the Selfsame, and the Selfsame, Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God Almighty — You, in the Beginning, which is of You, in Your Wisdom, which was born of Your own Substance, created something, and created it out of nothing. For You made heaven and earth, but not out of Yourself; if You had, they would be equal to Your Only Begotten Son, and through that to You as well, whereas it would in no way be right for anything to be equal to You that was not of You. And there was nothing else besides You out of which You could create them, O God, one Trinity and threefold Unity; and so You created heaven and earth out of nothing, a great thing and a small thing. For You are Almighty and Good, to make all things good, both the great heaven and the little earth. You were, and there was nothing else out of which You created heaven and earth: two kinds of thing, one near to You, the other near to nothing; one to which You alone would be superior, the other to which nothing would be inferior.

But that heaven of heaven was for Yourself, Lord; while the earth which You gave to the sons of men, to be seen and touched, was not such as we see and touch now. For it was invisible and unformed, and there was a deep over which there was no light; or, darkness was above the deep, that is, more than in the deep. For this deep of waters, which is now visible, has even in its depths a light proper to its own nature, perceptible in some degree to the fish and the creeping things on its bottom. But that whole deep was almost nothing, because it was still entirely without form; yet there was already something that could be formed. For You, Lord, made the world out of formless matter, which You made out of nothing as something almost nothing, so that from it You might make the great things that we sons of men marvel at. For this bodily heaven is truly wonderful, this firmament between water and water, of which You said on the second day, after the creation of light, Let it be made, and it was made. This firmament You called heaven: the heaven, that is, of this earth and sea, which You made on the third day by giving a visible shape to the formless matter which You had made before any day. For You had already made a heaven before any day, but that was the heaven of this heaven, because In the beginning You had made heaven and earth. But this earth itself which You had made was formless matter, because it was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep. Out of this invisible and unformed earth, out of this formlessness, out of this almost-nothing, You were to make all the things of which this changeable world consists and yet does not hold firm; a world in which changeableness itself shows, in that times can be perceived and counted in it. For times are produced by the changes of things, as their shapes vary and turn; and the matter of those shapes is the invisible earth spoken of above.

That is why the Spirit, the teacher of Your servant, when He relates that You in the beginning created heaven and earth, says nothing about times and is silent about days. For clearly that heaven of heaven which You created in the beginning is some intellectual creature. Although it is in no way coeternal with You, the Trinity, it still shares in Your eternity; through the sweetness of that most blessed contemplation of You it firmly holds its own changeableness in check; and, clinging to You without any fall from the moment it was created, it stands beyond all the turning succession of times. Nor is this formlessness itself, the earth invisible and unformed, counted among the days. For where there is no shape and no order, nothing comes and nothing passes away; and where this does not happen, there are certainly no days, nor any succession of spans of time.

O let the Truth, the Light of my heart, speak to me, and not my own darkness! I slid down into that darkness and was darkened; but even from there, even from there, I loved You. I went astray, and I remembered You. I heard Your voice behind me, calling me to come back, and I could hardly hear it for the uproar of the enemies of peace. And now, look, I am coming back, burning and panting for Your fountain. Let no one stop me! From this I will drink, and so I will live. Let me not be my own life: living from myself, I lived badly; I was death to myself; in You I come alive again. Speak to me Yourself; talk with me Yourself. I have believed Your Books, and their words are full of deep mystery.

You have already told me, Lord, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that You are eternal, You who alone have immortality, since You are not changed by any shape or motion, and Your will does not vary with times; for no will that becomes now one thing and now another is immortal. In Your sight this is clear to me; let it become clearer and clearer to me, I beg You, and in that revelation let me remain soberly under Your wings. You have also told me, Lord, with a strong voice in my inner ear, that You made all natures and substances which are not what You are and yet exist; and that the only thing not from You is what does not exist, together with the movement of the will away from You, who are, toward what exists to a lesser degree, because such a movement is transgression and sin; and that no one's sin either harms You or disturbs the order of Your rule, whether at its highest or at its lowest. In Your sight this is clear to me; let it become clearer and clearer to me, I beg You, and in that revelation let me remain soberly under Your wings.

You have also told me with a strong voice in my inner ear that not even that creature is coeternal with You whose happiness is You alone, and which, drawing its nourishment from You with a most persevering purity, never and nowhere puts forth its natural changeableness; and which, with You always present to it, to whom it holds fast with its whole affection, has no future to wait for and does not pass into the past what it remembers, and so is neither altered by any change nor drawn apart into any times. O blessed creature, if such a one exists, blessed in clinging to Your Blessedness, blessed in You, its eternal Inhabitant and its Enlightener! Nor can I find any name I would more gladly give to the heaven of heaven which is the Lord's than Your house, which contemplates Your delights without ever failing by going out to anything else: one pure mind, most harmoniously one, through the settled peace of holy spirits, the citizens of Your city in the heavenly places, far above these heavenly places that we see.

By this may the soul whose pilgrimage has become long and far away, by this may she understand — if she now thirsts for You, if her tears have now become her bread while they say to her every day, Where is your God? — if she now asks one thing of You and seeks after it, that she may dwell in Your house all the days of her life (and what is her life but You? and what are Your days but Your eternity, like Your years which do not fail, because You are always the same?) — by this, then, may the soul that is able understand how far above all times You are eternal, since Your house, which never went off into a far country, though it is not coeternal with You, still suffers no changeableness of times, because it clings to You continually and unfailingly. In Your sight this is clear to me; let it become clearer and clearer to me, I beg You, and in that revelation let me remain soberly under Your wings.

Look: there is some formlessness, I do not know what, in the changes of these last and lowest creatures. And who will tell me — unless it is someone who, through the emptiness of his own heart, wanders and tosses himself about among his own fantasies — who but such a person would tell me that if every shape were so diminished and used up that only that formlessness remained through which the thing was changed and turned from one shape into another, that formlessness could display the succession of times? For plainly it could not, because without variety of motions there are no times, and there is no variety where there is no shape.

Having considered these things, as far as You grant, my God, as far as You rouse me to knock, and as far as You open to me when I knock, I find two things that You have made outside the reach of time, though neither of them is coeternal with You. The one is so formed that, without any pause in its contemplation, without any interval of change, changeable yet never changed, it fully enjoys Your eternity and unchangeableness. The other was so formless that it had nothing that could be changed from one form into another, whether of motion or of rest, so as to become subject to time. But You did not leave this formless, because before any day, in the beginning, You created heaven and earth, the two things I was speaking of. But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep. In these words formlessness is conveyed to us, so that those who cannot conceive of a complete absence of all form which still does not come down to nothing may be led on by degrees. Out of it another heaven was to be created, together with a visible and well-formed earth, and the waters set in their various order, and whatever else in the forming of the world is recorded as having been created, not without days; and this because such things are of a nature in which the successive changes of times can take place, since they are subject to appointed changes of motions and of forms.

This, then, is how I understand it for now, my God, when I hear Your Scripture say, In the beginning God made heaven and earth: and the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep, without mentioning on what day You created them. This is how I understand it: that it is because of the heaven of heaven — that intellectual heaven, whose understanding knows all at once, not in part, not darkly, not through a glass, but as a whole, openly, face to face; not this thing now and that thing later, but (as I said) knows all at once, without any succession of times — and because of the earth invisible and unformed, which is without any succession of times, the succession that brings "this thing now, that thing later," since where there is no form there is no distinguishing of this and that; it is, then, on account of these two, the one formed from the first and the other wholly formless, the one heaven, but the heaven of heaven, the other earth, but the earth invisible and unformed; because of these two, I understand, Your Scripture said without mention of days, In the beginning God made heaven and earth. For it immediately added which earth it meant; and also, by recording that the firmament was created on the second day and called heaven, it shows us which heaven it had spoken of before, without mention of days.

Wonderful depth of Your words! Look, their surface lies before us, coaxing the little ones; and yet they are a wonderful depth, my God, a wonderful depth! It makes one shudder to look into it: a shudder of reverence and a trembling of love. Its enemies I hate fiercely. Oh, that You would slay them with Your two-edged sword, so that they would no longer be its enemies! For this is how I love to have them slain: slain to themselves, so that they may live to You. But look, there are others, not fault-finders but admirers of the book of Genesis. "The Spirit of God," they say, "who wrote these things through His servant Moses, did not want those words to be understood this way. He did not want them understood as you say, but in another way, as we say." To them, with You Yourself, God of us all, as judge, I answer as follows.

"Will you say that what Truth tells me with a strong voice in my inner ear about the eternity of the Creator is false: that His substance is in no way changed by time, and that His will is not separate from His substance? It follows that He does not will one thing now and another thing later, but wills all that He wills once, and at once, and always; not again and again, not now this and now that; He does not afterward will what He did not will before, nor cease to will what He willed before, because such a will is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal; but our God is eternal. Again, He tells me in my inner ear that the expectation of things to come becomes direct sight when they have come, and this same sight becomes memory when they have passed. Now every act of thought that varies in this way is changeable, and nothing changeable is eternal; but our God is eternal." I gather these things and put them together, and I find that my God, the eternal God, did not make any creature by some new act of will, and that His knowledge admits of nothing transitory. "What, then, will you say, you who contradict me? Are these things false?" "No," they say. "What then? Is it false that every nature already formed, or matter capable of form, exists only from Him who is supremely good because He supremely is?" "We do not deny this either," they say. "What then? Do you deny that there is a certain sublime creature, cleaving with so chaste a love to the true and truly eternal God that, although it is not coeternal with Him, it does not break away from Him or dissolve into the variety and succession of times, but rests in the truest contemplation of Him alone?" For You, God, show Yourself to the one who loves You as much as You command, and You are enough for him; and so he does not turn aside from You, nor toward himself. This is the house of God, not of earthly mold, nor of any bodily heavenly mass, but spiritual, and sharing in Your eternity, because it is without any falling away forever. For You have established it for ever and ever; You have given it a law which it shall not pass. Yet it is not coeternal with You, God, because it is not without beginning; for it was made.

For although we find no time before it, since wisdom was created before all things, this is not that Wisdom which is entirely equal and coeternal with You, our God, His Father, the Wisdom through whom all things were created and in whom, as the Beginning, You created heaven and earth. It is rather the wisdom that is created, namely the intellectual nature, which becomes light by contemplating the light. For this too, though created, is called wisdom. But as great as the difference is between the Light that enlightens and the light that is enlightened, so great is the difference between the Wisdom that creates and the wisdom that is created; just as between the Righteousness that justifies and the righteousness that is brought about by justification. For we too are called Your righteousness; as a certain servant of Yours says, That we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. Since, then, a certain created wisdom was created before all things, the rational and intellectual mind of that chaste city of Yours, our mother, which is above and is free and eternal in the heavens (in what heavens, if not those that praise You, the heavens of heavens? for this is also the heaven of heaven which is the Lord's); although we find no time before it, because what was created before all things also comes before the creation of time, still the eternity of the Creator Himself is before it. From Him, when it was made, it took its beginning, not indeed a beginning in time, since time did not yet exist, but the beginning of its own creation.

So it comes from You, our God, in such a way that it is plainly something other than You, and not the Selfsame. For although we find time neither before it nor even in it, since it is fit always to behold Your face and is never turned away from it, so that it is not varied by any change, there is still in it a liability to change, by which it would grow dark and cold if it did not cling to You with a great love and so, like an everlasting noon, shine and glow from You. O house full of light and beauty! I have loved your beauty, and the place of the habitation of the glory of my Lord, your builder and owner. Let my pilgrimage sigh for you; and I say to Him who made you that He should take possession of me too in you, since He made me as well. I have gone astray like a lost sheep; yet on the shoulders of my Shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried back to you.

"What do you say to me, you who contradict me, whom I was just addressing, and who nevertheless believe that Moses was the holy servant of God and that his books are the oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is not this house of God, though not coeternal with God, yet eternal after its own measure in the heavens, where you look in vain for changes of times, because you will not find them? For what it is always good to cling fast to God rises above all extension and every revolving span of time." "It is," they say. "Then of all that my heart cried out to my God when it heard inwardly the voice of His praise, which part do you claim is false? Is it that the matter was formless, and that there, because there was no form, there was no order? But where there was no order, there could be no succession of times; and yet this 'almost nothing,' insofar as it was not altogether nothing, was certainly from Him from whom is whatever is, in whatever degree it is anything at all." "This too," they say, "we do not deny."

With these, my God, I want to talk a little in Your presence: with those who grant that all these things are true which Your Truth whispers to my soul. As for those who deny them, let them bark and deafen themselves with their own noise as much as they like; I will try to persuade them to be quiet and to open in themselves a way for Your word. But if they refuse and push me away, I beg You, my God, do not be silent toward me. Speak truly in my heart, for You alone speak in that way; and I will leave them outside, blowing on the dust and raising it into their own eyes, and I will enter my chamber and sing there a song of love to You, groaning with groanings that cannot be uttered in my pilgrimage, and remembering Jerusalem, with my heart lifted up toward it: Jerusalem my homeland, Jerusalem my mother, and You who reign over it, the Enlightener, Father, Guardian, Husband, the pure and strong delight and solid joy, and all good things beyond words, all of them at once, because You are the one supreme and true Good. And I will not be turned away until You gather all that I am out of this scattered and disordered state into the peace of that dearest mother of ours, where the first fruits of my spirit already are, and from which I am made certain of these things, and until You conform and confirm it forever, my God, my Mercy. But as for those who do not call all these truths false, who honor Your holy Scripture, set forth by holy Moses, placing it, as we do, at the summit of authority to be followed, and who still contradict me on some point, to them I answer this: be the judge, our God, between my Confessions and these people's contradictions.

For they say, "Even though these things are true, Moses did not have those two in mind when, by revelation of the Spirit, he said, In the beginning God made heaven and earth. By the word heaven he did not mean that spiritual or intellectual creature which always beholds the face of God, nor by the word earth that formless matter." "What, then?" "That man of God," they say, "meant what we say; this is what he declared by those words." "And what is that?" "By the words heaven and earth," they say, "he wanted first to signify, in a general and summary way, this whole visible world, so that afterward, by listing the days one by one, he could set out in detail and, as it were, piece by piece, all the things that it pleased the Holy Spirit to express in this way. For the people he was speaking to were so unlearned and carnal that he judged them fit to be entrusted only with those works of God that are visible." They do agree, however, that the earth invisible and unformed and that dark deep (out of which, as is shown afterward, all these visible things that everyone knows were made and set in order during those "days") may, not unfittingly, be understood as this formless first matter.

What if someone else were to say that "this same formlessness and confusion of matter was first conveyed under the name of heaven and earth because out of it this visible world was created and completed, with all the natures that appear most plainly in it, a world often called by the name of heaven and earth"? What, again, if another were to say that "invisible and visible nature is indeed not unfittingly called heaven and earth, and so the whole creation, which God made in His Wisdom, that is, in the Beginning, was included under those two words? Yet since all things were made not from the substance of God but out of nothing (because they are not the same as what God is, and there is a changeable nature in them all, whether they abide, as the eternal house of God does, or are changed, as the soul and body of man are), therefore the common matter of all things visible and invisible (still unformed, though capable of form), out of which both heaven and earth were to be created (that is, the invisible and the visible creation once formed), was called by the same names that were given to the earth invisible and unformed and to the darkness upon the deep; but with this distinction, that by the earth invisible and unformed is understood corporeal matter before it was given the quality of any form, and by the darkness upon the deep, spiritual matter before its boundless, as it were fluid, restlessness was held in check, and before it received any light from Wisdom"?

It still remains for someone else to say, if he wishes, that "the natures already completed and formed, visible and invisible, are not what is meant by the name of heaven and earth when we read, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but that the still unformed beginning of things, the material capable of receiving form and of being made, was called by these names, because in it were contained in confusion, not yet distinguished by their qualities and forms, all those things which, now arranged in their order, are called heaven and earth, the one the spiritual, the other the corporeal, creation."

Having heard and weighed all these things, I will not quarrel over words, for that is useful for nothing except the ruin of those who listen. But the law is good for building up, if a man uses it lawfully, because its end is charity, out of a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith. And our Master knew well on which two commandments He hung the whole Law and the Prophets. So as I confess these things with zeal, O my God, light of my eyes in secret, what harm does it do me, since different things can be understood from these words and yet all of them are true — what harm, I say, does it do me if I think differently from the way someone else thinks the writer thought? All of us who read are indeed trying to track down and grasp what the author we are reading meant; and since we believe he speaks truly, we do not dare suppose that he said anything which we ourselves either know or think to be false. So while each person tries to understand in the Holy Scriptures what the writer understood there, what harm is there if someone understands what You, the light of all truthful minds, show him to be true, even if the author he is reading did not understand this, since he too understood something true, though not this truth?

For it is true, O Lord, that You made heaven and earth. It is also true that the Beginning is Your Wisdom, in which You create all things. It is true again that this visible world has heaven and earth as its great parts, which in brief sum up all the natures that have been made and created. It is true, too, that everything mutable suggests to our understanding a certain formlessness, by which it takes on a form, or is changed and turned. It is true that nothing is subject to times which cleaves so closely to the unchangeable Form that, though it is changeable, it is never changed. It is true that the formlessness which is almost nothing cannot undergo the alternations of times. It is true that the thing from which something is made can, by a certain way of speaking, be called by the name of the thing made from it; and so the formlessness from which heaven and earth were made could be called heaven and earth. It is true that of all things having form, none is nearer to formlessness than the earth and the deep. It is true that You, from whom are all things, made not only everything created and formed, but also whatever is capable of being created and formed. It is true that whatever is formed out of what had no form was formless before it was formed.

From all these truths — which are not doubted by those whose inner eye You have enabled to see such things, and who firmly believe that Your servant Moses spoke in the Spirit of truth — from all of these, then, one person takes one when he says, In the Beginning God made the heaven and the earth; that is, "in His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made the intelligible and the sensible creation, or the spiritual and the corporeal." Another takes another when he says, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth; that is, "in His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made the whole mass of this corporeal world, together with all the evident and familiar natures it contains." Another takes another when he says, In the Beginning God made heaven and earth; that is, "in His Word, coeternal with Himself, God made the formless matter of the spiritual and the corporeal creation." Another takes another when he says, In the Beginning God created heaven and earth; that is, "in His Word, coeternal with Himself, God created the formless matter of the corporeal creation, in which heaven and earth still lay mixed together; and these, now distinguished and formed, we see today in the mass of this world." Another takes another when he says, In the beginning God made heaven and earth; that is, "at the very start of His creating and working, God made formless matter which held heaven and earth within it in a confused state; out of it, once they were formed, they now stand out and appear, with everything that is in them."

And as for understanding the words that follow, out of all those truths one person chooses one for himself when he says, But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep; that is, "that corporeal thing which God made was still a formless matter of corporeal things, without order and without light." Another does so when he says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep; that is, "this whole, which is called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, from which the corporeal heaven and the corporeal earth were to be made, with everything in them that is known to our bodily senses." Another does so when he says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep; that is, "this whole, which is called heaven and earth, was still a formless and dark matter, from which were to be made both that intelligible heaven which elsewhere is called the heaven of heaven, and the earth, meaning the whole corporeal nature, under which name this corporeal heaven is also included; in short, the matter from which every visible and invisible creature was to be created." Another does so when he says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep: "Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth; rather, he says, that formlessness already existed, and it was this that Scripture called the invisible and unformed earth and the darkness upon the deep; and of this it had said before that God made heaven and earth from it, meaning the spiritual and the corporeal creation." Another does so when he says, The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was upon the deep; that is, "there was already a certain formless matter, from which, as Scripture said before, God made heaven and earth, meaning the whole corporeal mass of the world, divided into two great parts, upper and lower, with all the common and familiar creatures that are in them."

For suppose someone tries to argue against these last two opinions in this way: "If you will not grant that this formlessness of matter appears to be called by the name of heaven and earth, then there was something God had not made, out of which He was to make heaven and earth. For Scripture has not told us that God made this matter, unless we take it to be signified by the name of heaven and earth, or of earth alone, when it says, In the beginning God made heaven and earth. In that way, in the words that follow, and the earth was invisible and unformed (even though it pleased Him to call the formless matter by that name), we are to understand no other matter than the one God made, of which it is written above, God made heaven and earth." Those who hold either of these two last opinions will hear this and answer: "We do not deny that this formless matter was indeed created by God, that God from whom are all things, very good. For just as we say that what is created and formed is a greater good, so we admit that what is made capable of being created and formed is a lesser good, but still a good. We do say, however, that Scripture has not recorded that God made this formlessness, just as it has not recorded many other things, such as the Cherubim and the Seraphim, and those which the Apostle names distinctly: Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers. Yet it is perfectly plain that God made all of these. Or if everything is included in the words He made heaven and earth, what shall we say about the waters over which the Spirit of God moved? For if they are included in the word earth, how can formless matter be meant by the name earth, when we see the waters so beautiful? Or if it is taken that way, why is it written that out of the same formlessness the firmament was made and called heaven, while it is not written that the waters were made? For the waters do not remain formless and invisible, since we see them flowing in so lovely a form. But if they received that beauty when God said, Let the waters under the firmament be gathered together, so that the gathering together was itself their forming, what will be said about the waters that are above the firmament? For if they had been formless they would not have deserved so honorable a place, and it is not written by what word they were formed. So if Genesis is silent about God's making something which, all the same, neither sound faith nor well-grounded understanding doubts that God made; and if, again, no sober teaching will dare to say that these waters are coeternal with God on the ground that we hear them mentioned in the book of Genesis but do not find when they were created — why should we not also understand, since truth teaches us so, that the formless matter which this Scripture calls the invisible and unformed earth and the dark deep was created by God out of nothing, and therefore is not coeternal with Him, even though this narrative has left out saying when it was created?"

Having heard and examined these things, as far as my weak capacity allows (which I confess to You, O Lord, who know it), I see that two kinds of disagreement can arise when truthful messengers report something in words: one concerns the truth of the things, the other concerns the meaning of the one who reports them. For we ask in one way what is true about the making of the creation, and in another way what Moses, that excellent minister of Your faith, wanted his reader and hearer to understand by those words. As for the first kind, let all those depart from me who imagine that they know as true what is false; and as for the second, let all those depart from me too who imagine that Moses wrote things that are false. But let me be united in You, O Lord, with those who feed on Your truth in the breadth of love, and let me delight in You with them; and let us approach the words of Your book together, and seek in them Your meaning through the meaning of Your servant, by whose pen You have dispensed them.

But which of us, among the many truths that meet those who search in those words as they are understood in different ways, can so find that one meaning as to say, "This is what Moses thought," and "This is what he wanted understood in that narrative," with the same confidence with which he would say, "This is true," whether Moses thought this or something else? For look, O my God: I, Your servant, who in this book have vowed to You a sacrifice of confession, and who pray that by Your mercy I may pay my vows to You — can I, with the same confidence with which I affirm that in Your unchangeable Word You created all things visible and invisible, also affirm that Moses meant nothing other than this when he wrote, In the beginning God made heaven and earth? No. For I do not see in his mind that he was thinking of this when he wrote these things, as I see it to be certain in Your truth. He might have been thinking of the very start of God's creating when he said In the beginning; and by heaven and earth in this place he might have meant no nature already formed and perfected, whether spiritual or corporeal, but both of them only begun and still formless. For I see that whichever of the two had been said, it could have been said truly; but which of the two he had in mind in these words, I do not see in the same way. And yet, whether it was one of these, or some other sense I have not mentioned here, that so great a man saw in his mind when he uttered these words, I have no doubt that he saw it truly and expressed it fittingly.

So let no one trouble me any more by saying, Moses did not think what you say, but what I say. For if he asked me, "How do you know that Moses thought what you draw out of his words?" I ought to take it calmly, and I would answer perhaps as I answered above, or at somewhat greater length if he were stubborn. But when he says, "Moses did not mean what you say, but what I say," and yet does not deny that what each of us says may both be true, then, O my God, life of the poor, in whose bosom there is no contradiction, rain a softening dew into my heart, so that I may bear patiently with those who say this to me. They say it not because they are divinely inspired and have seen what they say in the heart of Your servant, but because they are proud. They do not know Moses' opinion; they love their own, not because it is true but because it is theirs. Otherwise they would love another true opinion just as much, as I love what they say when they say what is true — not because it is theirs but because it is true, and for that very reason it is no longer theirs, since it is true. But if they love it because it is true, then it is both theirs and mine, since it is common property of all lovers of truth. But their insistence that Moses did not mean what I say but what they say — this I do not like, I do not love. For even if it were so, that rashness of theirs comes not from knowledge but from audacity; it was born not of insight but of vanity. And therefore, O Lord, Your judgments are to be feared, since Your truth is neither mine, nor his, nor anyone else's, but belongs to all of us, whom You call openly to share in it, warning us terribly not to treat it as our private possession, lest we be deprived of it. For whoever claims as his own what You set before all to enjoy, and wants to have for himself what belongs to all, is driven from what is common to what is his own — that is, from truth to a lie. For he who speaks a lie speaks of his own.

Listen, O God, best of judges, Truth itself: listen to what I will say to this opponent, listen. For I speak before You, and before my brothers, who use Your law lawfully, to the end of charity. Listen, and see, if it pleases You, what I will say to him. This is the brotherly and peaceful word I give him in reply: "If we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true, where, I ask you, do we see it? Certainly I do not see it in you, nor you in me; we both see it in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our souls." Since, then, we do not quarrel about the very light of the Lord our God, why do we quarrel about the thoughts of our neighbor, which we cannot see in the way the unchangeable Truth is seen? For even if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, "This is what I meant," we would not see it even then; we would believe it. So let us not be puffed up, one against another, beyond what is written. Let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves. Unless we believe that whatever Moses meant in those books, he meant with a view to these two precepts of charity, we shall make God a liar, by holding an opinion of our fellow servant's mind different from what He has taught us. See now how foolish it is, amid such an abundance of most true meanings as can be drawn out of those words, rashly to assert which of them Moses chiefly meant, and by harmful disputes to offend charity itself, for whose sake he said everything, he whose words we are trying to explain.

And yet, O my God, You who lift up my lowliness and are the rest of my labor, who hear my confessions and forgive my sins: since You command me to love my neighbor as myself, I cannot believe that You gave Moses, Your faithful servant, a lesser gift than I would wish and desire You to have given me, had I been born in the time he was, and had You set me in that office, so that through the service of my heart and tongue those books might be dispensed which were to benefit all nations for so long afterward, and throughout the whole world, from such a height of authority, were to overcome the words of all false and proud teachings. For I would certainly have wished, had I then been Moses (for we all come from the same lump, and what is man, except that You are mindful of him?) — I would have wished, then, had I been what he was, and had You charged me with writing the book of Genesis, to be given such a power of expression and such a way of weaving my words that those who cannot yet understand how God creates would not reject what was said as beyond their capacity; and that those who had already reached that understanding would find, not passed over in those few words of Your servant, whatever true opinion they had arrived at by thinking; and that if another person had discovered another by the light of truth, that too would not fail to be found in the same words.

For just as a spring in a small space is more abundant, and supplies its flow to more streams over wider areas than any one of the streams that is drawn from that same spring and carried a long way off, so the account given by Your dispenser, which was to benefit many who would discourse on it, pours out of a small measure of language streams of clear truth, from which each person may draw for himself whatever truth he can on these matters, one this truth, another that, through longer windings of discussion. For some, when they read or hear these words, imagine that God, like a man or like some mass endowed with boundless power, made heaven and earth by some new and sudden decision, outside itself, as if at a distance: two great bodies, above and below, in which all things were to be contained. And when they hear, God said, Let it be made, and it was made, they imagine words that began and ended, sounding in time and passing away, and that after they had passed, the thing that was commanded to come into being came into being; and whatever else of that sort their familiarity with the material world suggests to them. In these, who are still little ones and carnal, while their weakness is carried along by this humble kind of speech as if in a mother's arms, faith is built up in a healthy way, by which they hold as certain that God made all the natures that their eyes see around them in wonderful variety. But if any of them despises these words as too plain, and in proud weakness stretches himself out beyond the nest that shelters him, alas, he will fall miserably. Have pity, O Lord God, so that those who pass along the way do not trample on the unfledged chick, and send Your angel to put it back in the nest, so that it may live until it can fly.

But others, for whom these words are no longer a nest but shady orchards, see the fruit hidden in them, fly about joyfully, and with glad chirping search it out and pluck it. For when they read or hear these words, they see that all times past and to come are surpassed by Your eternal and stable abiding; and yet that there is no creature formed in time which You did not make. They see that by Your will, which is the same as what You are, You made all things, not through any change of will, nor by a will that did not exist before; and that You made these things not out of Yourself, in Your own likeness, which is the form of all things, but out of nothing, a formless unlikeness, which was to be formed by Your likeness (turning back to Your unity according to their appointed capacity, as far as is given to each thing in its kind), so that all things might be made very good, whether they abide close around You, or, removed by degrees in time and place, make or undergo the beautiful changes of the universe. These things they see, and they rejoice in the light of Your truth, in the small measure they can here.

One of them fixes his mind on the words In the beginning God made heaven and earth, and sees in them Wisdom, the Beginning, because It also speaks to us. Another likewise fixes his mind on the same words, and by beginning understands the start of created things, taking In the beginning He made as if it said, At first He made. And among those who understand In the Beginning to mean "In Your Wisdom You created heaven and earth," one believes that the matter from which heaven and earth were to be created is there called heaven and earth; another, natures already formed and distinguished; another, one formed nature, and that a spiritual one, under the name Heaven, and the other, formless corporeal matter, under the name Earth. Those, again, who understand by the names heaven and earth a matter still formless, from which heaven and earth were to be formed, do not all understand it in one way either: one takes it as the matter from which both the intelligible and the sensible creation were to be completed; another, only the matter from which this sensible corporeal mass was to be made, holding in its vast bosom these visible and familiar natures. Nor do those who believe that creatures already ordered and arranged are called heaven and earth in this place understand it in the same way: one takes it as both the invisible and the visible, the other as the visible only, in which we see this bright heaven and dark earth, with the things they contain.

But the one who understands In the beginning He made only as if it said At first He made has no way of truly understanding heaven and earth except as the matter of heaven and earth, that is, of the whole creation, intelligible and corporeal. For if he wants to understand by it the universe as already formed, he could rightly be asked, "If God made this first, what did He make afterward?" After the universe he will find nothing, and so, against his will, he will have to hear another question: "How did God make this first, if nothing came after?" But when he says that God made matter first formless and then formed, there is nothing absurd in that, provided he is able to distinguish what comes before by eternity, what by time, what by choice, and what by origin. By eternity, as God is before all things; by time, as the flower is before the fruit; by choice, as the fruit is before the flower; by origin, as the sound is before the tune. Of these four, the first and the last I have mentioned are understood with the greatest difficulty, the two in the middle very easily. For it is a rare and exceedingly lofty vision to behold Your eternity, O Lord, unchangeably making changeable things, and in that way being before them. And again, who has so sharp an understanding as to be able to discern without great effort how the sound is before the tune? It is so because a tune is formed sound; and something unformed can certainly exist, but what does not exist cannot be formed. In this way the matter is before the thing made from it: not before because it makes it, since it is rather itself made; nor before by an interval of time. For we do not first, at an earlier time, utter formless sounds without singing, and then later fit or fashion them into the form of a tune, as is done with wood, from which a chest is made, or silver, from which a vessel is fashioned. Such materials do precede in time as well the forms of the things made from them; but with singing it is not so. For when a tune is sung, its sound is heard; there is not first a formless sound which is afterward formed into a tune. For each sound passes away as soon as it is made, and you could find nothing of it to call back and put together by art. So the tune has its being in its sound, and that sound is its matter. This sound is formed so that it may be a tune; and therefore, as I said, the matter of the sound is before the form of the tune. It is not before through any power of making it a tune, for a sound is in no way the craftsman of the tune; rather, it is something bodily, placed under the soul that sings, for it to make a tune from. Nor is it first in time, for it is given out together with the tune. Nor is it first by choice, for a sound is not better than a tune, since a tune is not only a sound but a beautiful sound. But it is first in origin, because a tune does not receive form in order to become a sound; a sound receives form in order to become a tune. By this example, let whoever can understand how the matter of things was made first and was called heaven and earth, because heaven and earth were made from it. Yet it was not made first in time, because it is the forms of things that give rise to time; but that matter was without form, and now it is perceived in time together with its form. And yet nothing can be said about that matter except as if it were prior in time, whereas in value it ranks last (because formed things are better than formless ones), and it is preceded by the eternity of the Creator, so that there might be, out of nothing, something from which something could be made.

In this diversity of true opinions, let Truth itself bring forth concord. And may our God have mercy on us, so that we may use the law lawfully, for the end of the commandment, pure charity. And so, if anyone asks me, "Which of these was the meaning of Your servant Moses?" these would not be the words of my Confessions if I did not confess to You, "I do not know." And yet I know that those meanings are true, except the carnal ones, about which I have said what seemed necessary. And even those little ones of good hope who think that way have this benefit: the words of Your Book do not frighten them, since they convey lofty things humbly, and a rich meaning in few words. And all of us who, I confess, see and speak the truth conveyed in those words, let us love one another, and together love You, our God, the fountain of truth, if it is truth we thirst for and not vanities. Yes, let us so honor this servant of Yours, the dispenser of this Scripture, full of Your Spirit, as to believe that when he wrote these things by Your revelation, he intended the meaning among them that most excels both in the light of truth and in fruitfulness of profit.

So when one person says, "Moses meant what I mean," and another, "No, he meant what I mean," I think it more reverent to say, "Why not rather both, if both are true?" And if there is a third meaning, or a fourth, and indeed if anyone sees any other truth in those words, why should he not be believed to have seen all of them, he through whom the one God tempered the holy Scriptures to the understanding of many, who were to see in them things true but different? For my part — and I say this fearlessly, from my heart — if I were writing anything meant to carry supreme authority, I would rather write in such a way that whatever truth anyone could grasp on these matters would be conveyed in my words, than set down my own meaning so plainly as to exclude the rest, which, not being false, could not offend me. So I will not be so rash, O my God, as to refuse to believe that You granted as much to that great man. Without doubt, when he wrote those words, he perceived and thought of whatever truth we have been able to find in them, and whatever we have not been able to find, and cannot yet find, but which can still be found in them.

Finally, O Lord, You who are God and not flesh and blood: even if a man saw less, could anything be hidden from Your good Spirit, who will lead me into the land of uprightness, anything that You Yourself were going to reveal through those words to readers in times to come, even though the man through whom they were spoken perhaps had in mind only one among many true meanings? If that is so, then let the meaning he had in mind be the highest of all. But to us, O Lord, reveal either that same meaning or any other true one that pleases You, so that whether You disclose to us the same thing You disclosed to that servant of Yours, or something else on the occasion of those words, it may still be You who feed us, and not error that deceives us. See, O Lord my God, how much we have written about a few words, how much, I beg You! What strength of ours, what ages, would be enough for all Your books at this rate? Allow me, then, to confess to You more briefly in them, and to choose some one true, certain and good meaning that You inspire in me, even if many should occur to me, where many can occur. Let this be the rule of my confession: if I say what Your minister intended, that is right and best, for that is what I ought to strive for; and if I do not attain it, I shall still say what Your Truth willed to tell me through his words, the Truth which also told him what It willed.

chapters.title: Book 13
paragraphs: I call upon You, O my God, my mercy, who made me and did not forget me when I had forgotten You. I call You into my soul, which You are preparing to receive You through the longing that You Yourself breathed into it. Do not abandon me now that I call upon You, for You came to meet me before I ever called, and pressed on me with many repeated calls of every kind, so that I would hear You from far off, and be turned back, and call upon You who were calling me. For You, Lord, blotted out all my evil deserts, so as not to repay my hands, with which I fell away from You; and You went ahead of all my good deserts, so as to repay the work of Your own hands, with which You made me. For before I existed, You were; nor was I anything to which You could grant existence; and yet, see, I exist, out of Your goodness, which went before all that You have made me to be and all that You have made me from. For You had no need of me, nor am I any such good as could be of help to You, my Lord and my God. I do not serve You as though You might grow tired in working, or as though Your power would be less if it lacked my service. Nor do I cultivate You, as one cultivates land, as though You would lie uncultivated unless I cultivated You. Rather, I serve You and worship You so that I may receive well-being from You, from whom it comes that I have a being capable of well-being.

For it is out of the fullness of Your goodness that Your creation stands in being, so that a good which could in no way profit You, and which was not of Your own being (for then it would have been equal to You), might still exist, since it could be made by You. For what did heaven and earth, which You made in the Beginning, deserve from You? Let those spiritual and corporeal natures which You made in Your Wisdom tell how they deserved from You to depend on it, even in their inchoate and formless state, each in its own kind, whether spiritual or corporeal, drifting toward boundless excess and a far-off unlikeness to You. (The spiritual, even without form, was higher than the corporeal even with form; and the corporeal, even without form, was better than if it had been nothing at all.)
